In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him)

Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him) is Meccan, according to unanimous agreement. It was revealed before the conversion of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Umar went out with a sword slung on him. It was said to him: "Your brother-in-law [and your sister [from B, J, Z, T, K]] have turned away [sabaw (sabā al-rajul: he left one religion for another)]." So Umar came to them, and with them was a man from the Muhajirun called Khabbab, and they were reading: "Ta-Ha." He said: "Give me the book you have, so that I may read it." Umar used to read books. His sister said to him: "You are impure, and none touches it except the purified. So get up and perform ghusl, or wudu." Umar stood up, performed wudu, took the book and read: "Ta-Ha."

Ibn Ishaq mentioned it at length: Umar went out with his sword girded, intending to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kill him. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah met him and said: "Where are you going, O Umar?" He said: "I am going to Muhammad, this Sabian who has divided the affair of Quraysh, belittled their minds, reviled their religion, and cursed their gods; I will kill him." Nu'aym said to him: "By Allah, your own self has deluded you, O Umar. Do you think the Banu Abd Manaf will leave you walking on the earth after you have killed Muhammad? Will you not return to your family and set their affairs right?" He said: "Which family of mine?" He said: "Your brother-in-law and paternal cousin Sa'id ibn Zayd, and your sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab. By Allah, they have both embraced Islam and followed Muhammad in his religion, so go to them." Umar returned intending to go to his sister and brother-in-law, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Arat, who had a sheet on which was "Ta-Ha," teaching it to them. When they heard Umar's sound, Khabbab hid in a small room of theirs or in part of the house, and Fatimah bint al-Khattab took the sheet and put it under her thigh. Umar had heard the recitation of Khabbab to them as he approached the house. When he entered he said: "What is this murmuring [al-haynamah: low speech that cannot be understood] that I heard?" They said to him: "You heard nothing." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, I have been informed that you both have followed Muhammad in his religion." He attacked his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd, so his sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab stood up to restrain him from her husband, and he struck her and wounded her. When he did that, his sister and brother-in-law said to him: "Yes, we have embraced Islam and believed in Allah and His Messenger, so do what you wish." When Umar saw the blood on his sister, he regretted what he had done, and he relented and said to his sister: "Give me this sheet which I heard you reading just now, so I can see what this is that Muhammad has brought." He was a scribe. When he said that, his sister said to him: "We fear for it on your account." He said to her: "Do not fear," and swore to her by his gods that he would return it once he had read it. When he said that, she hoped for his Islam, and said to him: "O my brother, you are impure in your polytheism, and none touches it except the pure." So Umar stood up and performed ghusl, and she gave him the sheet, in which was "Ta-Ha." When he read a portion of it, he said: "How excellent this speech is, and how noble!" When Khabbab heard that, he came out to him and said: "O Umar, by Allah, I hope that Allah has singled you out with the supplication of His Prophet, for I heard him yesterday saying: (O Allah, strengthen Islam with Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or with Umar ibn al-Khattab)." So, fear Allah, O Umar. He said to him at that: "Guide me, O Khabbab, to Muhammad so that I may go to him and embrace Islam," and he mentioned the hadith.

Issue: Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad narrated in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down, blessed are the bodies that carry this, and blessed are the tongues that speak this.'" Ibn Furak said the meaning of his saying: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin," i.e., He made His speech manifest, audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He willed among the angels at that time. The Arabs say: "I read the thing" when they followed it, and they say: "This she-camel never gave birth in her womb" meaning no offspring appeared in her. On this basis the statement is valid, and its recitation is its making them hear and comprehend through expressions He creates and writing He produces. This is the meaning of our saying "we recited the speech of Allah," and the meaning of His saying: "Recite what is easy of the Qur'an" ("recite what is easy of it") [see vol. 19 p. 50 onward]. Some of our companions said the meaning of His saying "recited" is "spoke it," and this is metaphorical, like their saying "I tasted this statement" (dhuqtu hadha al-qawl dhawaqan) meaning "I tested it." From it is the saying of the Exalted: "So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing" [see vol. 10 p. 193 onward], i.e., Allah tested them with it, and that was called tasting, though fear is not tasted in the literal sense, because tasting in reality is with the mouth and not other limbs. Ibn Furak said: What we said first is more correct in interpreting this report, because the speech of Allah, the Exalted, is eternal, pre-existent, preceding all created things; He only makes audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He wills, according to what He wills, in times and periods, not that the very essence of His speech is tied in its existence to a duration and time.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Ha. (1) We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed. (2) But as a reminder to whoever fears. (3) A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens. (4) The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne. (5) To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil. (6) And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden. (7) Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names. (8)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. The scholars differed about its meaning. Al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is among the secrets. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it from Ibn Abbas; its meaning is "O man." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. It was also said: it is a well-known dialect among the tribe of Ukl. It was said also of Akk. Al-Kalbi said: If you say to a man in Akk "O man," he will not respond until you say "Ta-Ha." Al-Tabari recited in this regard, saying:

"I called 'Ta-Ha' in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be a fugitive [wa'il: seeking deliverance]."

It is also narrated as "muzayilan." Abd Allah ibn Umar said: "O my beloved" in the dialect of Akk, mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Qutrub said: it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited for Yazid ibn al-Muhalhal:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your traits; may Allah not bless the cursed people."

Likewise al-Hasan said: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "O man." Ikrimah also said it. He said it is in Syriac likewise, mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Mawardi related it from Ibn Abbas as well and Mujahid. Al-Tabari related that in Nabataean it means "O man." This is the view of al-Suddi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and also Ibn Abbas. He said:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your characteristics; may Allah not sanctify the souls of the cursed."

Ikrimah also said: it is like your saying "O man" in the language of Abyssinia, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The correct view is that although it is found in another language, it is from the language of the Arabs as we have mentioned, and that it is a Yemeni dialect among Akk, Tayy and Ukl also. It was also said: it is one of the names of Allah, and an oath which He swore by. This too is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It was also said: it is a name of the Prophet (ﷺ), which Allah named him by, just as He named him Muhammad. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have ten names with my Lord," and he mentioned that among them are Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin. It was also said: it is the name of the surah and its key. It was also said: it is an abbreviation from the speech of Allah, which Allah singled out His Messenger with knowledge of. It was also said: they are disjointed letters, each letter of which indicates a meaning, and this was disputed. It was said: the Ta is the tree of Tuba and the Ha is the Hawiyah fire; the Arabs express the whole by a part, as if He swore by Paradise and Hell. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Ta is the opening of His name Tahir and Tayyib, and the Ha is the opening of His name Hadi. It was said: "Ta" means "O one who hopes for intercession for the community," "Ha" means "O guide of creation to Allah." It was said: the Ta is from purity and the Ha is from guidance, as if He says to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "O one purified from sins, O guide of creation to the Knower of the unseen." It was said: the Ta is the drums of the warriors and the Ha is their awe in the hearts of the disbelievers. Its clarification is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [see vol. 4 p. 232 onward] and His saying: "And He cast terror into their hearts" [see vol. 18 p. 3 onward]. It was said: the Ta is the joy of the people of Paradise in Paradise, and the Ha is the grief of the people of the Fire in the Fire. A sixth view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "Tuba li-man ihtada" (blessed is whoever is guided), said by Mujahid and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah. A seventh view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "ta' al-ard" (tread the earth), because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bear the hardship of prayer until his feet nearly swelled and he needed to rest between his feet, so it was said to him: "tread the earth," i.e., do not exert yourself until you need rest; related by Ibn al-Anbari. Qadi Iyad mentioned in al-Shifa that al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other, so Allah revealed: "Ta-Ha," meaning, "Tread the earth, O Muhammad."

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed﴾ [20:2]. Al-Zamakhshari: It is also narrated from al-Hasan that "Ta-Ha" was explained as an order to tread, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to stand in his tahajjud on one of his feet, so he was commanded to set his feet on the earth together, and that the original is "ta'" whose hamza was changed to ha, just as alif was changed in "yata" according to the one who said:

"...... may the pasture not be pleasant for you"

[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, and the full line is: "They went with the mules of Maslamah in the evening, so pasture, O Fazarah, may the pasture not be pleasant for you." He said this when Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik was removed from Iraq and Umar ibn Hubayrah al-Fazari was appointed over it, so al-Farazdaq satirized them and invoked against his people not to congratulate themselves on the favor of his governorship. By the mules of the postal service he meant those that brought Maslamah at his removal.] (Shawahid Sibawayh).

Then He established this matter upon it, and the hā' is for pausal (sakt) purposes. Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ and his companions used to tie ropes to their chests during the night prayer because of the length of standing, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by the obligatory command, and this verse was revealed. Al-Kalbi said: When revelation came down upon the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, he exerted himself greatly in worship, and his worship intensified; he would pray the whole night for a time, until this verse was revealed, and Allah the Exalted commanded him to lighten the burden on himself, so that he would pray and sleep. Thus this verse abrogated the qiyam of the night, and after this verse he would pray and sleep. Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: When the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he and his companions stood and prayed. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah has not sent down this Qur'an upon Muhammad except that he may be wretched." So Allah the Exalted revealed "Ta Ha," saying: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2), meaning: to make you toil, as will come. According to this view, "Ta Ha" means "tā" as in "trample" (ṭa'), so the hā' and alif are a pronoun referring to the earth, meaning: trample the earth with your feet in your prayers; the hamza was lightened and became a silent alif. A group read "Ta Ha" with its origin being ṭa' meaning ṭi (trample), so the hamza was dropped and the hā' of pausal was added. Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: A man recited to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2). Abdullah said to him: "Ṭih." The man said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, is it not that he was commanded to trample the earth with his feet or his two feet?" He said: "Ṭih, thus did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it to me." Abu Amr and Abu Ishaq inclined the hā' and made the ṭā' open. Abu Bakr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read between the two pronunciations, and Abu Ubayd chose this. The rest read with emphasis (tafkhim). Al-Tha'labi said: All of these are correct and eloquent dialects. Al-Nahhas said: According to most Arabic grammarians there is no basis for imala (inclination), for two reasons: first, there is no yā' or kasra here that would call for imala; and second, the ṭā' is among the letters that prevent imala. These are two clear reasons.

His saying, Exalted is He: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:2). It was read: "The Qur'an was not sent down upon you to make you wretched." Al-Nahhas said: Some grammarians say this is the lam of negation, and some say it is the lam of denial (juhud). Abu Ja'far said: I heard Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lam of jarr (preposition), and the meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you for wretchedness." Al-shaqa' (wretchedness) may be pronounced with a long or short vowel, and it is from the roots with waw. The original linguistic meaning of shaqa' is hardship and fatigue, i.e., "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should toil." The poet said:

The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect,
while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.

So the meaning of "li-tashqa" is "that you should toil," from your excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your distress that they should believe, like His saying, Exalted is He: "Perhaps you would destroy yourself over their traces" (18:6), meaning: your only duty is to convey and remind, and it was not prescribed upon you that they must believe, after you have not fallen short in delivering the message and good admonition. It is narrated that Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are wretched because you have abandoned the religion of your fathers." So it was intended to refute this by stating that the religion of Islam and this Qur'an are the ladder to attaining every success, and the means of reaching every happiness, while what the disbelievers are in is wretchedness itself. According to the previous views, the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, prayed at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril said to him: "Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you." Meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you so that you would exhaust yourself in worship and make it suffer grave hardship; you were sent only with the easy, tolerant monotheistic way (hanifiyyah samhah).

His saying, Exalted is He: "As a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3). Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: It is a substitute (badal) for "tashqa", meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder. Al-Nahhas said: This is a distant interpretation, and Abu Ali rejected it, because a reminder is not wretchedness. Rather, it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be wretched through it; We sent it down only as a reminder. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it; its sense is: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you except as a reminder for whoever fears, and so that you would not be wretched.

(Tanzilan) is a verbal noun: We sent it down as a sending down. It was also said to be a substitute for His saying "a reminder." Abu Haywah al-Shami read "tanzilun" in the nominative, meaning: this is a sending down.

(From He who created the earth and the high heavens) — i.e., the lofty, exalted ones, being the plural of "al-'ulya," like "kubra" and "sughra," and "kabura" and "saghura." He informed of His greatness, majesty and sublimity, then said: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5). The accusative is permissible as praise. Abu Ishaq said: The genitive is by way of substitution. Sa'id ibn Mas'adah said: The nominative is in the sense of "He is the Merciful." Al-Nahhas said: The nominative is permissible as the subject with a predicate, "to Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," so one does not stop at "istawa"; and as a substitute for the pronoun in "khalaqa," in which case one may stop at "istawa." Likewise if it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and one does not stop at "al-'ulya." The discussion of the meaning of istiwa' has already preceded in "al-A'raf". What Shaykh Abu al-Hasan and others adopted is that He is established upon His Throne without limit and without modality, as the establishment of created beings is. Ibn Abbas said: He means He created what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection and after the Resurrection. "To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth and what is between them and what is beneath the soil" (20:6): he means what is beneath the rock, of which no one knows what lies beneath except Allah the Exalted. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He means the seventh earth. Ibn Abbas [this report and similar ones were narrated from Ibn Abbas by non-trustworthy transmitters, and scholars have spoken against this report and its like]: The earth is upon a nun (fish), the nun is upon the sea, and the two ends of the nun, its head and tail, meet beneath the Throne; the sea is upon a green rock, whose greenness is the color of the sky, and it is the one of which Allah the Exalted said: "It would be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth" (31:16); the rock is upon the horn of a bull, and the bull is upon the soil, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah the Exalted. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: On the surface of the earth are seven seas, and the earths are seven, with a sea between every two earths; the lowest sea encloses the rim of Hell, and were it not for its vastness, abundance of water and coldness, Hell would burn everyone upon it. He said: Hell is upon the back of the wind, and the back of the wind is upon a veil of darkness whose thickness none knows except Allah the Exalted; and that veil is upon the soil, and to the soil the knowledge of creation ends.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden" (20:7). Ibn Abbas said: The secret is what a person tells another privately, and more hidden than that is what he conceals in himself which he has not told anyone. It is also narrated from him: The secret is the discourse of your soul, and more hidden than the secret is what you will yet say to yourself of what has not yet occurred but will occur; you know what you conceal today but do not know what you will conceal tomorrow, while Allah knows what you concealed today and what you will conceal tomorrow. The meaning: Allah knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret. Ibn Abbas also said: "The secret" is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and "what is more hidden" is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself will do and does not know; so Allah the Exalted knows all of that, and His knowledge of what has passed and what is to come is one knowledge, and all creation in His knowledge is like a single soul. Qatadah and others said: "The secret" is what a person conceals in himself, and "what is more hidden" is what has not yet occurred and no one has concealed. Ibn Zayd said: "The secret" is the secret of creation, and "what is more hidden" is His own secret, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Tabari rejected this and said: What is more hidden is what is not in a person's secret but will be in his soul, as Ibn Abbas said.

(Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names) (20:8). "Allah" is nominative by way of beginning (mubtada'), or by implying an omitted subject, or as a substitute for the pronoun in "ya'lamu." He declared His own oneness, glory be to Him, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the polytheists to worship Allah alone, with no partner, and this was grievous to them. When Abu Jahl heard him mention "the Merciful," he said to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "Muhammad forbids us to call upon another god with Allah, yet he calls upon Allah and the Merciful." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5), and revealed: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names" (17:110). He is one, and His names are many. Then He said: "Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names" (20:8). These have already been noted in Surat al-A'raf.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him)

Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him) is Meccan, according to unanimous agreement. It was revealed before the conversion of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Umar went out with a sword slung on him. It was said to him: "Your brother-in-law [and your sister [from B, J, Z, T, K]] have turned away [sabaw (sabā al-rajul: he left one religion for another)]." So Umar came to them, and with them was a man from the Muhajirun called Khabbab, and they were reading: "Ta-Ha." He said: "Give me the book you have, so that I may read it." Umar used to read books. His sister said to him: "You are impure, and none touches it except the purified. So get up and perform ghusl, or wudu." Umar stood up, performed wudu, took the book and read: "Ta-Ha."

Ibn Ishaq mentioned it at length: Umar went out with his sword girded, intending to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kill him. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah met him and said: "Where are you going, O Umar?" He said: "I am going to Muhammad, this Sabian who has divided the affair of Quraysh, belittled their minds, reviled their religion, and cursed their gods; I will kill him." Nu'aym said to him: "By Allah, your own self has deluded you, O Umar. Do you think the Banu Abd Manaf will leave you walking on the earth after you have killed Muhammad? Will you not return to your family and set their affairs right?" He said: "Which family of mine?" He said: "Your brother-in-law and paternal cousin Sa'id ibn Zayd, and your sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab. By Allah, they have both embraced Islam and followed Muhammad in his religion, so go to them." Umar returned intending to go to his sister and brother-in-law, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Arat, who had a sheet on which was "Ta-Ha," teaching it to them. When they heard Umar's sound, Khabbab hid in a small room of theirs or in part of the house, and Fatimah bint al-Khattab took the sheet and put it under her thigh. Umar had heard the recitation of Khabbab to them as he approached the house. When he entered he said: "What is this murmuring [al-haynamah: low speech that cannot be understood] that I heard?" They said to him: "You heard nothing." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, I have been informed that you both have followed Muhammad in his religion." He attacked his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd, so his sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab stood up to restrain him from her husband, and he struck her and wounded her. When he did that, his sister and brother-in-law said to him: "Yes, we have embraced Islam and believed in Allah and His Messenger, so do what you wish." When Umar saw the blood on his sister, he regretted what he had done, and he relented and said to his sister: "Give me this sheet which I heard you reading just now, so I can see what this is that Muhammad has brought." He was a scribe. When he said that, his sister said to him: "We fear for it on your account." He said to her: "Do not fear," and swore to her by his gods that he would return it once he had read it. When he said that, she hoped for his Islam, and said to him: "O my brother, you are impure in your polytheism, and none touches it except the pure." So Umar stood up and performed ghusl, and she gave him the sheet, in which was "Ta-Ha." When he read a portion of it, he said: "How excellent this speech is, and how noble!" When Khabbab heard that, he came out to him and said: "O Umar, by Allah, I hope that Allah has singled you out with the supplication of His Prophet, for I heard him yesterday saying: (O Allah, strengthen Islam with Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or with Umar ibn al-Khattab)." So, fear Allah, O Umar. He said to him at that: "Guide me, O Khabbab, to Muhammad so that I may go to him and embrace Islam," and he mentioned the hadith.

Issue: Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad narrated in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down, blessed are the bodies that carry this, and blessed are the tongues that speak this.'" Ibn Furak said the meaning of his saying: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin," i.e., He made His speech manifest, audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He willed among the angels at that time. The Arabs say: "I read the thing" when they followed it, and they say: "This she-camel never gave birth in her womb" meaning no offspring appeared in her. On this basis the statement is valid, and its recitation is its making them hear and comprehend through expressions He creates and writing He produces. This is the meaning of our saying "we recited the speech of Allah," and the meaning of His saying: "Recite what is easy of the Qur'an" ("recite what is easy of it") [see vol. 19 p. 50 onward]. Some of our companions said the meaning of His saying "recited" is "spoke it," and this is metaphorical, like their saying "I tasted this statement" (dhuqtu hadha al-qawl dhawaqan) meaning "I tested it." From it is the saying of the Exalted: "So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing" [see vol. 10 p. 193 onward], i.e., Allah tested them with it, and that was called tasting, though fear is not tasted in the literal sense, because tasting in reality is with the mouth and not other limbs. Ibn Furak said: What we said first is more correct in interpreting this report, because the speech of Allah, the Exalted, is eternal, pre-existent, preceding all created things; He only makes audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He wills, according to what He wills, in times and periods, not that the very essence of His speech is tied in its existence to a duration and time.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Ha. (1) We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed. (2) But as a reminder to whoever fears. (3) A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens. (4) The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne. (5) To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil. (6) And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden. (7) Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names. (8)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. The scholars differed about its meaning. Al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is among the secrets. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it from Ibn Abbas; its meaning is "O man." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. It was also said: it is a well-known dialect among the tribe of Ukl. It was said also of Akk. Al-Kalbi said: If you say to a man in Akk "O man," he will not respond until you say "Ta-Ha." Al-Tabari recited in this regard, saying:

"I called 'Ta-Ha' in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be a fugitive [wa'il: seeking deliverance]."

It is also narrated as "muzayilan." Abd Allah ibn Umar said: "O my beloved" in the dialect of Akk, mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Qutrub said: it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited for Yazid ibn al-Muhalhal:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your traits; may Allah not bless the cursed people."

Likewise al-Hasan said: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "O man." Ikrimah also said it. He said it is in Syriac likewise, mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Mawardi related it from Ibn Abbas as well and Mujahid. Al-Tabari related that in Nabataean it means "O man." This is the view of al-Suddi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and also Ibn Abbas. He said:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your characteristics; may Allah not sanctify the souls of the cursed."

Ikrimah also said: it is like your saying "O man" in the language of Abyssinia, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The correct view is that although it is found in another language, it is from the language of the Arabs as we have mentioned, and that it is a Yemeni dialect among Akk, Tayy and Ukl also. It was also said: it is one of the names of Allah, and an oath which He swore by. This too is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It was also said: it is a name of the Prophet (ﷺ), which Allah named him by, just as He named him Muhammad. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have ten names with my Lord," and he mentioned that among them are Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin. It was also said: it is the name of the surah and its key. It was also said: it is an abbreviation from the speech of Allah, which Allah singled out His Messenger with knowledge of. It was also said: they are disjointed letters, each letter of which indicates a meaning, and this was disputed. It was said: the Ta is the tree of Tuba and the Ha is the Hawiyah fire; the Arabs express the whole by a part, as if He swore by Paradise and Hell. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Ta is the opening of His name Tahir and Tayyib, and the Ha is the opening of His name Hadi. It was said: "Ta" means "O one who hopes for intercession for the community," "Ha" means "O guide of creation to Allah." It was said: the Ta is from purity and the Ha is from guidance, as if He says to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "O one purified from sins, O guide of creation to the Knower of the unseen." It was said: the Ta is the drums of the warriors and the Ha is their awe in the hearts of the disbelievers. Its clarification is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [see vol. 4 p. 232 onward] and His saying: "And He cast terror into their hearts" [see vol. 18 p. 3 onward]. It was said: the Ta is the joy of the people of Paradise in Paradise, and the Ha is the grief of the people of the Fire in the Fire. A sixth view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "Tuba li-man ihtada" (blessed is whoever is guided), said by Mujahid and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah. A seventh view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "ta' al-ard" (tread the earth), because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bear the hardship of prayer until his feet nearly swelled and he needed to rest between his feet, so it was said to him: "tread the earth," i.e., do not exert yourself until you need rest; related by Ibn al-Anbari. Qadi Iyad mentioned in al-Shifa that al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other, so Allah revealed: "Ta-Ha," meaning, "Tread the earth, O Muhammad."

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed﴾ [20:2]. Al-Zamakhshari: It is also narrated from al-Hasan that "Ta-Ha" was explained as an order to tread, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to stand in his tahajjud on one of his feet, so he was commanded to set his feet on the earth together, and that the original is "ta'" whose hamza was changed to ha, just as alif was changed in "yata" according to the one who said:

"...... may the pasture not be pleasant for you"

[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, and the full line is: "They went with the mules of Maslamah in the evening, so pasture, O Fazarah, may the pasture not be pleasant for you." He said this when Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik was removed from Iraq and Umar ibn Hubayrah al-Fazari was appointed over it, so al-Farazdaq satirized them and invoked against his people not to congratulate themselves on the favor of his governorship. By the mules of the postal service he meant those that brought Maslamah at his removal.] (Shawahid Sibawayh).

Then He established this matter upon it, and the hā' is for pausal (sakt) purposes. Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ and his companions used to tie ropes to their chests during the night prayer because of the length of standing, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by the obligatory command, and this verse was revealed. Al-Kalbi said: When revelation came down upon the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, he exerted himself greatly in worship, and his worship intensified; he would pray the whole night for a time, until this verse was revealed, and Allah the Exalted commanded him to lighten the burden on himself, so that he would pray and sleep. Thus this verse abrogated the qiyam of the night, and after this verse he would pray and sleep. Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: When the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he and his companions stood and prayed. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah has not sent down this Qur'an upon Muhammad except that he may be wretched." So Allah the Exalted revealed "Ta Ha," saying: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2), meaning: to make you toil, as will come. According to this view, "Ta Ha" means "tā" as in "trample" (ṭa'), so the hā' and alif are a pronoun referring to the earth, meaning: trample the earth with your feet in your prayers; the hamza was lightened and became a silent alif. A group read "Ta Ha" with its origin being ṭa' meaning ṭi (trample), so the hamza was dropped and the hā' of pausal was added. Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: A man recited to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2). Abdullah said to him: "Ṭih." The man said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, is it not that he was commanded to trample the earth with his feet or his two feet?" He said: "Ṭih, thus did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it to me." Abu Amr and Abu Ishaq inclined the hā' and made the ṭā' open. Abu Bakr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read between the two pronunciations, and Abu Ubayd chose this. The rest read with emphasis (tafkhim). Al-Tha'labi said: All of these are correct and eloquent dialects. Al-Nahhas said: According to most Arabic grammarians there is no basis for imala (inclination), for two reasons: first, there is no yā' or kasra here that would call for imala; and second, the ṭā' is among the letters that prevent imala. These are two clear reasons.

His saying, Exalted is He: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:2). It was read: "The Qur'an was not sent down upon you to make you wretched." Al-Nahhas said: Some grammarians say this is the lam of negation, and some say it is the lam of denial (juhud). Abu Ja'far said: I heard Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lam of jarr (preposition), and the meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you for wretchedness." Al-shaqa' (wretchedness) may be pronounced with a long or short vowel, and it is from the roots with waw. The original linguistic meaning of shaqa' is hardship and fatigue, i.e., "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should toil." The poet said:

The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect,
while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.

So the meaning of "li-tashqa" is "that you should toil," from your excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your distress that they should believe, like His saying, Exalted is He: "Perhaps you would destroy yourself over their traces" (18:6), meaning: your only duty is to convey and remind, and it was not prescribed upon you that they must believe, after you have not fallen short in delivering the message and good admonition. It is narrated that Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are wretched because you have abandoned the religion of your fathers." So it was intended to refute this by stating that the religion of Islam and this Qur'an are the ladder to attaining every success, and the means of reaching every happiness, while what the disbelievers are in is wretchedness itself. According to the previous views, the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, prayed at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril said to him: "Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you." Meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you so that you would exhaust yourself in worship and make it suffer grave hardship; you were sent only with the easy, tolerant monotheistic way (hanifiyyah samhah).

His saying, Exalted is He: "As a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3). Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: It is a substitute (badal) for "tashqa", meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder. Al-Nahhas said: This is a distant interpretation, and Abu Ali rejected it, because a reminder is not wretchedness. Rather, it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be wretched through it; We sent it down only as a reminder. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it; its sense is: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you except as a reminder for whoever fears, and so that you would not be wretched.

(Tanzilan) is a verbal noun: We sent it down as a sending down. It was also said to be a substitute for His saying "a reminder." Abu Haywah al-Shami read "tanzilun" in the nominative, meaning: this is a sending down.

(From He who created the earth and the high heavens) — i.e., the lofty, exalted ones, being the plural of "al-'ulya," like "kubra" and "sughra," and "kabura" and "saghura." He informed of His greatness, majesty and sublimity, then said: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5). The accusative is permissible as praise. Abu Ishaq said: The genitive is by way of substitution. Sa'id ibn Mas'adah said: The nominative is in the sense of "He is the Merciful." Al-Nahhas said: The nominative is permissible as the subject with a predicate, "to Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," so one does not stop at "istawa"; and as a substitute for the pronoun in "khalaqa," in which case one may stop at "istawa." Likewise if it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and one does not stop at "al-'ulya." The discussion of the meaning of istiwa' has already preceded in "al-A'raf". What Shaykh Abu al-Hasan and others adopted is that He is established upon His Throne without limit and without modality, as the establishment of created beings is. Ibn Abbas said: He means He created what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection and after the Resurrection. "To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth and what is between them and what is beneath the soil" (20:6): he means what is beneath the rock, of which no one knows what lies beneath except Allah the Exalted. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He means the seventh earth. Ibn Abbas [this report and similar ones were narrated from Ibn Abbas by non-trustworthy transmitters, and scholars have spoken against this report and its like]: The earth is upon a nun (fish), the nun is upon the sea, and the two ends of the nun, its head and tail, meet beneath the Throne; the sea is upon a green rock, whose greenness is the color of the sky, and it is the one of which Allah the Exalted said: "It would be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth" (31:16); the rock is upon the horn of a bull, and the bull is upon the soil, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah the Exalted. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: On the surface of the earth are seven seas, and the earths are seven, with a sea between every two earths; the lowest sea encloses the rim of Hell, and were it not for its vastness, abundance of water and coldness, Hell would burn everyone upon it. He said: Hell is upon the back of the wind, and the back of the wind is upon a veil of darkness whose thickness none knows except Allah the Exalted; and that veil is upon the soil, and to the soil the knowledge of creation ends.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden" (20:7). Ibn Abbas said: The secret is what a person tells another privately, and more hidden than that is what he conceals in himself which he has not told anyone. It is also narrated from him: The secret is the discourse of your soul, and more hidden than the secret is what you will yet say to yourself of what has not yet occurred but will occur; you know what you conceal today but do not know what you will conceal tomorrow, while Allah knows what you concealed today and what you will conceal tomorrow. The meaning: Allah knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret. Ibn Abbas also said: "The secret" is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and "what is more hidden" is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself will do and does not know; so Allah the Exalted knows all of that, and His knowledge of what has passed and what is to come is one knowledge, and all creation in His knowledge is like a single soul. Qatadah and others said: "The secret" is what a person conceals in himself, and "what is more hidden" is what has not yet occurred and no one has concealed. Ibn Zayd said: "The secret" is the secret of creation, and "what is more hidden" is His own secret, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Tabari rejected this and said: What is more hidden is what is not in a person's secret but will be in his soul, as Ibn Abbas said.

(Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names) (20:8). "Allah" is nominative by way of beginning (mubtada'), or by implying an omitted subject, or as a substitute for the pronoun in "ya'lamu." He declared His own oneness, glory be to Him, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the polytheists to worship Allah alone, with no partner, and this was grievous to them. When Abu Jahl heard him mention "the Merciful," he said to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "Muhammad forbids us to call upon another god with Allah, yet he calls upon Allah and the Merciful." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5), and revealed: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names" (17:110). He is one, and His names are many. Then He said: "Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names" (20:8). These have already been noted in Surat al-A'raf.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him)

Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him) is Meccan, according to unanimous agreement. It was revealed before the conversion of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Umar went out with a sword slung on him. It was said to him: "Your brother-in-law [and your sister [from B, J, Z, T, K]] have turned away [sabaw (sabā al-rajul: he left one religion for another)]." So Umar came to them, and with them was a man from the Muhajirun called Khabbab, and they were reading: "Ta-Ha." He said: "Give me the book you have, so that I may read it." Umar used to read books. His sister said to him: "You are impure, and none touches it except the purified. So get up and perform ghusl, or wudu." Umar stood up, performed wudu, took the book and read: "Ta-Ha."

Ibn Ishaq mentioned it at length: Umar went out with his sword girded, intending to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kill him. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah met him and said: "Where are you going, O Umar?" He said: "I am going to Muhammad, this Sabian who has divided the affair of Quraysh, belittled their minds, reviled their religion, and cursed their gods; I will kill him." Nu'aym said to him: "By Allah, your own self has deluded you, O Umar. Do you think the Banu Abd Manaf will leave you walking on the earth after you have killed Muhammad? Will you not return to your family and set their affairs right?" He said: "Which family of mine?" He said: "Your brother-in-law and paternal cousin Sa'id ibn Zayd, and your sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab. By Allah, they have both embraced Islam and followed Muhammad in his religion, so go to them." Umar returned intending to go to his sister and brother-in-law, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Arat, who had a sheet on which was "Ta-Ha," teaching it to them. When they heard Umar's sound, Khabbab hid in a small room of theirs or in part of the house, and Fatimah bint al-Khattab took the sheet and put it under her thigh. Umar had heard the recitation of Khabbab to them as he approached the house. When he entered he said: "What is this murmuring [al-haynamah: low speech that cannot be understood] that I heard?" They said to him: "You heard nothing." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, I have been informed that you both have followed Muhammad in his religion." He attacked his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd, so his sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab stood up to restrain him from her husband, and he struck her and wounded her. When he did that, his sister and brother-in-law said to him: "Yes, we have embraced Islam and believed in Allah and His Messenger, so do what you wish." When Umar saw the blood on his sister, he regretted what he had done, and he relented and said to his sister: "Give me this sheet which I heard you reading just now, so I can see what this is that Muhammad has brought." He was a scribe. When he said that, his sister said to him: "We fear for it on your account." He said to her: "Do not fear," and swore to her by his gods that he would return it once he had read it. When he said that, she hoped for his Islam, and said to him: "O my brother, you are impure in your polytheism, and none touches it except the pure." So Umar stood up and performed ghusl, and she gave him the sheet, in which was "Ta-Ha." When he read a portion of it, he said: "How excellent this speech is, and how noble!" When Khabbab heard that, he came out to him and said: "O Umar, by Allah, I hope that Allah has singled you out with the supplication of His Prophet, for I heard him yesterday saying: (O Allah, strengthen Islam with Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or with Umar ibn al-Khattab)." So, fear Allah, O Umar. He said to him at that: "Guide me, O Khabbab, to Muhammad so that I may go to him and embrace Islam," and he mentioned the hadith.

Issue: Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad narrated in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down, blessed are the bodies that carry this, and blessed are the tongues that speak this.'" Ibn Furak said the meaning of his saying: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin," i.e., He made His speech manifest, audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He willed among the angels at that time. The Arabs say: "I read the thing" when they followed it, and they say: "This she-camel never gave birth in her womb" meaning no offspring appeared in her. On this basis the statement is valid, and its recitation is its making them hear and comprehend through expressions He creates and writing He produces. This is the meaning of our saying "we recited the speech of Allah," and the meaning of His saying: "Recite what is easy of the Qur'an" ("recite what is easy of it") [see vol. 19 p. 50 onward]. Some of our companions said the meaning of His saying "recited" is "spoke it," and this is metaphorical, like their saying "I tasted this statement" (dhuqtu hadha al-qawl dhawaqan) meaning "I tested it." From it is the saying of the Exalted: "So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing" [see vol. 10 p. 193 onward], i.e., Allah tested them with it, and that was called tasting, though fear is not tasted in the literal sense, because tasting in reality is with the mouth and not other limbs. Ibn Furak said: What we said first is more correct in interpreting this report, because the speech of Allah, the Exalted, is eternal, pre-existent, preceding all created things; He only makes audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He wills, according to what He wills, in times and periods, not that the very essence of His speech is tied in its existence to a duration and time.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Ha. (1) We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed. (2) But as a reminder to whoever fears. (3) A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens. (4) The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne. (5) To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil. (6) And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden. (7) Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names. (8)

According to this view, "Ta Ha" means "tā" as in "trample" (ṭa'), so the hā' and alif are a pronoun referring to the earth, meaning: trample the earth with your feet in your prayers; the hamza was lightened and became a silent alif. We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2). Abdullah said to him: "Ṭih." The man said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, is it not that he was commanded to trample the earth with his feet or his two feet?" He said: "Ṭih, thus did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it to me." Abu Amr and Abu Ishaq inclined the hā' and made the ṭā' open. Abu Bakr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read between the two pronunciations, and Abu Ubayd chose this. The rest read with emphasis (tafkhim). Al-Tha'labi said: All of these are correct and eloquent dialects. Al-Nahhas said: According to most Arabic grammarians there is no basis for imala (inclination), for two reasons: first, there is no yā' or kasra here that would call for imala; and second, the ṭā' is among the letters that prevent imala. These are two clear reasons.

His saying, Exalted is He: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:2). It was read: "The Qur'an was not sent down upon you to make you wretched." Al-Nahhas said: Some grammarians say this is the lam of negation, and some say it is the lam of denial (juhud). Abu Ja'far said: I heard Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lam of jarr (preposition), and the meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you for wretchedness." Al-shaqa' (wretchedness) may be pronounced with a long or short vowel, and it is from the roots with waw. The original linguistic meaning of shaqa' is hardship and fatigue, i.e., "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should toil." The poet said:

The man of intellect suffers in comfort because of his intellect,
while the ignorant one in misery enjoys ease.

So the meaning of "li-tashqa" is "that you should toil," from your excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your distress that they should believe, like His saying, Exalted is He: "Perhaps you would destroy yourself over their traces" (18:6), meaning: your only duty is to convey and remind, and it was not prescribed upon you that they must believe, after you have not fallen short in delivering the message and good admonition. It is narrated that Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are wretched because you have abandoned the religion of your fathers." So it was intended to refute this by stating that the religion of Islam and this Qur'an are the ladder to attaining every success, and the means of reaching every happiness, while what the disbelievers are in is wretchedness itself. According to the previous views, the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, prayed at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril said to him: "Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you." Meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you so that you would exhaust yourself in worship and make it suffer grave hardship; you were sent only with the easy, tolerant monotheistic way (hanifiyyah samhah).

His saying, Exalted is He: "As a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3). Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: It is a substitute (badal) for "tashqa", meaning: We did not send it down except as a reminder. Al-Nahhas said: This is a distant interpretation, and Abu Ali rejected it, because a reminder is not wretchedness. Rather, it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: We sent it down so that you would remind by it a reminder; or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be wretched through it; We sent it down only as a reminder. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it; its sense is: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you except as a reminder for whoever fears, and so that you would not be wretched.

(Tanzilan) is a verbal noun: We sent it down as a sending down. It was also said to be a substitute for His saying "a reminder." Abu Haywah al-Shami read "tanzilun" in the nominative, meaning: this is a sending down.

(From He who created the earth and the high heavens) — i.e., the lofty, exalted ones, being the plural of "al-'ulya," like "kubra" and "sughra," and "kabura" and "saghura." He informed of His greatness, majesty and sublimity, then said: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5). The accusative is permissible as praise. Abu Ishaq said: The genitive is by way of substitution. Sa'id ibn Mas'adah said: The nominative is in the sense of "He is the Merciful." Al-Nahhas said: The nominative is permissible as the subject with a predicate, "to Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," so one does not stop at "istawa"; and as a substitute for the pronoun in "khalaqa," in which case one may stop at "istawa." Likewise if it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and one does not stop at "al-'ulya." The discussion of the meaning of istiwa' has already preceded in "al-A'raf". What Shaykh Abu al-Hasan and others adopted is that He is established upon His Throne without limit and without modality, as the establishment of created beings is. Ibn Abbas said: He means He created what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection and after the Resurrection. "To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth and what is between them and what is beneath the soil" (20:6): he means what is beneath the rock, of which no one knows what lies beneath except Allah the Exalted. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He means the seventh earth. Ibn Abbas [this report and similar ones were narrated from Ibn Abbas by non-trustworthy transmitters, and scholars have spoken against this report and its like]: The earth is upon a nun (fish), the nun is upon the sea, and the two ends of the nun, its head and tail, meet beneath the Throne; the sea is upon a green rock, whose greenness is the color of the sky, and it is the one of which Allah the Exalted said: "It would be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth" (31:16); the rock is upon the horn of a bull, and the bull is upon the soil, and none knows what is beneath the soil except Allah the Exalted. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: On the surface of the earth are seven seas, and the earths are seven, with a sea between every two earths; the lowest sea encloses the rim of Hell, and were it not for its vastness, abundance of water and coldness, Hell would burn everyone upon it. He said: Hell is upon the back of the wind, and the back of the wind is upon a veil of darkness whose thickness none knows except Allah the Exalted; and that veil is upon the soil, and to the soil the knowledge of creation ends.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden" (20:7). Ibn Abbas said: The secret is what a person tells another privately, and more hidden than that is what he conceals in himself which he has not told anyone. It is also narrated from him: The secret is the discourse of your soul, and more hidden than the secret is what you will yet say to yourself of what has not yet occurred but will occur; you know what you conceal today but do not know what you will conceal tomorrow, while Allah knows what you concealed today and what you will conceal tomorrow. The meaning: Allah knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret. Ibn Abbas also said: "The secret" is what the son of Adam conceals within himself, and "what is more hidden" is what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he himself will do and does not know; so Allah the Exalted knows all of that, and His knowledge of what has passed and what is to come is one knowledge, and all creation in His knowledge is like a single soul. Qatadah and others said: "The secret" is what a person conceals in himself, and "what is more hidden" is what has not yet occurred and no one has concealed. Ibn Zayd said: "The secret" is the secret of creation, and "what is more hidden" is His own secret, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Tabari rejected this and said: What is more hidden is what is not in a person's secret but will be in his soul, as Ibn Abbas said.

(Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names) (20:8). "Allah" is nominative by way of beginning (mubtada'), or by implying an omitted subject, or as a substitute for the pronoun in "ya'lamu." He declared His own oneness, glory be to Him, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the polytheists to worship Allah alone, with no partner, and this was grievous to them. When Abu Jahl heard him mention "the Merciful," he said to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: "Muhammad forbids us to call upon another god with Allah, yet he calls upon Allah and the Merciful." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "The Merciful, established upon the Throne" (20:5), and revealed: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names" (17:110). He is one, and His names are many. Then He said: "Allah, there is no god but He; to Him belong the most beautiful names" (20:8). These have already been noted in Surat al-A'raf.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him)

Surat Ta-Ha (peace be upon him) is Meccan, according to unanimous agreement. It was revealed before the conversion of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Umar went out with a sword slung on him. It was said to him: "Your brother-in-law [and your sister [from B, J, Z, T, K]] have turned away [sabaw (sabā al-rajul: he left one religion for another)]." So Umar came to them, and with them was a man from the Muhajirun called Khabbab, and they were reading: "Ta-Ha." He said: "Give me the book you have, so that I may read it." Umar used to read books. His sister said to him: "You are impure, and none touches it except the purified. So get up and perform ghusl, or wudu." Umar stood up, performed wudu, took the book and read: "Ta-Ha."

Ibn Ishaq mentioned it at length: Umar went out with his sword girded, intending to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kill him. Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah met him and said: "Where are you going, O Umar?" He said: "I am going to Muhammad, this Sabian who has divided the affair of Quraysh, belittled their minds, reviled their religion, and cursed their gods; I will kill him." Nu'aym said to him: "By Allah, your own self has deluded you, O Umar. Do you think the Banu Abd Manaf will leave you walking on the earth after you have killed Muhammad? Will you not return to your family and set their affairs right?" He said: "Which family of mine?" He said: "Your brother-in-law and paternal cousin Sa'id ibn Zayd, and your sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab. By Allah, they have both embraced Islam and followed Muhammad in his religion, so go to them." Umar returned intending to go to his sister and brother-in-law, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Arat, who had a sheet on which was "Ta-Ha," teaching it to them. When they heard Umar's sound, Khabbab hid in a small room of theirs or in part of the house, and Fatimah bint al-Khattab took the sheet and put it under her thigh. Umar had heard the recitation of Khabbab to them as he approached the house. When he entered he said: "What is this murmuring [al-haynamah: low speech that cannot be understood] that I heard?" They said to him: "You heard nothing." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, I have been informed that you both have followed Muhammad in his religion." He attacked his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd, so his sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab stood up to restrain him from her husband, and he struck her and wounded her. When he did that, his sister and brother-in-law said to him: "Yes, we have embraced Islam and believed in Allah and His Messenger, so do what you wish." When Umar saw the blood on his sister, he regretted what he had done, and he relented and said to his sister: "Give me this sheet which I heard you reading just now, so I can see what this is that Muhammad has brought." He was a scribe. When he said that, his sister said to him: "We fear for it on your account." He said to her: "Do not fear," and swore to her by his gods that he would return it once he had read it. When he said that, she hoped for his Islam, and said to him: "O my brother, you are impure in your polytheism, and none touches it except the pure." So Umar stood up and performed ghusl, and she gave him the sheet, in which was "Ta-Ha." When he read a portion of it, he said: "How excellent this speech is, and how noble!" When Khabbab heard that, he came out to him and said: "O Umar, by Allah, I hope that Allah has singled you out with the supplication of His Prophet, for I heard him yesterday saying: (O Allah, strengthen Islam with Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or with Umar ibn al-Khattab)." So, fear Allah, O Umar. He said to him at that: "Guide me, O Khabbab, to Muhammad so that I may go to him and embrace Islam," and he mentioned the hadith.

Issue: Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad narrated in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will be sent down, blessed are the bodies that carry this, and blessed are the tongues that speak this.'" Ibn Furak said the meaning of his saying: "Allah, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin," i.e., He made His speech manifest, audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He willed among the angels at that time. The Arabs say: "I read the thing" when they followed it, and they say: "This she-camel never gave birth in her womb" meaning no offspring appeared in her. On this basis the statement is valid, and its recitation is its making them hear and comprehend through expressions He creates and writing He produces. This is the meaning of our saying "we recited the speech of Allah," and the meaning of His saying: "Recite what is easy of the Qur'an" ("recite what is easy of it") [see vol. 19 p. 50 onward]. Some of our companions said the meaning of His saying "recited" is "spoke it," and this is metaphorical, like their saying "I tasted this statement" (dhuqtu hadha al-qawl dhawaqan) meaning "I tested it." From it is the saying of the Exalted: "So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing" [see vol. 10 p. 193 onward], i.e., Allah tested them with it, and that was called tasting, though fear is not tasted in the literal sense, because tasting in reality is with the mouth and not other limbs. Ibn Furak said: What we said first is more correct in interpreting this report, because the speech of Allah, the Exalted, is eternal, pre-existent, preceding all created things; He only makes audible and comprehensible to whomever of His creation He wills, according to what He wills, in times and periods, not that the very essence of His speech is tied in its existence to a duration and time.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Ha. (1) We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed. (2) But as a reminder to whoever fears. (3) A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens. (4) The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne. (5) To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil. (6) And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden. (7) Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names. (8)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. The scholars differed about its meaning. Al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is among the secrets. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it from Ibn Abbas; its meaning is "O man." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. It was also said: it is a well-known dialect among the tribe of Ukl. It was said also of Akk. Al-Kalbi said: If you say to a man in Akk "O man," he will not respond until you say "Ta-Ha." Al-Tabari recited in this regard, saying:

"I called 'Ta-Ha' in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be a fugitive [wa'il: seeking deliverance]."

It is also narrated as "muzayilan." Abd Allah ibn Umar said: "O my beloved" in the dialect of Akk, mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Qutrub said: it is in the dialect of Tayy, and he recited for Yazid ibn al-Muhalhal:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your traits; may Allah not bless the cursed people."

Likewise al-Hasan said: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "O man." Ikrimah also said it. He said it is in Syriac likewise, mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Mawardi related it from Ibn Abbas as well and Mujahid. Al-Tabari related that in Nabataean it means "O man." This is the view of al-Suddi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and also Ibn Abbas. He said:

"Indeed, folly is Ta-Ha among your characteristics; may Allah not sanctify the souls of the cursed."

Ikrimah also said: it is like your saying "O man" in the language of Abyssinia, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The correct view is that although it is found in another language, it is from the language of the Arabs as we have mentioned, and that it is a Yemeni dialect among Akk, Tayy and Ukl also. It was also said: it is one of the names of Allah, and an oath which He swore by. This too is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It was also said: it is a name of the Prophet (ﷺ), which Allah named him by, just as He named him Muhammad. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have ten names with my Lord," and he mentioned that among them are Ta-Ha and Ya-Sin. It was also said: it is the name of the surah and its key. It was also said: it is an abbreviation from the speech of Allah, which Allah singled out His Messenger with knowledge of. It was also said: they are disjointed letters, each letter of which indicates a meaning, and this was disputed. It was said: the Ta is the tree of Tuba and the Ha is the Hawiyah fire; the Arabs express the whole by a part, as if He swore by Paradise and Hell. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Ta is the opening of His name Tahir and Tayyib, and the Ha is the opening of His name Hadi. It was said: "Ta" means "O one who hopes for intercession for the community," "Ha" means "O guide of creation to Allah." It was said: the Ta is from purity and the Ha is from guidance, as if He says to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "O one purified from sins, O guide of creation to the Knower of the unseen." It was said: the Ta is the drums of the warriors and the Ha is their awe in the hearts of the disbelievers. Its clarification is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [see vol. 4 p. 232 onward] and His saying: "And He cast terror into their hearts" [see vol. 18 p. 3 onward]. It was said: the Ta is the joy of the people of Paradise in Paradise, and the Ha is the grief of the people of the Fire in the Fire. A sixth view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "Tuba li-man ihtada" (blessed is whoever is guided), said by Mujahid and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah. A seventh view: the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "ta' al-ard" (tread the earth), because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to bear the hardship of prayer until his feet nearly swelled and he needed to rest between his feet, so it was said to him: "tread the earth," i.e., do not exert yourself until you need rest; related by Ibn al-Anbari. Qadi Iyad mentioned in al-Shifa that al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he stood on one foot and raised the other, so Allah revealed: "Ta-Ha," meaning, "Tread the earth, O Muhammad."

﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you for you to be distressed﴾ [20:2]. Al-Zamakhshari: It is also narrated from al-Hasan that "Ta-Ha" was explained as an order to tread, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to stand in his tahajjud on one of his feet, so he was commanded to set his feet on the earth together, and that the original is "ta'" whose hamza was changed to ha, just as alif was changed in "yata" according to the one who said:

"...... may the pasture not be pleasant for you"

[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, and the full line is: "They went with the mules of Maslamah in the evening, so pasture, O Fazarah, may the pasture not be pleasant for you." He said this when Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik was removed from Iraq and Umar ibn Hubayrah al-Fazari was appointed over it, so al-Farazdaq satirized them and invoked against his people not to congratulate themselves on the favor of his governorship. By the mules of the postal service he meant those that brought Maslamah at his removal.] (Shawahid Sibawayh).

Then He established this matter upon it, and the hā' is for pausal (sakt) purposes. Mujahid said: The Prophet ﷺ and his companions used to tie ropes to their chests during the night prayer because of the length of standing, and then this was abrogated (naskh) by the obligatory command, and this verse was revealed. Al-Kalbi said: When revelation came down upon the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, he exerted himself greatly in worship, and his worship intensified; he would pray the whole night for a time, until this verse was revealed, and Allah the Exalted commanded him to lighten the burden on himself, so that he would pray and sleep. Thus this verse abrogated the qiyam of the night, and after this verse he would pray and sleep. Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: When the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he and his companions stood and prayed. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Allah has not sent down this Qur'an upon Muhammad except that he may be wretched." So Allah the Exalted revealed "Ta Ha," saying: "O man, We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2), meaning: to make you toil, as will come. According to this view, "Ta Ha" means "tā" as in "trample" (ṭa'), so the hā' and alif are a pronoun referring to the earth, meaning: trample the earth with your feet in your prayers; the hamza was lightened and became a silent alif. A group read "Ta Ha" with its origin being ṭa' meaning ṭi (trample), so the hamza was dropped and the hā' of pausal was added. Zirr ibn Hubaysh said: A man recited to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched" (20:1-2). Abdullah said to him: "Ṭih." The man said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, is it not that he was commanded to trample the earth with his feet or his two feet?" He said: "Ṭih, thus did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it to me." Abu Amr and Abu Ishaq inclined the hā' and made the ṭā' open. Abu Bakr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash inclined both. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' read between the two pronunciations, and Abu Ubayd chose this. The rest read with emphasis (tafkhim). Al-Tha'labi said: All of these are correct and eloquent dialects. These are two clear reasons.
