His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So take off your sandals; indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa﴾ [20:12]. In this there are five issues.

**The first issue:** His words, may He be exalted, "So take off your sandals" [20:12]. al-Tirmidhi related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Moses, on the day his Lord spoke to him, wore a woolen cloak, a woolen jubba, a woolen kummah, woolen trousers, and his sandals were of the skin of a dead donkey." He said: "This is a strange ḥadīth, which we know only through the ḥadīth of Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj [Ḥumayd is Ibn ʿAlī al-Kūfī] [[the addition is from al-Tirmidhi]], who is munkar al-ḥadīth (rejected in narration). But Ḥumayd ibn Qays al-Aʿraj al-Makkī, the companion of Mujāhid, is trustworthy." The kummah is a small cap.

The majority read "innī" with a kasra, meaning: he was called, and it was said to him, "O Moses, indeed I..." Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading. Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥaysin and Ḥumayd read "annī" with a fatḥa on the alif, by making the call govern it.

The scholars differed about the reason for which he was commanded to take off the two sandals. Khalʿ means removal, and naʿl (sandal) is that which you make as a protection for your feet from the ground.

It was said: he was commanded to cast off the two sandals because they were impure, being made of the skin of an animal that was not slaughtered lawfully (ghayr mudhakkā). This was said by Kaʿb, ʿIkrima and Qatāda.

It was said: he was commanded to do so in order to obtain the blessing of the sacred valley, and so that his feet would touch the dust of the valley. This was said by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj.

It was said: he was commanded to remove the two sandals for humility and lowliness when privately communing with Allah, may He be exalted. The early generations (al-salaf) did likewise when they circumambulated the House.

It was said: [he was commanded to do so] as a means of magnifying that place, just as the sacred precinct (al-Ḥaram) is not entered wearing sandals, out of reverence for it. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It was said to him, "Walk upon the ground barefoot, just as you enter the Kaʿba barefoot."

The custom among kings is that sandals are removed, and a person reaches the utmost of humility. So it is as if Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded in this manner, and it does not matter whether his sandals were of carrion or of something else.

Mālik would not allow himself to ride an animal in Medina, out of reverence for its soil, which contains the noble bones and the honored body [of the Prophet (ﷺ)].

In this same sense is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, to Bashīr ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyya, when he was walking among the graves wearing his sandals: "If you are in a place like this, take off your sandals." He said: "So I took them off."

**A fifth view:** that this is an expression for emptying his heart of concern for family and children. The family is sometimes expressed by the sandal. Likewise in interpretation (taʿbīr, the interpretation of dreams): [[His words, "in interpretation," mean the interpretation of dreams.]] whoever sees himself wearing two sandals, he will marry.

It was said: because Allah, may He be exalted, spread out for him the carpet of light and guidance, and it is not fitting to tread upon the carpet of the Lord of the worlds with one's sandal. [[From b, j, z, ṭ and y.]]

It is also possible that Moses was commanded to take off his sandals, and that this was the first obligation upon him, just as the first thing said to Muḥammad (ﷺ) was: "Arise and warn. And your Lord, magnify. And your garments, purify. And uncleanness, shun" [74:2–5]. And Allah knows best what is meant by that.

**The second issue:** It is reported that Moses, peace be upon him, took off his sandals and threw them behind the valley. Abū al-Aḥwaṣ said: ʿAbd Allah visited Abū Mūsā in his house. The prayer was called, and Abū Mūsā led the prayer. Then Abū Mūsā said to ʿAbd Allah, "Go forward." ʿAbd Allah said, "You go forward, in your own house." So he went forward and took off his sandals. ʿAbd Allah said, "Are you, O Abū Mūsā, the one of the sacred valley?"

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Yazīd, who said: I asked Anas, "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray in his sandals?" He said: "Yes."

al-Nasāʾī related it from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Sāʾib: that the Prophet (ﷺ), on the day of the Conquest, placed his sandals on his left.

Abū Dāwūd related from the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was leading his companions in prayer, he took off his sandals and placed them on his left. When the people saw that, they threw down their sandals. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished the prayer, he said: "What made you throw down your sandals?" They said: "We saw you throw down your sandals, so we threw down ours." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibrīl came to me and informed me that there was filth on them." And he said: "When one of you comes to the mosque, let him look; if he sees filth or harm on his sandals, let him wipe it off and pray in them." Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq authenticated it. It combines the two ḥadīths before it, and removes the contradiction between them.

The scholars did not differ regarding the permissibility of praying in sandals when they are pure, made of lawfully slaughtered (dhakī) skin. Indeed, some scholars said: praying in them is better. This is the meaning of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Take your adornment at every mosque﴾ [7:31], as has preceded.

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said, concerning those who take off their sandals: "I wish that a needy person would come and take them."

**The third issue:** If you take them off, then take them off between your feet, for Abū Hurayra said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you prays, let him take off his sandals between his feet." Abū Hurayra also said to al-Maqburī: "Take them off between your feet, and do not harm a Muslim with them." And [there is] what ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Sāʾib, may Allah be pleased with him, related: that he, peace and blessings be upon him, took them off to his left, because he was the imam. So if you are an imam or praying alone, do so if you wish. But if you are a follower (maʾmūm) in the row, do not harm the one to your left with them, and do not place them between your feet so that they distract you, but in front of your feet.

It is related from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim that he said: a man placing his sandals between his feet is an innovation (bidʿa).

**The fourth issue:** If there is definitely an impurity on them that is agreed upon as making them impure, such as blood and excrement, or the urine of the sons of Adam, then only washing with water purifies them, according to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and most scholars. If the impurity is disputed, such as the urine of animals and their fresh dung, then does wiping them with earth purify the sandal and the leather sock or not? There are two opinions in our school. al-Awzāʿī and Abū Thawr allowed unconditionally that wiping such things with earth suffices, without distinction.

Abū Ḥanīfa said: it removes [the impurity] if it has dried, by scraping and rubbing, but it does not remove the moist portion except by washing, except for urine, for which only washing suffices according to him.

al-Shāfiʿī said: nothing of all that is purified except by water.

The correct view is that of the one who said that wiping purifies the sock and the sandal, based on the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd. As for if the sandal and the sock are made of the skin of carrion, then if it is not tanned (ghayr madbūgh), it is impure by consensus, except for the view of al-Zuhrī and al-Layth, as has preceded in explanation in Surat al-Naḥl. The discussion of removing impurity has passed in Surat Barāʾa, and praise be to Allah.

**The fifth issue:** His words, may He be exalted: "indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa" [20:12]. al-Muqaddas means the purified. al-Quds means purity. The sacred land (al-arḍ al-muqaddasa) means the purified, and it was so named because Allah, may He be exalted, expelled the disbelievers from it and populated it with the believers.

Allah, may He be exalted, has given some places more excellence than others, just as He has given some times more excellence than others, and some animals likewise. Allah may prefer whatever He wills. In light of this, there is no consideration in its being sacred due to the expulsion of the disbelievers and the settling of the believers, since others share that with it.

"Ṭuwā" is the name of the valley, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others. Qatāda said: it is a deep valley, round like a well (ṭawī). ʿIkrima read "Ṭiwan." The rest read "Ṭuwā."

al-Jawharī said: "Ṭuwā" is the name of a place in Syria. Its ṭāʾ may be pronounced with a kasra or a ḍamma, and it may be declined or not declined. Whoever declines it makes it the name of a valley and a place, and makes it indefinite. Whoever does not decline it makes it a town and a plot, and makes it definite.

Some said: "Ṭuwā" is like "ṭiwan," which is the folded thing (al-shayʾ al-mathnī). They said regarding His words "the sacred valley, Tuwa": it was folded twice, that is, made holy. al-Ḥasan said: blessing and sanctification were folded in it twice.

al-Mahdawī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was said to him: "Ṭuwā" because Moses folded it (ṭawāhu) by night when he passed by it, and he ascended to the upper part of the valley. So it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) governing what is not from its own root. It is as if He said: "indeed, you are in the sacred valley" that you folded (ṭawaytahu) by folding (ṭuwan), that is, you passed beyond it and folded it by your traveling. al-Ḥasan: its meaning is that it was made holy twice, so it is also a verbal noun from "ṭawaytuhu ṭuwan."

**His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾ [20:13]**, that is, I have chosen you for the message (risāla).

The people of Medina, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read "And I have chosen you" [20:13]. Ḥamza read "wa-annā ikhtarnāka" (And We have chosen you). The meaning is one, except that "wa-anā ikhtartuka" [20:13] is preferable here from two aspects: first, that it is closer to the written form (al-khaṭṭ); second, that it is more suitable to the arrangement of the speech, given His words, mighty and majestic: "O Moses, indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals" [20:11–12]. And the address proceeded in this arrangement. This was said by al-Naḥḥās.

**His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ [20:13].** In this there is one issue. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, told me that he heard Abū al-Faḍl al-Jawharī, may Allah have mercy on him, say: When it was said to Moses, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, "So listen to what is revealed" [20:13], he stood upon a stone, leaned against a stone, placed his right hand upon his left, lowered his chin onto his chest, and stood listening. All of his clothing was wool.

I say: Good listening, as it must be, is what Allah has praised, saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it—those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ [39:18]. And He censured the opposite of this description, saying: ﴿We know best what they listen to with it﴾ [[see vol. 10, p. 272]] and so on. So He praised the one who is silent in order to listen to His speech with presence of mind, and He commanded His servants to do so as a courtesy to them, saying: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy﴾ [7:204]. And here He said: "So listen to what is revealed" [20:13], because by that understanding from Allah, may He be exalted, is attained.

It is reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: Among the etiquette of listening is stillness of the limbs, lowering the gaze, attentive hearing, presence of mind, and resolve to act. That is listening as Allah, may He be exalted, loves it: that the servant restrains his limbs and does not busy them, so that his heart is not occupied with other than what he hears; he lowers his gaze so that his heart is not diverted by what he sees; he confines his mind so that he speaks to himself of nothing except what he is listening to; and he resolves to understand, so that he acts upon what he understands.

Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said: The beginning of knowledge is listening, then understanding, then memorization, then action, then dissemination. When the servant listens to the Book of Allah, may He be exalted, and the Sunna of His Prophet, peace be upon him, with a sincere intention, in accordance with what Allah loves, Allah makes him understand as He loves, and places light in his heart.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 9–16 (part 3 of 4)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am Allah; there is no god except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. On this there are seven issues.

**The first issue:** Scholars differed concerning the interpretation of His words "for My remembrance." It was said that it may mean: so that you remember Me in it, or it may mean: so that I mention you with praise in the highest place (ʿIlliyyin) because of it. On this reading, the verbal noun (maṣdar) may be read as an annexation to the subject or to the object. It was also said that the meaning is: after affirming the Oneness of God, be steadfast in the prayer. This is a reminder of the great rank of prayer, since it is a humble supplication to Allah, Exalted is He, and a standing before Him. On this reading, prayer is itself the remembrance. Allah, Exalted is He, has called prayer a remembrance in His words: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 9].[[See vol. 18, p. 97 onward.]] It was also said that the intended meaning is: if you forget and then recall, then pray, as in the report: "Let him pray it when he remembers it," meaning: do not let forgetfulness cause the prayer to be dropped.

**The second issue:** Malik and others narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [20:14]." Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Ghani ibn Saʿid also narrated, through the ḥadīth of Ḥajjaj ibn Ḥajjaj[[In sources j, t, k and y: "Ibn Abi al-Hajjaj." What we have written in the original is what appears in al-Tahdhib.]]—he is the first Ḥajjaj, from whom Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated—who said: Qatada narrated to us from Anas ibn Malik[[From sources j and k.]], who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a man who sleeps through the prayer and neglects it. He said: "Its expiation is that he pray it when he remembers it." Ibrahim ibn Tahman narrated it similarly from Ḥajjaj, and Hammam ibn Yahya narrates it likewise from Qatada. Al-Daraqutni also narrated from Abu Hurayrah[[From sources j and k.]] that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, its time is when he remembers it."

His saying, "let him pray it when he remembers it," is evidence that making up (qaḍāʾ, performing a missed act after its time) is obligatory for the one who sleeps or is heedless, whether the missed prayers are many or few. This is the position of the majority of scholars. A weak, disregarded dissent has been reported from some people, that for more than five prayers there is no obligation to make them up, but this contradicts the explicit text of the ḥadīth.

I say: Allah commanded the establishment of prayer and specified fixed times, saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾[[See vol. 10, p. 302 onward.]] [al-Isrāʾ: 78], and other verses. Whoever establishes at night what he was commanded to establish by day, or the reverse, has not performed what he was commanded, and he has no reward for his act, since he is disobedient. On this basis, it would not be obligatory for him to make up what has passed its time. Were it not for the statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it," no one would benefit from a prayer performed outside its time. For this reason it is qaḍāʾ (making up) and not adāʾ (performing on time), because qaḍāʾ is by a new command and not by the first command.

**The third issue:** As for one who abandons prayer deliberately, the majority likewise hold that making it up is obligatory for him, even though he is sinful. The exception is Dawud. He was agreed with by Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥman al-Ashʿari al-Shafiʿi, as Ibn al-Qassar reported from him.

The difference between the deliberate, the forgetful and the sleeper is the removal of sin. The deliberate one is sinful, but all of them must make it up.

The proof for the majority is His saying: ﴿Establish prayer﴾[[See vol. 1, p. 344 onward.]] [al-Anʿām: 72], and He did not distinguish between performing it within its time or after it. It is a command, which implies obligation. Also, the command to make up prayer for the one who sleeps and the one who forgets has been established, even though they are not sinful; so the deliberate one is more deserving of it. Also, His words, "whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it," and forgetting means abandoning, as Allah says: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and ﴿They forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 19], whether accompanied by inattention or not, because Allah does not forget. Its meaning is only that He abandoned them. And ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾[[See vol. 2, p. 61.]] [al-Baqarah: 106] means: We leave it aside. Likewise, remembrance occurs after forgetting and after other states. Allah said: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself." He, Exalted is He, does not forget, so His remembrance would not follow forgetting; its meaning is only "I know." Thus the meaning of His words, "when he remembers it," is: when he knows it.

Also, debts owed to human beings, if they are tied to a time, and that time arrives, the obligation to make them up does not lapse after it has become due, and they are of the kind that release (ibrāʾ) can cancel. If release is not valid in the debts of Allah, Exalted is He, then it is more appropriate that making them up not lapse except by His permission.

Also, we agree that if a person deliberately abandons a day of Ramadan without excuse, its making up is obligatory; so likewise for prayer.

If it is said: it has been reported from Malik that "one who deliberately abandons prayer never makes it up," then the reference is that what has passed does not return, or it is a statement that came as a severe warning, as was reported from Ibn Masʿud and ʿAli: that whoever breaks his fast in Ramadan deliberately, fasting the whole year will not atone for it, even if he fasts it.

Even so, it is necessary to fulfill the obligation's right by performing the making up in place of the performance on time, and to follow it with repentance, and Allah does after that what He wills.

Abu al-Mutawwas narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever breaks a day of Ramadan deliberately, fasting the whole year will not suffice for it, even if he fasts it." This may, if authentic, mean severity. It is a weak ḥadīth, which Abu Dawud recorded. Expiation has come in sound ḥadīths[[In sources b, z and k: "with sound chains (asānīd)."]], and in some of them is the making up of the day, and praise belongs to Allah, Exalted is He.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it..." This ḥadīth specifies the generality of His saying, peace be upon him: "The pen is lifted from three: from the sleeper until he awakes..." Here "lifting" means the lifting of sin, not the lifting of the obligation itself. This is not of the type of His saying: "and from the child until he reaches puberty," although that also came in a single report. So grasp this principle.

**The fifth issue:** Scholars differed concerning this matter for one who remembers a missed prayer while he is at the end of the time of another prayer, or who remembers a prayer while he is in a prayer. The general position of Malik is: one who remembers a prayer when the time of another prayer has arrived begins with the one he forgot, if the prayers are five or fewer, even if the time of this one passes. If they are more than that, he begins with the one whose time has arrived. The position of Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and al-Layth is similar to this, except that Abu Hanifa and his companions said: the sequence (tartīb, performing the prayers in order) is obligatory for us within the day and night when there is room in the time for the missed prayer and for the prayer of the present time. If he fears that the time of the present prayer will pass, he begins with it. If the missed prayers exceed the prayers of one day and night, the sequence is not obligatory according to them. It has been reported from al-Thawri that the sequence is obligatory, and he did not distinguish between few and many. This is the established position of al-Shafiʿi.

Al-Shafiʿi said: The preferred course is to begin with the missed prayer as long as he does not fear the passing of this one. If he does not do so, and begins with the prayer of the present time, it suffices him.

Al-Athram reported that the sequence is obligatory according to Ahmad when the missed prayers are sixty years' worth or more. He said: No one should perform a prayer while he is aware of an earlier one, because it will be spoiled for him.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If one of you remembers a prayer while he is in an obligatory prayer, let him begin with the one he is in. When he finishes it, let him pray the one he forgot." ʿUmar ibn Abi ʿUmar is unknown[[ʿUmar ibn Abi ʿUmar is one of the narrators of this ḥadīth from Makhul from Ibn ʿAbbas. The wording of the ḥadīth in al-Daraqutni is as follows: "If one of you forgets the prayer and remembers it while he is in an obligatory prayer, let him begin with the one he is in. When he finishes it, let him pray the one he forgot." This is as in sources b, z and k.]].

I say: If this were authentic, it would be a proof for al-Shafiʿi in beginning with the prayer of the present time. But the authentic report is what the compilers of the Ṣaḥīḥ transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: that ʿUmar, on the day of the Trench, began cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh and said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I almost did not pray ʿAṣr until the sun nearly set!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Allah, I have not prayed it[[In, meaning "not."]]." Then we went down to al-Biṭḥān[[Biṭḥān (with a damma, or more correctly a fatḥa with the ṭāʾ kasra): a place in Medina.]], and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed wuḍūʾ, and we performed wuḍūʾ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed ʿAṣr after the sun had set, and then prayed Maghrib after it.

This is an explicit text for beginning with the missed prayer before the prayer of the present time, especially since the time of Maghrib is a single, restricted time, not extended, according to the more correct view among us, and according to al-Shafiʿi, as has preceded.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu ʿUbaydah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, from his father, that the polytheists distracted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from four prayers on the day of the Trench, until a part of the night passed, as Allah willed. So he commanded Bilal to call the adhan. He stood and called the adhan, then gave the iqāma and prayed Ẓuhr, then gave the iqāma and prayed ʿAṣr, then gave the iqāma and prayed Maghrib, then gave the iqāma and prayed ʿIshāʾ.

From this, scholars inferred that whoever has missed prayers makes them up in order, just as they were missed, when he remembers them within one time.

They differed when one remembers a missed prayer during the restricted time of a present prayer, on three views:

The first: he begins with the missed prayer even if the time of the present prayer passes. This was said by Malik, al-Layth, al-Zuhri and others, as we have already mentioned.

The second: he begins with the present prayer. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Shafiʿi, the jurists of the people of ḥadīth, al-Muḥasibi and Ibn Wahb, from among our companions.

The third: he chooses, and puts forward whichever of the two he wishes. This was said by Ashhab.

The reason for the first view is the multitude of prayers, and there is no disagreement that one begins with the present prayer when the number is large. This was stated by al-Qadi ʿIyad.

They differed about what counts as a small number. According to Malik: five or fewer. It has also been said: four or fewer, based on the ḥadīth of Jabir. The school has not differed that six is a large number.

**The sixth issue:** As for one who remembers a prayer while he is in a prayer: if he is behind the imam, then everyone who holds the obligation of the sequence and everyone who does not hold it[[In sources k, t and y: "says."]] continues with the imam until he completes his prayer. The basis for this is what Malik and al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "If one of you forgets a prayer and does not remember it except while he is with the imam, let him pray with the imam. When he finishes his prayer, let him pray the prayer he forgot, then let him repeat the prayer he prayed with the imam." This is the wording of al-Daraqutni. Musa ibn Harun said: Abu Ibrahim al-Tarjumani narrated it to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us [with it][[The addition is from al-Daraqutni.]], and raised it to the Prophet ﷺ, and he erred in raising it. If he retracted his raising, then he was guided to what is correct.

Then they differed. Abu Hanifa and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: he prays the one he remembered, then prays the one he prayed with the imam, unless there are more than five prayers between them, according to what we have mentioned from the Kufans.

This is also the position of a group of Malik's Medinan companions.

Al-Kharaqi[[This nisba refers to the trade in rags and clothing.]] mentioned from Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he said: Whoever remembers a prayer while he is in another, he completes the one he is in, and makes up the one he remembered. If the time was wide, he repeats the one he was in. If he fears the time will pass while he is in it, I believe he does not need to repeat it, and it has sufficed him, and he makes up the one that is owed to him.

Malik said:

Whoever remembers a prayer while he is in a prayer, having already prayed two rak'ahs of it, and then ends (the prayer) with a salam after two rak'ahs; if he was an imam, it collapses upon him and upon those behind him, and it is nullified.

This is the apparent position of the school of Malik, but among the people of analysis (ahl al-nazar) of his companions it is not so, because his statement regarding one who remembers a prayer during a prayer in which he has prayed one rak'ah, that he adds another to it and makes salam, implies...

And if he remembered it during a prayer in which he had prayed three rak'ahs, he adds a fourth to it and makes salam, and it becomes a supererogatory prayer (nafilah) that is not invalid. Even if it collapsed upon him as mentioned and was nullified, he would not be commanded to add another to it, just as if he had broken his wudu' after one rak'ah, he would not add another to it.

Seventh: Muslim narrated from Abu Qatadah, who said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us, and the hadith of the water vessel was mentioned in full, and in it he said, then he said:

"Is there not for you in me an example?" Then he said:

"Indeed, there is no negligence in sleep. Negligence is only upon the one who does not pray until the time of the next prayer comes. Whoever does that, let him pray it when he wakes up for it, and when the next day comes, let him pray it at its time."

Al-Daraqutni also narrated it in exactly the wording of Muslim. Its apparent meaning requires repeating the missed prayer twice: upon remembering it, and upon the arrival of a similar time later on. This apparent meaning is supported by what Abu Dawud narrated from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn, who mentioned the story and said at its end:

"Whoever among you catches the morning prayer tomorrow in its proper state, let him make up with it a similar one."

I say: This is not on its apparent meaning, and it is not repeated more than once, because of what al-Daraqutni narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, who said:

We travelled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a campaign, or he said on a raid. When it was the time of the pre-dawn, we stopped to rest, and we did not awaken until the heat of the sun woke us. Each man among us jumped up startled and bewildered. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) awoke, he commanded us, and we set out, then we travelled until the sun had risen. The people then attended to their needs. Then he commanded Bilal, who gave the adhan, and we prayed two rak'ahs. Then he commanded him, and he gave the iqamah, and we prayed the morning prayer. We said:

"O Prophet of Allah, should we not make it up at its time tomorrow?"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Does Allah forbid you from usury while accepting it from you?"

Al-Khattabi said: I do not know of anyone who held this to be obligatory. It seems that the command to do so was for recommendation (istihbab), in order to obtain the virtue of the time in making up the prayer.

The correct position is to abandon acting upon it, because of his statement, peace be upon him: "Does Allah forbid you from usury while accepting it from you?" And because the sound chains from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn contain none of that addition, except what was mentioned from the hadith of Abu Qatadah, and it is open to interpretation as we have explained.

I say: Al-Kiya al-Tabari mentioned in his [Ahkam al-Qur'an] that some of the early generation (salaf) opposed his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it except that." He said: He should wait until the similar time and then pray; if the morning prayer has passed, then he should pray it on the next day.

This is a distant, anomalous (shadhdh) opinion.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [20:15] is a problematic verse. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read "akadu ukhfiha" [20:15] with a fatha on the hamza, and said: "I make it manifest." And "li-tujza" means the manifestation is for the recompense. Abu Ubayd narrated it from al-Kisa'i, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Wiqa' ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Nahhas said: This narration has no chain other than this one. I say: Abu Bakr al-Anbari likewise narrated it in the Kitab al-Radd: my father told me, Muhammad ibn al-Jahm told us, al-Farra' told us, al-Kisa'i told us; and 'Abd Allah ibn Naji'a told us, Yusuf told us, Yahya al-Himmani told us, Muhammad ibn Sahl told us. Al-Nahhas said: The better chain than this is what Yahya al-Qattan narrated from al-Thawri, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he read: "akadu ukhfiha" [20:15] with a damma on the hamza. I say: As for Ibn Jubayr's reading "akhfiha" with a fatha on the hamza by the chain mentioned, Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: al-Farra' said: its meaning is "I make it manifest," from "khafaytu al-shay'" "akhfihi," when I reveal it. Al-Farra' cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you bury the disease, we shall not conceal it, and if you stir up war, we shall not sit idle."

He meant: we shall not reveal it. Some lexicographers said: it is permissible that "ukhfiha" [20:15] with a damma on the hamza means "I make it manifest," because it is said: "khafaytu al-shay'" and "akhfaytuhu" when I reveal it; so "akhfaytuhu" is among the words of opposites, applying to both concealing and revealing. Abu Ubayda said: "khafaytu" and "akhfaytu" have one meaning. Al-Nahhas said: This is good, and he related it from Abu al-Khattab [the Akhfash al-Akbar, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn 'Abd al-Majid], who is one of the leaders of the language, whose truthfulness is not doubted, and Sibawayh narrated from him.

He recited:

"And if you conceal the disease, we shall not conceal it, and if you stir up war, we shall not sit idle."

Abu Ubayda narrated it likewise from Abu al-Khattab with a damma on the nun. Imru' al-Qays also said:

"He revealed them from their holes, as if the rain of an evening, pouring down, had revealed them."

That is, he revealed them. It is also narrated: "from a cloud piled up" instead of "from an evening pouring down."

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: There is another explanation of the verse: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, I almost [20:15]" — the speech stops at "akadu" [20:15], and after it there is an implied: "I almost bring it," and the beginning is "ukhfiha li-tujza kullu nafs" [20:15]. Daba'i al-Burjumi said (he said it while imprisoned, imprisoned by our master 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, for satirizing some of the Banu Jarwal ibn Nahshal, and he remained in his prison until he died):

"I intended and did not do it, and I almost did, and I wish I had left upon 'Uthman weeping his wives."

He meant: "wa-kidtu af'al" (and I almost did), so he implied a verb with "kidtu" similar to the implied verb with it in the Qur'an.

I say: This is what al-Nahhas chose, and he rejected the view before it, saying: It is said "khafa al-shay'" yukhfihi when he revealed it, and it has been related that it is also said "akhfahu" when he revealed it, but this is not well known. He said: I have seen 'Ali ibn Sulayman, when the meaning of "ukhfiha" [20:15] became unclear to him, turn to this view, and he said: its meaning is like the meaning of "ukhfiha" [20:15]. Al-Nahhas said: The meaning is not "reveal," especially since "ukhfiha" [20:15] is a shadhdh reading; how can the sound, widespread reading be referred back to the shadhdh one? The meaning of the implied is better, and the sense would be: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, I almost bring it," and "ataya" indicates "ati biha," then he said "ukhfiha" [20:15] as a new beginning. This is a sound meaning, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has concealed the Hour, which is the Resurrection, and the hour in which a person dies, so that a person may keep working, and the matter is ambiguous to him, so he does not delay repentance.

I say: According to this view, the lam in "li-tujza" is connected to "ukhfiha" [20:15]. Abu 'Ali said: This is from the category of negation of a quality (al-salb), not from the category of opposites, and the meaning of "ukhfiha" [20:15] is: its concealment is removed from it, and its concealment is its covering, like the khafa' of the coverings, and its singular is khafa' with a kasra on the kha' — what is wrapped around a waterskin. When its covering is removed, it becomes manifest. From this is their saying: "akshaytuhu," meaning I removed his complaint, and "a'datuhu," meaning I accepted his request for aid and did not make him need to repeat it. Abu Hatim related from al-Akhfash that "kada" is an emphatic redundant particle. He said: Similar to it is ﴿When he extends his hand, he almost does not see it﴾ [24:40], because the darknesses Allah mentioned, some of them intervene between the viewer and what is viewed. The same meaning is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, and the estimate is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives." The poet said (he is Zayd al-Khayl):

"Swift to the battle, his weapons on him; he almost does not breathe, his opponent."

He meant: "fa-ma yatanaffasu," (he does not breathe). Another said:

"And that I should not blame myself for what befell me, and that I should not almost succeed with what I attained."

Meaning: "and that I should not succeed with what I attained," so "akadu" is an emphasis of the speech. It was also said: the meaning of "akadu ukhfiha" [20:15] is "I approach that," because when you say "kada Zayd yaqumu," it is possible that he stood and possible that he did not stand. This indicates that He had concealed it, by an indication other than this, toward this answer. The lexicographers said: "kidtu af'al" in the Arabs' usage means: I approached the act and did not do it; and "ma kidtu af'al" means: I did it after delay. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, whose greatness is exalted: ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾ [2:71], meaning: they did it after delay, because of the difficulty of finding the cow for them. It may also be that "ma kidtu af'al" means "I did not do it and did not even approach it," when the speech is emphasized with "akadu." It was also said: the meaning of "akadu ukhfiha" [20:15] is "uridu ukhfiha" (I intend to conceal it). Al-Anbari said: The evidence for this is the saying of the eloquent poets:

"She almost, and I almost, and that is the best of intentions, if what passed of the play of passion were to return."

Meaning: "aradat wa-aradtu" (she intended and I intended). Ibn 'Abbas and most of the commentators said, as related by al-Tha'labi: the meaning is "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi" (I almost conceal it from myself), and so it is in the Mushaf of Ubayy. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud: "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi," so how would a created being know it? In some readings: "fa-kayfa uzhiruha lakum" (how then would I make it manifest to you). This is taken to mean that it came according to the custom of the Arabs in their speech, that when one of them exaggerates in concealing a matter, he says: "kidtu ukhfihi min nafsi" (I almost concealed it from myself). Allah, the Exalted, is not hidden from anything. Qutrub and others said this. [And Allah knows best.] The poet said:

"In the days when Hind accompanies me, and I inform her of what I conceal of my need and my secrets..."

How would he inform her of what he conceals within himself? From this category is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "And a man who gave charity and concealed it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." (al-Zamakhshari). It was also said: its meaning is "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi," and there is no indication in the speech for this implied element, and an implied element without an indication is discarded. What deceived them about it is that in the Mushaf of Ubayy: "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi," and in some Mushafs: "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi fa-kayfa ukhbiruku 'alayha" (how then would I inform you of it). I say: It was also said that the meaning of those who said "akadu ukhfiha min nafsi" is that its concealment was from Me and from My side, not from the side of anyone else. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "akada ukhfiha min nafsi," and Talha ibn 'Amr narrated it from 'Ata'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I do not make it manifest to anyone." It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "He has concealed it." This is on the basis that "kada" is redundant, meaning: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I conceal it," and the benefit of concealing it is intimidation and awe. It was also said: "li-tujza" is connected to the saying of the Exalted: "And establish the prayer" (wa-aqimi al-salah), so there is inversion in the speech, meaning: "establish the prayer so that you remember Me."

﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [20:15], meaning: for its striving.

﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾ [20:15]. And Allah knows best. It was also said: it is connected to His saying "coming" (ati-yah), meaning: "Indeed, the Hour is coming, so that..." (li-tujza), ﴿so let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it﴾ [20:16], meaning: let him not divert you from belief in it and affirmation of it.

﴿whoever does not believe in it and follows his desire, lest you perish﴾ [20:16], meaning: lest you be ruined. It is in a position of accusative (nasb) as the answer to the prohibition.

There are five issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** Concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿And what is that in your right hand?﴾ [20:17]. It has been said that this address from God the Exalted to Moses was by revelation, because He said: (So listen to what is revealed) [20:13]. A prophet must have, within himself, a miracle through which he knows the truth of his own prophethood. So He showed him in the staff and in himself what He showed him for that purpose. It is also possible that what He showed him in the tree was a sufficient sign for him within himself, and then the hand and the staff served as added confirmation and a proof with which he would confront his people.

There is disagreement about "mā" in His words: (And what is that) [20:17]. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it is an incomplete noun (ism nāqis) joined to "bi-yamīnika" (in your right hand), meaning "what is it that is in your right hand?" Al-Farra' also said: "tilka" has the sense of "hādhihi" (this), and had he said "mā dhālika" it would have been permissible, meaning "what is that thing?" The purpose of the question was to establish the matter, so that Moses would say, "It is my staff," and the proof would be established against him after he had acknowledged it. Otherwise God already knew what it was from eternity.

Ibn al-Jawhari said: in some reports, God the Exalted rebuked Moses for attributing the staff to himself at that moment. It was said to him: "Throw it down, so that you may see from it a wonder, and know that it has no ownership over you and is not attributed to you."

Ibn Abi Ishaq read "‘aṣayya" (my staff) in the dialect of Hudhayl, and similar to it are "yā bushrāya" [see vol. 9, pp. 152 and 357] and "maḥyayya" [see vol. 7, p. 152], which have been mentioned before. Al-Hasan read "‘aṣāya" [20:18] with a kasra on the yā' because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters. A similar reading is that of Hamzah: ﴿And you are not one to help me [bi-muṣrikhiyya]﴾ [14:22]. It is also reported from Ibn Abi Ishaq that the yā' was vocalised with sukūn.

**The second issue:** In this verse there is evidence that the answer to a question may exceed what was asked. When He said: "And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?" [20:17], Moses mentioned four meanings: the attribution of the staff to himself (though it should have been "‘aṣā," the staff), the leaning on it (al-tawakkuʾ), the beating down of leaves (al-hashsh), and the various other uses (al-ma'ārib al-muṭlaqa). Moses mentioned from the benefits of his staff its size and its bulk, and summarised the rest.

In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the water of the sea, and he said: "Its water is pure and its dead animals are lawful." A woman asked him about a child whom she lifted up to him, saying: "Does this one have a pilgrimage?" He said: "Yes, and you have a reward." Similar examples in hadith are many.

**The third issue:** The words of the Exalted: (I lean upon it) [20:18], meaning I lean heavily upon it while walking and standing; from this comes "al-ittikā'" (reclining). Also (And I beat down with it) [20:18], "wa-ahushshu," also reported by al-Nahhas. It is the recitation of al-Nakha'i [it is also transmitted from al-Nakha'i that he read (wa-ahushshu) with a ḍamma on the hamza and the shīn, from the fourth-form verb "ahusha"], meaning I strike the leaves from it, that is, I strike the branches of the tree so that its leaves fall, and thus it becomes easy for my sheep to take and eat them. The reciter says:

I beat down with the staff upon my sheep
from the tender arak and basham trees.

It is said: "hashsha ʿalā ghanamihi, yahushshu" with a ḍamma on the hā' in the present tense; "hashsha ilā al-rajul, yahashshu" with a fatḥa; likewise "hashsha lil-maʿrūf, yahashshu." I myself [the author] "hashishtu." In the hadith of ʿUmar: "I was excited one day and kissed [my wife] while I was fasting." Shimr said: that is, I rejoiced and desired. He said: it is permissible to say "hāsha" with the meaning of "hashsha." The shepherd (al-rāʿī) says:

So he exclaimed at the vision, and his heart was stirred,
and he gave good news to a soul that had once been blaming it.

That is, it was delighted. The original root meaning of the word is softness. One says "rajulun hashshun" (a soft, gentle man) and "zawjun hashshun" (a gentle husband). Ikrimah read "wa-ahussu" with an unpointed sīn. It has been said that both are dialects with one meaning. It has also been said that their meanings differ: "al-hashsh" with the dots means striking trees, and "al-hass" without dots means driving away sheep; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi, and al-Zamakhshari likewise mentioned it. From Ikrimah, "wa-ahussu" with a sīn means "I incline over it, driving it away," and "al-hass" is driving sheep.

**The fourth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿And I have in it other uses﴾ [20:18], that is, needs. Its singular is "ma'raba," "ma'raba," or "ma'ribah." He said "ukhrā" in the singular form, because "ma'ārib" has the sense of a plural. However, the well-known (al-mahyaʿ) practice in the adjectives of plurals of non-rational things is the singular and the pronoun referring to them in that form, since it functions like a feminine singular. Like His words: ﴿And to God belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [7:180], and like His words: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [34:10]. This has been discussed before in Surat al-A'raf [see vol. 14, pp. 264 ff.].

**The fifth issue:** Some people have undertaken to enumerate the benefits of the staff, among them Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When you reach the mouth of a well and the rope falls short, you join it with the staff. When the heat of the sun reaches me, I plant it in the ground and cast over it what shades me. When I fear any of the creeping creatures of the earth, I kill it with it. When I walk, I place it on my shoulder and hang on it the bow, the quiver, and the food-bag, and I fight off the beasts of prey from the sheep with it."

Maymun ibn Mihran narrated from him: "Holding the staff is a sunnah (practice) of the prophets and a sign of the believer." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "In it are six qualities: a sunnah of the prophets, an adornment of the righteous, a weapon against enemies, a help to the weak, a grief to the hypocrites, and an increase in acts of obedience." It is also said: "When the staff is with the believer, Satan flees from him, the hypocrite and the wicked humble themselves before him, it becomes his qibla when he prays, and a strength when he is weary."

Al-Hajjaj met a Bedouin and said: "From where have you come, O Bedouin?" He said: "From the desert." He said: "And what is in your hand?" He said: "My staff. I plant it for my prayer, I prepare it for my enemies, I drive my animal with it, I strengthen myself with it on my journey, I rely on it in my walking so that my stride lengthens, I leap over the river with it, it saves me from stumbling, I throw my cloak over it and it shields me from the heat, and it warms me from the cold. It brings near to me what is far from me. It is the carrier of my travel provisions and the strap of my water-skin. I drive off with it at the time of mating, I knock on doors with it, I protect myself with it from the biting dogs, it takes the place of the spear in combat and of the sword when facing equals. I inherited it from my father, and I will bequeath it to my son after me. I beat down with it upon my sheep, and I have in it other uses, many and uncountable."

I say: the benefits of the staff are many, and it has a place in various matters of the Sharia. Among them: it is taken as a qibla (direction of prayer) in the open desert. The Prophet, peace be upon him, had an ʿanaza (a spear-like staff, about half a spear or larger, with a point like a spearhead) which was planted for him, and he prayed toward it. When he went out on the day of ʿEid, the spear was brought and placed before him, and he prayed toward it. This is established in the Sahih. The ḥarba, the ʿanaza, the naizak, and the ālah are names for one referent. He also had a miḥjan, which is a staff with a curved end, with which he pointed to the Black Stone when he could not kiss it; this too is established in the Sahih. In the Muwatta' from Sa'ib ibn Yazid, he said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, ordered Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Tamim al-Dari to lead the people in eleven rakʿahs. The reciter would recite the hundred-verse sections until we would lean on staves because of the length of the standing, and we would not leave except at the break of dawn." In the two Sahihs: the Prophet, peace be upon him, had a mikhṣarah (a stick held in the hand, a staff, crutch, whip, or rod on which one may lean).

There is a consensus (ijmaʿ) that the preacher delivers the khutbah leaning on a sword or staff. The staff is thus derived from a noble origin and a distinguished substance, and none denies it except an ignorant person. God gathered for Moses in his staff great proofs and mighty signs, which led the obstinate sorcerers to faith. Sulayman used it for his sermon, his exhortation, and his lengthy prayer. Ibn Mas'ud was the companion of the staff and spear of the Prophet, ﷺ, and he used to preach with a rod. That suffices as a virtue for the honour of the staff. The caliphs and the great preachers did likewise, and it was the custom of the pure Arabs, the eloquent, clear-tongued, and articulate, to take up the mikhṣarah or staff and lean upon it when speaking, in assemblies and sermons. The Shu'ubiyyah (a movement that disparaged Arabs and favoured non-Arabs) objected to Arab preachers taking the mikhṣarah and pointing with it to meanings. The Shu'ubiyyah hates the Arabs and prefers the non-Arabs.

Malik said: "ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib used to hold the mikhṣarah, seeking help from it." Malik said: "A man, when he grows old and is not like a young man, is strengthened by it when he stands."

I say: As someone said about his walking:

I used to walk on two legs, leaning,
then I walked on another, of wood.

Malik, may God have mercy on him and be pleased with him, said: "When rain came, people would go out with staves, leaning on them, to the point that the young men would hold back their staves, and sometimes Rabi'ah would take the staff from one of those sitting with him until he stood up."

Among the benefits of the staff is a man striking his wife with it in what improves them, and what improves his situation and theirs with him. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "As for Abu Jahm, he does not lay down his staff from his shoulder." This is from the hadith of Fatimah bint Qays, when she came to the Prophet, ﷺ, and mentioned that Abu Jahm ibn Hudhayfah and Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan had proposed to her. He said: "As for Abu Jahm, he is a man who does not lift his staff from women; as for Mu'awiyah, he is a pauper with no wealth." [al-Tirmidhi] in one of the narrations. It is also narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said to a man whom he advised: "Do not lift your staff from your family; frighten them for the sake of God." Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated it, and al-Nasa'i recorded it. In this same meaning is his, ﷺ, saying: "Hang your whip where your family can see it." This has been mentioned before in Surat al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 174].

Among its benefits is an alert to moving on from this world, as it was said to one of the ascetics: "Why do you walk with a staff when you are neither old nor sick?" He said: "I know that I am a traveller, that this is a house of departure, and that the staff is one of the tools of travel." One of the poets took this up and said:

I carried the staff, not because weakness made me carry it,
nor because I bent with old age,
but I bound myself to carrying it,
to make it known to myself that the one who stays is on a journey.

When he went out on the day of ʿEid, the spear was brought and placed before him, and he prayed toward it. This is established in the Sahih. The ḥarba, the ʿanaza, the naizak, and the ālah are names for one referent. He also had a miḥjan, which is a staff with a curved end, with which he pointed to the Black Stone when he could not kiss it; this too is established in the Sahih. In the Muwatta' from Sa'ib ibn Yazid, he said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, ordered Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Tamim al-Dari to lead the people in eleven rakʿahs. The reciter would recite the hundred-verse sections until we would lean on staves because of the length of the standing, and we would not leave except at the break of dawn." In the two Sahihs: the Prophet, peace be upon him, had a mikhṣarah (a stick held in the hand, a staff, crutch, whip, or rod on which one may lean).

There is a consensus (ijmaʿ) that the preacher delivers the khutbah leaning on a sword or staff. The staff is thus derived from a noble origin and a distinguished substance, and none denies it except an ignorant person. God gathered for Moses in his staff great proofs and mighty signs, which led the obstinate sorcerers to faith. Sulayman used it for his sermon, his exhortation, and his lengthy prayer. Ibn Mas'ud was the companion of the staff and spear of the Prophet, ﷺ, and he used to preach with a rod. That suffices as a virtue for the honour of the staff. The caliphs and the great preachers did likewise, and it was the custom of the pure Arabs, the eloquent, clear-tongued, and articulate, to take up the mikhṣarah or staff and lean upon it when speaking, in assemblies and sermons. The Shu'ubiyyah (a movement that disparaged Arabs and favoured non-Arabs) objected to Arab preachers taking the mikhṣarah and pointing with it to meanings. The Shu'ubiyyah hates the Arabs and prefers the non-Arabs.

Malik said: "ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib used to hold the mikhṣarah, seeking help from it." Malik said: "A man, when he grows old and is not like a young man, is strengthened by it when he stands."

I say: As someone said about his walking:

I used to walk on two legs, leaning,
then I walked on another, of wood.

Malik, may God have mercy on him and be pleased with him, said: "When rain came, people would go out with staves, leaning on them, to the point that the young men would hold back their staves, and sometimes Rabi'ah would take the staff from one of those sitting with him until he stood up."

Among the benefits of the staff is a man striking his wife with it in what improves them, and what improves his situation and theirs with him. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "As for Abu Jahm, he does not lay down his staff from his shoulder." This is from the hadith of Fatimah bint Qays, when she came to the Prophet, ﷺ, and mentioned that Abu Jahm ibn Hudhayfah and Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan had proposed to her. He said: "As for Abu Jahm, he is a man who does not lift his staff from women; as for Mu'awiyah, he is a pauper with no wealth." [al-Tirmidhi] in one of the narrations. It is also narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said to a man whom he advised: "Do not lift your staff from your family; frighten them for the sake of God." Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated it, and al-Nasa'i recorded it. In this same meaning is his, ﷺ, saying: "Hang your whip where your family can see it." This has been mentioned before in Surat al-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 174].

Among its benefits is an alert to moving on from this world, as it was said to one of the ascetics: "Why do you walk with a staff when you are neither old nor sick?" He said: "I know that I am a traveller, that this is a house of departure, and that the staff is one of the tools of travel." One of the poets took this up and said:

I carried the staff, not because weakness made me carry it,
nor because I bent with old age,
but I bound myself to carrying it,
to make it known to myself that the one who stays is on a journey.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 19–23:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa."﴾ [20:19]. When Allah, may He be exalted, wished to train him in receiving prophethood and its obligations, He commanded him to throw down the staff. ﴿So he threw it down, O Musa﴾ [20:20]. Allah then transformed its attributes and qualities. It had been a staff with two prongs, and the two prongs became a mouth for it. It became a serpent ﴿moving swiftly﴾, meaning it moved about, walked, and swallowed stones. When Musa, peace be upon him, saw it, he saw it as a sign, so ﴿he turned and fled without looking back﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. [See vol. 13, p. 283.] Then Allah said to him: ﴿"Take it and do not fear"﴾ [20:21]. That was because ﴿he felt fear within himself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 67], meaning that what afflicts human beings befell him. It is narrated that Musa took hold of it with the sleeves of his robe, so he was forbidden from doing so. He then took it in his hand, and it became a staff as it was the first time, in its original form. Allah showed him this sign only so that he would not be alarmed by it when he threw it down before Pharaoh. It is said that after this, the staff would walk with him and converse with him, he would hang his loads on it, its two prongs would shine for him at night like a candle, and when he wished for water, the two prongs would turn like a bucket. When he desired a fruit, he would plant it in the ground and it would bear that fruit. It was also said that it was from the myrtle (ās) of Paradise. It was also said that Jibril brought it to him, and it was also said that it was an angel. It was said that Shu'ayb told him: "Take a staff from that house," and that staff came into his hand. It was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, which he brought down with him from Paradise. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then behold, it was a serpent moving swiftly﴾ [20:20]. Al-Nahhas said: it is permissible to read ﴿ḥayyatan﴾ in the accusative, as in the construction "I went out and behold, Zayd was sitting" (jālisan), in which the word is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The pause form is ﴿ḥayyah﴾ with the ha'. Al-sa'y (sa'y) means walking with speed and lightness. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it turned into a male serpent (thu'bān) that swallowed rocks and trees. When he saw it swallowing everything, he feared it and fled from it. It is also narrated from some of them that he feared it only because he knew what Adam had suffered from it. It was also said that when his Lord said to him: ﴿"Do not fear"﴾, his fear departed and his soul was so reassured that he put his hand into its mouth and seized its jaws.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We shall return it to its original form﴾ [20:21]. I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: the estimated meaning is "to its original form," like His saying: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning "from his people." He said: it is permissible.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And draw your hand to your side [janah]﴾ [20:22]. Outside the Qur'an, it is permissible to read ﴿ḍum﴾ with a fatha or a kasra on the mim, due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The fatha is better because it is lighter, and the kasra is the original form. The ḍamm is also permissible by imitation (ittibā'). The original form of ﴿yad﴾ is yadyun on the pattern of fa'l, as evidenced by ayd. Its diminutive is ﴿yuday﴾. Al-janāḥ means the upper arm (al-'aḍud), as stated by Mujahid. He said: ﴿ilā﴾ here means "beneath" (taḥta). Qutrub said: ﴿ilā janāḥika﴾ means "to your breast pocket (jayb)," and from this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"I press him to the chest and the janāḥ"

It was also said: it means "to your side (janb)," so the side was expressed by the word janāḥ, because it is inclined in the place of the wing. It was also said: it means "to your presence (ʻindika)." Muqatil said: ﴿ilā﴾ means "with" (ma'a), i.e., "with your janāḥ."

﴿Will come forth white, without harm﴾: without leprosy, a shining light that illuminates by night and day like the light of the sun and the moon, and even brighter. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others: it came forth as light, unlike its color. The word ﴿bayḍā'﴾ is in the accusative as a ḥāl. It does not take nunation (lā yanṣarif) because it contains two feminine suffixes (alifayi al-ta'nīth) which never leave it, so their constant presence serves as a second cause, and therefore it is not declined even when indefinite. These two differ from the ha' (ta' marbuta), because the ha' separates from the noun. The phrase ﴿min ghayri sū'﴾: the ﴿min﴾ is a complement (ṣila) of ﴿bayḍā'﴾, just as you say "it turned white (ibyaḍḍat) without harm."

﴿Another sign﴾ besides the staff. He drew his hand out from a Egyptian woolen garment (midra'a) he had, which had a radiance like the radiance of the sun, dazzling the sight. ﴿Ayatan﴾ is in the accusative as a badal (substitution, apposition) for ﴿bayḍā'﴾, as al-Akhfash said. Al-Nahhas said: this is a good opinion. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "We gave you another sign," or "We shall give you," because when He said ﴿will come forth white, without harm﴾, this indicated that He had already given him another sign.

﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [20:23]: meaning the greatest. It would have been more proper to say al-kabīrah, but He said ﴿al-kubrā﴾ to match the endings of the verses. It was also said that there is an implied element, meaning: "That We may show you of Our signs the greatest sign." The evidence for this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "The hand of Musa was the greatest of his signs."

When Allah, may He be exalted, wished to train him in receiving prophethood and its obligations, He commanded him to throw down the staff. ﴿So he threw it down, O Musa﴾ [20:20]. Allah then transformed its attributes and qualities. It had been a staff with two prongs, and the two prongs became a mouth for it. It became a serpent ﴿moving swiftly﴾, meaning it moved about, walked, and swallowed stones. When Musa, peace be upon him, saw it, he saw it as a sign, so ﴿he turned and fled without looking back﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. He then took it in his hand, and it became a staff as it was the first time, in its original form. Allah showed him this sign only so that he would not be alarmed by it when he threw it down before Pharaoh. It is said that after this, the staff would walk with him and converse with him, he would hang his loads on it, its two prongs would shine for him at night like a candle, and when he wished for water, the two prongs would turn like a bucket. When he desired a fruit, he would plant it in the ground and it would bear that fruit. It was also said that it was from the myrtle (ās) of Paradise. It was also said that Jibril brought it to him, and it was also said that it was an angel. It was said that Shu'ayb told him: "Take a staff from that house," and that staff came into his hand. It was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, which he brought down with him from Paradise. And Allah knows best.

The pause form is ﴿ḥayyah﴾ with the ha'. Al-sa'y (sa'y) means walking with speed and lightness. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it turned into a male serpent (thu'bān) that swallowed rocks and trees. When he saw it swallowing everything, he feared it and fled from it. It is also narrated from some of them that he feared it only because he knew what Adam had suffered from it. It was also said that when his Lord said to him: ﴿"Do not fear"﴾, his fear departed and his soul was so reassured that he put his hand into its mouth and seized its jaws.

"I press him to the chest and the janāḥ"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 24–35:**

Allah's words: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ When He had made Moses feel at ease with the staff and the hand, and had shown him what proves that he is a messenger, He commanded him to go to Pharaoh and to call him (to faith). The word "ṭagha" [20:24] means: he disobeyed, became arrogant, disbelieved, acted tyrannically, and exceeded the limit.

﴿He said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me, and ease my task for me, and loosen the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech, and appoint for me a minister from my family, Aaron, my brother."﴾ [20:25–30] He asked for help in conveying the message. It is said that Allah had informed him that He had strengthened Pharaoh's heart and that Pharaoh would not believe. Moses said: "My Lord, how can You command me to go to him when You have strengthened his heart?" Then an angel from the keepers of the wind came to him and said: "O Moses, set out to what Allah has commanded you." At that, Moses said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me" [20:25], meaning: widen it and illuminate it with faith and prophethood.

﴿And ease my task for me﴾ [20:26], meaning: make easy for me what You have commanded me of conveying the message to Pharaoh.

﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾ [20:27]. This refers to the incompetence in speech that was in him, from the ember of fire that (Gabriel) placed in his mouth when he was a child. Ibn Abbas said: there was a speech defect (rutta) in his tongue. This happened because one day he was in Pharaoh's lap as a child, and he slapped Pharaoh and took hold of his beard and plucked it. Pharaoh said to Asiya: "This is my enemy; bring the executioners." Asiya said: "Be patient, for he is a child who does not distinguish between things." Then she brought two basins; she put an ember in one and a jewel in the other. Gabriel took Moses' hand and placed it on the fire until he lifted an ember and put it in his mouth, on his tongue, and that became the speech defect. It is also narrated that his hand was burned, and Pharaoh strove to treat it but it did not heal. When (Moses) called (Pharaoh), he said: "Which Lord are you calling me to?" (Moses) said: "To the One who healed my hand, which you could not heal."

It is also reported from some of them: his hand was not healed only so that he would not put it into one bowl with Pharaoh, lest a bond of eating together be established between them.

Then scholars differed as to whether that speech defect was removed. It was said: it was removed, as evidenced by His words: "You have been granted your request, O Moses" [20:36]. It was also said: it was not entirely removed, as evidenced by His words, relating Pharaoh's speech: ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ [43:52]. And because (Moses) did not say: "Loosen all of my tongue," which indicates that some tightness remained in his tongue. It was also said: it was removed completely, as evidenced by His words: "You have been granted your request" [20:36]. Pharaoh said ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ [43:52] only because he knew of that impediment from his upbringing, and it had not been established to him that the affliction had been removed.

I say: this is open to scrutiny, because if that were the case, Pharaoh would not have said "and he can hardly express himself clearly" when Moses spoke to him in an eloquent and fluent tongue. And Allah knows best. It was also said that this knot arose in his tongue at the time of his intimate conversation with his Lord, so that he would not speak to anyone else except by His permission.

﴿That they may understand my speech﴾ [20:28], meaning: that they may act upon what I say to them and comprehend it. In the Arabic language, "fiqh" means understanding. An Arab bedouin said to Isa ibn Umar: "I testify against you for fiqh." From it one says: "faqiha al-rajul" (with kasra), and "Fulan la yafqahu wa la yanqahu" (he does not know and does not comprehend). And "anqahtu al-hadith unqihu" means I understood the speech. And "afqahtuka al-shay'" means I made you understand the thing. Then fiqh was specialized to refer to the knowledge of the Sharia, and one who possesses it is a faqih. From it: "faqaha" with damma, "faqaha" as a noun; Allah made him faqih (granted him understanding), and "tafaqqaha" when he engaged in that. "Fa'qahtuhu" means I debated with him about knowledge, as al-Jawhari stated. The minister (wazir) is the one who supports, like the "akil" (table companion) and the "mu'akil", because he carries the sultan's burden (wizr), that is, his weight. In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad: I heard my aunt say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever among you is entrusted with a task, and Allah wills good for him, He will give him a righteous minister: if he forgets, the minister reminds him, and if he remembers, the minister helps him." And in this meaning is his statement, peace be upon him: "Allah did not send any prophet nor appoint any caliph except that he had two inner circles: an inner circle that commands him to good and urges him toward it, and an inner circle that commands him to evil and urges him toward it. The one protected is he whom Allah protects." Narrated by al-Bukhari. Moses therefore asked Allah, may He be exalted, to make a minister for him, but he did not want it to be restricted to a ministry alone, so that he would not be a partner to him in prophethood. Had it not been for that, it would have been permissible for him to appoint him as minister without asking.

He specified and said "Aaron" (Harun), and it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for his words "minister." Or it may be in the accusative governed by "ij'al" (appoint), by way of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the sense is: "Appoint for me Aaron, my brother, as minister." Aaron was one year older than Moses, and it was said: three years.

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ [20:31], meaning: my back, and "al-azr" is the back from the position of the waist. The meaning is: my self is strengthened through him. "Al-azr" means strength, and "azarahu" means he strengthened him. From it is His words: ﴿so he strengthened it and it became thick﴾ [48:29]. Abu Talib said: (this line is from a poem of his, which he composed concerning the matter of the Shi'b and the document):

"Did not our father Hashim strengthen his back,
and enjoin his sons to thrust and to strike?"

It was also said: "al-azr" means help, that is, he would be a help through which my affair is set right. The poet said:

"I strengthened my back through him, and I was certain that he
is a brother of poverty, one whose ways are straitened upon him."

Aaron was heavier in flesh than Moses, fuller in stature, fairer in complexion, and more eloquent in tongue. He died three years before Moses. There was a mole on Aaron's forehead, and on the tip of Moses' nose a mole, and on the tip of his tongue a mole; none had such before him, and none will have it after him. It was said that these were the cause of the knot that was in his tongue. And Allah knows best.

﴿And make him a partner in my affair﴾ [20:32], meaning: in prophethood and in conveying the message. The exegetes said: Aaron was in Egypt at that time. Allah commanded Moses to go to Aaron, and He revealed to Aaron, while he was in Egypt, to go out to meet Moses. He met him one stage (marhala) away and informed him of what had been revealed to him. Moses said to him: "Allah has commanded me to go to Pharaoh, and I asked my Lord to make you a messenger with me."

The majority of readers recited "akhi ushdud" with the alif connected (wasl). "Wa ashrikhu" [20:32] with a fatha on the hamza, as a supplication: that is, "Strengthen, O Lord, my back, and make him a partner with me in my affair." Ibn Amir, Yahya ibn al-Harith, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan, and Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq recited "ashuddu" with the alif cut (qat') and "wa ashrikhu" with a damma on the alif, meaning: "I do that: I strengthen my back through him, and I make him a partner in my affair, O Lord." Al-Nahhas said: they made the two verbs in the jussive position as an answer to His words "appoint for me a minister" [20:29]. This reading is anomalous and remote, because the answer to such a construction is only properly understood in the sense of a condition and a consequence, so the meaning would be: "If You appoint for me a minister from my family, I will strengthen my back through him and make him a partner in my affair." And his affair is prophethood and messengership, and this is not in his (Moses') hands, so that he could report it; rather he asked Allah, mighty and majestic, to make him a partner with him in prophethood. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr made the ya' of "akhi" fatha.

﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ [20:33]. It was said: the meaning of "nusabbihaka" [20:33] is "nusalli laka" (we pray to You). It may also be that glorification is by the tongue, that is, we declare You far above what is not fitting to Your majesty. "Kathiran" is an attribute of a verbal noun that is omitted. It may also be an attribute of a time. The idgham (assimilation of letters) is good. Likewise: ﴿and remember You much﴾ [20:34].

﴿Indeed You are ever, of us, Seeing﴾ [20:35]. Al-Khattabi said: "al-basir" can mean one who sees, and "al-basir" can also mean one who knows hidden matters. So the meaning is: knowing of us, and perceiving us in our youth, so You were good to us; so be good to us likewise, O Lord.
