Then an angel from the keepers of the wind came to him and said: "O Moses, set out to what Allah has commanded you." At that, Moses said: "My Lord, expand my breast for me" [20:25], meaning: widen it and illuminate it with faith and prophethood.

﴿And ease my task for me﴾ [20:26], meaning: make easy for me what You have commanded me of conveying the message to Pharaoh.

﴿And loosen the knot from my tongue﴾ [20:27]. This refers to the incompetence in speech that was in him, from the ember of fire that (Gabriel) placed in his mouth when he was a child. Ibn Abbas said: there was a speech defect (rutta) in his tongue. This happened because one day he was in Pharaoh's lap as a child, and he slapped Pharaoh and took hold of his beard and plucked it. Pharaoh said to Asiya: "This is my enemy; bring the executioners." Asiya said: "Be patient, for he is a child who does not distinguish between things." Then she brought two basins; she put an ember in one and a jewel in the other. Gabriel took Moses' hand and placed it on the fire until he lifted an ember and put it in his mouth, on his tongue, and that became the speech defect. It is also narrated that his hand was burned, and Pharaoh strove to treat it but it did not heal. When (Moses) called (Pharaoh), he said: "Which Lord are you calling me to?" (Moses) said: "To the One who healed my hand, which you could not heal."

It is also reported from some of them: his hand was not healed only so that he would not put it into one bowl with Pharaoh, lest a bond of eating together be established between them.

Then scholars differed as to whether that speech defect was removed. It was said: it was removed, as evidenced by His words: "You have been granted your request, O Moses" [20:36]. It was also said: it was not entirely removed, as evidenced by His words, relating Pharaoh's speech: ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ [43:52]. And because (Moses) did not say: "Loosen all of my tongue," which indicates that some tightness remained in his tongue. It was also said: it was removed completely, as evidenced by His words: "You have been granted your request" [20:36]. Pharaoh said ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ [43:52] only because he knew of that impediment from his upbringing, and it had not been established to him that the affliction had been removed.

I say: this is open to scrutiny, because if that were the case, Pharaoh would not have said "and he can hardly express himself clearly" when Moses spoke to him in an eloquent and fluent tongue. And Allah knows best. It was also said that this knot arose in his tongue at the time of his intimate conversation with his Lord, so that he would not speak to anyone else except by His permission.

﴿That they may understand my speech﴾ [20:28], meaning: that they may act upon what I say to them and comprehend it. In the Arabic language, "fiqh" means understanding. An Arab bedouin said to Isa ibn Umar: "I testify against you for fiqh." From it one says: "faqiha al-rajul" (with kasra), and "Fulan la yafqahu wa la yanqahu" (he does not know and does not comprehend). And "anqahtu al-hadith unqihu" means I understood the speech. And "afqahtuka al-shay'" means I made you understand the thing. Then fiqh was specialized to refer to the knowledge of the Sharia, and one who possesses it is a faqih. From it: "faqaha" with damma, "faqaha" as a noun; Allah made him faqih (granted him understanding), and "tafaqqaha" when he engaged in that. "Fa'qahtuhu" means I debated with him about knowledge, as al-Jawhari stated. The minister (wazir) is the one who supports, like the "akil" (table companion) and the "mu'akil", because he carries the sultan's burden (wizr), that is, his weight. In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad: I heard my aunt say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever among you is entrusted with a task, and Allah wills good for him, He will give him a righteous minister: if he forgets, the minister reminds him, and if he remembers, the minister helps him." And in this meaning is his statement, peace be upon him: "Allah did not send any prophet nor appoint any caliph except that he had two inner circles: an inner circle that commands him to good and urges him toward it, and an inner circle that commands him to evil and urges him toward it. The one protected is he whom Allah protects." Narrated by al-Bukhari. Moses therefore asked Allah, may He be exalted, to make a minister for him, but he did not want it to be restricted to a ministry alone, so that he would not be a partner to him in prophethood. Had it not been for that, it would have been permissible for him to appoint him as minister without asking.

He specified and said "Aaron" (Harun), and it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for his words "minister." Or it may be in the accusative governed by "ij'al" (appoint), by way of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the sense is: "Appoint for me Aaron, my brother, as minister." Aaron was one year older than Moses, and it was said: three years.

﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ [20:31], meaning: my back, and "al-azr" is the back from the position of the waist. The meaning is: my self is strengthened through him. "Al-azr" means strength, and "azarahu" means he strengthened him. From it is His words: ﴿so he strengthened it and it became thick﴾ [48:29]. Abu Talib said: (this line is from a poem of his, which he composed concerning the matter of the Shi'b and the document):

"Did not our father Hashim strengthen his back,
and enjoin his sons to thrust and to strike?"

It was also said: "al-azr" means help, that is, he would be a help through which my affair is set right. The poet said:

"I strengthened my back through him, and I was certain that he
is a brother of poverty, one whose ways are straitened upon him."

Aaron was heavier in flesh than Moses, fuller in stature, fairer in complexion, and more eloquent in tongue. He died three years before Moses. There was a mole on Aaron's forehead, and on the tip of Moses' nose a mole, and on the tip of his tongue a mole; none had such before him, and none will have it after him. It was said that these were the cause of the knot that was in his tongue. And Allah knows best.

﴿And make him a partner in my affair﴾ [20:32], meaning: in prophethood and in conveying the message. The exegetes said: Aaron was in Egypt at that time. Allah commanded Moses to go to Aaron, and He revealed to Aaron, while he was in Egypt, to go out to meet Moses. He met him one stage (marhala) away and informed him of what had been revealed to him. Moses said to him: "Allah has commanded me to go to Pharaoh, and I asked my Lord to make you a messenger with me."

The majority of readers recited "akhi ushdud" with the alif connected (wasl). "Wa ashrikhu" [20:32] with a fatha on the hamza, as a supplication: that is, "Strengthen, O Lord, my back, and make him a partner with me in my affair." Ibn Amir, Yahya ibn al-Harith, Abu Haywa, al-Hasan, and Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq recited "ashuddu" with the alif cut (qat') and "wa ashrikhu" with a damma on the alif, meaning: "I do that: I strengthen my back through him, and I make him a partner in my affair, O Lord." Al-Nahhas said: they made the two verbs in the jussive position as an answer to His words "appoint for me a minister" [20:29]. This reading is anomalous and remote, because the answer to such a construction is only properly understood in the sense of a condition and a consequence, so the meaning would be: "If You appoint for me a minister from my family, I will strengthen my back through him and make him a partner in my affair." And his affair is prophethood and messengership, and this is not in his (Moses') hands, so that he could report it; rather he asked Allah, mighty and majestic, to make him a partner with him in prophethood. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr made the ya' of "akhi" fatha.

﴿That we may glorify You much﴾ [20:33]. It was said: the meaning of "nusabbihaka" [20:33] is "nusalli laka" (we pray to You). It may also be that glorification is by the tongue, that is, we declare You far above what is not fitting to Your majesty. "Kathiran" is an attribute of a verbal noun that is omitted. It may also be an attribute of a time. The idgham (assimilation of letters) is good. Likewise: ﴿and remember You much﴾ [20:34].

﴿Indeed You are ever, of us, Seeing﴾ [20:35]. Al-Khattabi said: "al-basir" can mean one who sees, and "al-basir" can also mean one who knows hidden matters. So the meaning is: knowing of us, and perceiving us in our youth, so You were good to us; so be good to us likewise, O Lord.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 36–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Musa."﴾ [20:36] When he asked Him to expand his breast and to ease the matter in the manner he mentioned, He answered his request and granted him his petition and his desire. The su'l (request) is the talab (demand), a fu'l in the sense of maf'ul, like your saying khubz (bread) meaning makhbuz (baked), and ukl (food) meaning ma'kul (eaten).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already bestowed a favour upon you another time﴾ [20:37], i.e., before this, which was His protection of him from the evil of the enemies at the beginning, and that was at the time of the slaughter [of infants]. And Allah knows best. The mann (favour) is benevolence and bounty.

His saying: (When We inspired to your mother that which is inspired) [20:38]. It is said: "awhayna" means "alhamna" (We inspired/caused to intuit). It is also said: He inspired her during sleep. Ibn Abbas [may Allah be pleased with them both] said: He inspired her just as He inspired the Prophets.

(Saying: "Cast him into the chest") [20:39]. Muqatil said: The believer of Pharaoh's family is the one who made the chest and carpentered it, and his name was Hizqil. The chest was made of sycamore (jumayz).

(Then let the river throw him ashore) [20:39], i.e., cast him into the sea: the river, the Nile.

(fa-l-yulqihi) [20:39]. Al-Farra' said: "fa-qdhifihi fi l-yamm" [20:39] is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: i.e., cast him, and the sea will throw him up. Similarly His saying: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12] [see vol. 13, p. 330 onward].

(so that an enemy to Me and an enemy to him shall take him) [20:39], meaning Pharaoh. So she made a chest, placed in it a felt rug, put Musa in it, sealed its head and its cracks (khisasahu, i.e., its fissures) with pitch, then cast it into the Nile. A great river branched off from it into Pharaoh's house, and Allah carried him along in that river to Pharaoh's house. It is also reported that she placed in the chest carded cotton, put him in it, sealed it with pitch and plastered it with gypsum, then cast it into the sea. A great river branched from it to Pharaoh's garden, and while he was sitting at the edge of a pool with Asiya, behold, there was the chest; he ordered it brought out, it was opened, and there was the most beautiful child of people. The enemy of Allah loved him with an intense love, so that he could not bear to be parted from him. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the sea cast him onto its shore, which is its bank, and Pharaoh saw the chest on the shore and ordered it taken. It is possible that the casting of the sea occurred at a point on the shore where there was the mouth (fuwwahu) of a valley, i.e., the mouth of Pharaoh's river, and then the river carried it to where the pool was. And Allah knows best. It is also said: Pharaoh's daughter found him, and she had leprosy; when she opened the chest she was cured. It is also reported that when they picked up the chest they tried to open it but could not, and they tried to break it but were unable; then Asiya drew near and saw a light inside the chest, so she worked at it and opened it, and there was a child whose light was between his eyes, sucking his thumb for milk, and they loved him. Pharaoh had a leprous daughter, and the physicians told him: "She will not be healed except from the direction of the sea, where there is found a figure of a human whose saliva is her cure." So the leprous girl smeared her leprosy with his saliva and was healed. It is also said: when she looked at his face she was healed. And Allah knows best. It is also said: the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife found him, and when Pharaoh looked at him he saw a child of the most beautiful face of people, and Pharaoh loved him. This is His saying, exalted is He: (And I cast upon you love from Me) [20:39]. Ibn Abbas said: Allah loved him and made him beloved to His creation. Ibn Atiyya said: He placed upon him a radiance of beauty such that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be parted from him. Qatadah said: there was in the eyes of Musa a comeliness such that no one who saw him failed to love him and become enamoured. Ikrimah said: the meaning is: I placed in you beauty and comeliness, so no one sees you without loving you. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: I cast upon you My mercy. Ibn Zayd said: I made whoever saw you love you, until Pharaoh loved you and you were saved from his evil, and Asiya bint Muzahim loved you and adopted you.

(And that you might be reared under My eye) [20:39]. Ibn Abbas said: this means that it was under My eye where you were placed in the chest, where the chest was cast into the sea, and where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife picked you up. They wanted to open the chest to see what was in it. One of them said: Do not open it until you bring it to your mistress, for that will be more favourable to you with her, and more fitting so that she does not accuse you of having found something in it and taken it for yourselves. Pharaoh's wife would drink water only that those maidservants had drawn. So they took the chest to her sealed. When she opened it, she saw a child the like of whom had never been seen, and his love was cast upon her; she took him and went in with him to Pharaoh, and said to him: (A delight of the eye for me and for you) [al-Qasas: 9] [see vol. 13, p. 250 onward]. Pharaoh said to her: As for you, yes; as for me, no. It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If Pharaoh had said yes, that he is a delight of the eye for me and for you, he would have believed and affirmed." She said: Give him to me and do not kill him, so he gave him to her. It is also said: "And that you might be reared under My eye" means: that you be raised and nourished in My sight, as Qatadah said. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language; it is said: sana'tu al-faras and asna'tu when I tended the horse well. The meaning is: "And that you might be reared under My eye" [20:39], I did that. It is also said: the lam is connected to what follows it, His saying: "When your sister walked" [20:40], by way of fronting and postponement, and "idh" is an adverbial complement of tusna'a. It is also said: the waw in "wa-li-tusna'a" is superfluous. Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "wa-litusna'" with a sukun on the lam as an imperative, and its apparent address is to the one addressed while the one commanded is absent. Abu Nuhayk read "wa-litasna'a" with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning is: that your movement and conduct be by My will and under My eye. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. "When your sister walked" [20:40]: the governing element for "idh tamshi" [20:40] is "alqaytu" or "tusna'a". It is permissible that it be a substitute for "idh awhayna" [20:38]. His sister's name was Maryam.

(Then she said: "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?") That is because she went out seeking news of him. When Pharaoh had given him to his wife, they sought wet-nurses for him, but he would not take from anyone until his sister came; she took him, placed him in her lap, offered him her breast, and he sucked and rejoiced in her. They said to her: "Will you stay with us?" She said: "Indeed, I have no milk, but I will direct you to one who will nurse him, and they are sincere to him." They said: "Who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "The milk of my brother Harun." Harun was one year older than Musa. It is also said: three years; it is also said: four years, because Pharaoh had pity on the Children of Israel and lifted the killing from them for four years, and Harun was born in that period, as Ibn Abbas said. So the mother came and he took her breast. This is His saying, exalted is He: (So We returned you to your mother) [20:40]. In the Mushaf of Ubayy it reads: "fa-radadnaka".

(So that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve). Abd al-Hamid reported from Ibn Amir "kay taqarra 'aynuha" with a kasra on the qaf. Al-Jawhari said: qarirtu bihi 'aynan, and qarartu bihi qurratan and qururan in both. A man is qarir al-'ayn, and his eye has become cool (qarrat 'aynuhu, taqirru and taqurru), the opposite of "sakhunat". And Allah made his eye cool, i.e., gave him until it cooled so that he would not look longingly at someone above him; and it is said: until it becomes cold and not hot. For joy there is a cool tear, and for grief a hot tear. This meaning has already been discussed in (Maryam) [see p. 81 onward of this part]. "And that she would not grieve": i.e., over your loss.

(And you killed a person) [20:40]. Ibn Abbas said: he killed a Coptic unbeliever. Ka'b said: he was then twelve years old. In the Sahih of Muslim: his killing was by mistake, as will come.

(And We delivered you from distress) [20:40], i.e., We secured you from fear, killing and imprisonment.

(And We tried you with a trial) [20:40], i.e., We tested you with a test until you became fit for the message. Qatadah said: We afflicted you with an affliction. Mujahid: We made you sincere with sincerity. Ibn Abbas said: We tested you with things before the message; the first of them: his mother carried him in the year when Pharaoh was slaughtering the infants; then his being cast into the sea; then his being prevented from nursing except from his mother's breast; then his pulling at Pharaoh's beard; then his taking the coal instead of the pearl, whereby Pharaoh's killing of him was averted; then his killing of the Copt and his going out in fear, watching; then his tending of the sheep so that he would train himself in tending people. It is said that a kid of the sheep bolted from him, and he followed it for most of the day and tired himself out; then he caught it, kissed it, and pressed it to his chest, saying: "You have tired me, and you have pursued yourself," and he did not become angry with it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: for this reason Allah took him as a Kalim (one who speaks with Him), and this has passed in (al-Nisa') [see vol. 6, p. 18].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ [20:40].

He means ten years, fulfilling the better of the two terms. Wahb said: he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years, of which ten were the dowry for his wife Safura, daughter of Shu'ayb, and eighteen were his stay with him until a child was born to him there. And His saying: (Then you came according to a decree, O Musa) [20:40]. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan said: he means: in agreement with prophethood and messagehood, because prophets are sent only at the age of forty. Mujahid and Muqatil said: "ala qadar" means "ala wa'd" (according to a promise). Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: then you came according to the measure that We had decreed for you, that you would come in it. The meaning is one: you came at the time when We intended to send you. The poet said:

He attained the caliphate, or it was for him a decree, as Musa came to his Lord according to a measure.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾ [20:41]. Ibn Abbas said: i.e., I chose you for My revelation and My message. It is said: "istana'tuka" means "khalaqtuka" (I created you), derived from sun'ah (craft). It is also said: I strengthened you and taught you so that you might convey My command and My prohibition to My servants.

(Go, you and your brother, with My signs) [20:42]. Ibn Abbas said: he means the nine signs that were sent down upon him.

(And do not be slack in remembering Me) [20:42]. Ibn Abbas said: do not weaken, i.e., in the matter of the message, and Qatadah said the same. It is also said: do not slacken. The poet said: [it is al-Ajjaj]:

"Muhammad did not weaken since Allah forgave him what had passed and what remained."

Al-wana is weakness and languor, fatigue and exhaustion, and all of this is intended in the verse [from b, j, and y]. Imru' al-Qays said:

Swift-running, when the racing ones grow weary, they raise dust with the hard ground of Kadid...

It is said: wanaytu fi al-amr, anni wanan and wanyan, meaning I became weak; so I am wan, and a she-camel is wanyah; and awnaytuha, I weakened and tired her. And "fulan la yani kadha" means he does not cease doing such-and-such. Aban interpreted the verse this way and cited the words of Tarafa:

As though the great cauldrons before them were domes that they built, never ceasing to boil.

It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: do not delay. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la tahina fi dhikri", and [in it] My praise, My glorification and the conveying of My message.

They said to her: "Will you stay with us?" She said: "Indeed, I have no milk, but I will direct you to one who will nurse him, and they are sincere to him." They said: "Who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "The milk of my brother Harun." Harun was one year older than Musa. (fa-l-yulqihi) [20:39]. Al-Farra' said: "fa-qdhifihi fi l-yamm" [20:39] is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: i.e., cast him, and the sea will throw him up. Similarly His saying: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12] [see vol. 13, p. 330 onward].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already bestowed a favour upon you another time﴾ [20:37], i.e., before this, which was His protection of him from the evil of the enemies at the beginning, and that was at the time of the slaughter [of infants]. (Saying: "Cast him into the chest") [20:39]. Muqatil said: The believer of Pharaoh's family is the one who made the chest and carpentered it, and his name was Hizqil. The chest was made of sycamore (jumayz).

(Then let the river throw him ashore) [20:39], i.e., cast him into the sea: the river, the Nile.

(fa-l-yulqihi) [20:39]. Al-Farra' said: "fa-qdhifihi fi l-yamm" [20:39] is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: i.e., cast him, and the sea will throw him up. Similarly His saying: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12] [see vol. 13, p. 330 onward].

(so that an enemy to Me and an enemy to him shall take him) [20:39], meaning Pharaoh. Qatadah said: there was in the eyes of Musa a comeliness such that no one who saw him failed to love him and become enamoured. Ikrimah said: the meaning is: I placed in you beauty and comeliness, so no one sees you without loving you. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: I cast upon you My mercy. Ibn Zayd said: I made whoever saw you love you, until Pharaoh loved you and you were saved from his evil, and Asiya bint Muzahim loved you and adopted you.

"Muhammad did not weaken since Allah forgave him what had passed and what remained."

Al-wana is weakness and languor, fatigue and exhaustion, and all of this is intended in the verse [from b, j, and y]. Imru' al-Qays said:

Swift-running, when the racing ones grow weary, they raise dust with the hard ground of Kadid...

It is said: wanaytu fi al-amr, anni wanan and wanyan, meaning I became weak; so I am wan, and a she-camel is wanyah; and awnaytuha, I weakened and tired her. And "fulan la yani kadha" means he does not cease doing such-and-such. Aban interpreted the verse this way and cited the words of Tarafa:

As though the great cauldrons before them were domes that they built, never ceasing to boil.

It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: do not delay. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la tahina fi dhikri", and [in it] My praise, My glorification and the conveying of My message.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 36–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Musa."﴾ [20:36] When he asked Him to expand his breast and to ease the matter in the manner he mentioned, He answered his request and granted him his petition and his desire. The su'l (request) is the talab (demand), a fu'l in the sense of maf'ul, like your saying khubz (bread) meaning makhbuz (baked), and ukl (food) meaning ma'kul (eaten).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already bestowed a favour upon you another time﴾ [20:37], i.e., before this, which was His protection of him from the evil of the enemies at the beginning, and that was at the time of the slaughter [of infants]. And Allah knows best. The mann (favour) is benevolence and bounty.

His saying: (When We inspired to your mother that which is inspired) [20:38]. It is said: "awhayna" means "alhamna" (We inspired/caused to intuit). It is also said: He inspired her during sleep. Ibn Abbas [may Allah be pleased with them both] said: He inspired her just as He inspired the Prophets.

(Saying: "Cast him into the chest") [20:39]. Muqatil said: The believer of Pharaoh's family is the one who made the chest and carpentered it, and his name was Hizqil. The chest was made of sycamore (jumayz).

(Then let the river throw him ashore) [20:39], i.e., cast him into the sea: the river, the Nile.

(fa-l-yulqihi) [20:39]. Al-Farra' said: "fa-qdhifihi fi l-yamm" [20:39] is an imperative with the meaning of a conditional: i.e., cast him, and the sea will throw him up. Similarly His saying: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12] [see vol. 13, p. 330 onward].

(so that an enemy to Me and an enemy to him shall take him) [20:39], meaning Pharaoh. So she made a chest, placed in it a felt rug, put Musa in it, sealed its head and its cracks (khisasahu, i.e., its fissures) with pitch, then cast it into the Nile. A great river branched off from it into Pharaoh's house, and Allah carried him along in that river to Pharaoh's house. It is also reported that she placed in the chest carded cotton, put him in it, sealed it with pitch and plastered it with gypsum, then cast it into the sea. A great river branched from it to Pharaoh's garden, and while he was sitting at the edge of a pool with Asiya, behold, there was the chest; he ordered it brought out, it was opened, and there was the most beautiful child of people. The enemy of Allah loved him with an intense love, so that he could not bear to be parted from him. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the sea cast him onto its shore, which is its bank, and Pharaoh saw the chest on the shore and ordered it taken. It is possible that the casting of the sea occurred at a point on the shore where there was the mouth (fuwwahu) of a valley, i.e., the mouth of Pharaoh's river, and then the river carried it to where the pool was. And Allah knows best. It is also said: Pharaoh's daughter found him, and she had leprosy; when she opened the chest she was cured. It is also reported that when they picked up the chest they tried to open it but could not, and they tried to break it but were unable; then Asiya drew near and saw a light inside the chest, so she worked at it and opened it, and there was a child whose light was between his eyes, sucking his thumb for milk, and they loved him. Pharaoh had a leprous daughter, and the physicians told him: "She will not be healed except from the direction of the sea, where there is found a figure of a human whose saliva is her cure." So the leprous girl smeared her leprosy with his saliva and was healed. It is also said: when she looked at his face she was healed. And Allah knows best. It is also said: the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife found him, and when Pharaoh looked at him he saw a child of the most beautiful face of people, and Pharaoh loved him. This is His saying, exalted is He: (And I cast upon you love from Me) [20:39]. Ibn Abbas said: Allah loved him and made him beloved to His creation. Ibn Atiyya said: He placed upon him a radiance of beauty such that whoever saw him could hardly bear to be parted from him. Qatadah said: there was in the eyes of Musa a comeliness such that no one who saw him failed to love him and become enamoured. Ikrimah said: the meaning is: I placed in you beauty and comeliness, so no one sees you without loving you. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: I cast upon you My mercy. Ibn Zayd said: I made whoever saw you love you, until Pharaoh loved you and you were saved from his evil, and Asiya bint Muzahim loved you and adopted you.

(And that you might be reared under My eye) [20:39]. Ibn Abbas said: this means that it was under My eye where you were placed in the chest, where the chest was cast into the sea, and where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife picked you up. They wanted to open the chest to see what was in it. One of them said: Do not open it until you bring it to your mistress, for that will be more favourable to you with her, and more fitting so that she does not accuse you of having found something in it and taken it for yourselves. Pharaoh's wife would drink water only that those maidservants had drawn. So they took the chest to her sealed. When she opened it, she saw a child the like of whom had never been seen, and his love was cast upon her; she took him and went in with him to Pharaoh, and said to him: (A delight of the eye for me and for you) [al-Qasas: 9] [see vol. 13, p. 250 onward]. Pharaoh said to her: As for you, yes; as for me, no. It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If Pharaoh had said yes, that he is a delight of the eye for me and for you, he would have believed and affirmed." She said: Give him to me and do not kill him, so he gave him to her. It is also said: "And that you might be reared under My eye" means: that you be raised and nourished in My sight, as Qatadah said. Al-Nahhas said: this is known in the language; it is said: sana'tu al-faras and asna'tu when I tended the horse well. The meaning is: "And that you might be reared under My eye" [20:39], I did that. It is also said: the lam is connected to what follows it, His saying: "When your sister walked" [20:40], by way of fronting and postponement, and "idh" is an adverbial complement of tusna'a. It is also said: the waw in "wa-li-tusna'a" is superfluous. Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "wa-litusna'" with a sukun on the lam as an imperative, and its apparent address is to the one addressed while the one commanded is absent. Abu Nuhayk read "wa-litasna'a" with a fatha on the ta'. The meaning is: that your movement and conduct be by My will and under My eye. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. "When your sister walked" [20:40]: the governing element for "idh tamshi" [20:40] is "alqaytu" or "tusna'a". It is permissible that it be a substitute for "idh awhayna" [20:38]. His sister's name was Maryam.

(Then she said: "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?") That is because she went out seeking news of him. When Pharaoh had given him to his wife, they sought wet-nurses for him, but he would not take from anyone until his sister came; she took him, placed him in her lap, offered him her breast, and he sucked and rejoiced in her. They said to her: "Will you stay with us?" She said: "Indeed, I have no milk, but I will direct you to one who will nurse him, and they are sincere to him." They said: "Who is she?" She said: "My mother." They said: "Does she have milk?" She said: "The milk of my brother Harun." Harun was one year older than Musa. It is also said: three years; it is also said: four years, because Pharaoh had pity on the Children of Israel and lifted the killing from them for four years, and Harun was born in that period, as Ibn Abbas said. So the mother came and he took her breast. This is His saying, exalted is He: (So We returned you to your mother) [20:40]. In the Mushaf of Ubayy it reads: "fa-radadnaka".

(So that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve). Abd al-Hamid reported from Ibn Amir "kay taqarra 'aynuha" with a kasra on the qaf. Al-Jawhari said: qarirtu bihi 'aynan, and qarartu bihi qurratan and qururan in both. A man is qarir al-'ayn, and his eye has become cool (qarrat 'aynuhu, taqirru and taqurru), the opposite of "sakhunat". And Allah made his eye cool, i.e., gave him until it cooled so that he would not look longingly at someone above him; and it is said: until it becomes cold and not hot. For joy there is a cool tear, and for grief a hot tear. This meaning has already been discussed in (Maryam) [see p. 81 onward of this part]. "And that she would not grieve": i.e., over your loss.

(And you killed a person) [20:40]. Ibn Abbas said: he killed a Coptic unbeliever. Ka'b said: he was then twelve years old. In the Sahih of Muslim: his killing was by mistake, as will come.

(And We delivered you from distress) [20:40], i.e., We secured you from fear, killing and imprisonment.

(And We tried you with a trial) [20:40], i.e., We tested you with a test until you became fit for the message. Qatadah said: We afflicted you with an affliction. Mujahid: We made you sincere with sincerity. Ibn Abbas said: We tested you with things before the message; the first of them: his mother carried him in the year when Pharaoh was slaughtering the infants; then his being cast into the sea; then his being prevented from nursing except from his mother's breast; then his pulling at Pharaoh's beard; then his taking the coal instead of the pearl, whereby Pharaoh's killing of him was averted; then his killing of the Copt and his going out in fear, watching; then his tending of the sheep so that he would train himself in tending people. It is said that a kid of the sheep bolted from him, and he followed it for most of the day and tired himself out; then he caught it, kissed it, and pressed it to his chest, saying: "You have tired me, and you have pursued yourself," and he did not become angry with it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: for this reason Allah took him as a Kalim (one who speaks with Him), and this has passed in (al-Nisa') [see vol. 6, p. 18].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ [20:40].

He means ten years, fulfilling the better of the two terms. Wahb said: he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years, of which ten were the dowry for his wife Safura, daughter of Shu'ayb, and eighteen were his stay with him until a child was born to him there. And His saying: (Then you came according to a decree, O Musa) [20:40]. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan said: he means: in agreement with prophethood and messagehood, because prophets are sent only at the age of forty. Mujahid and Muqatil said: "ala qadar" means "ala wa'd" (according to a promise). Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: then you came according to the measure that We had decreed for you, that you would come in it. The meaning is one: you came at the time when We intended to send you. The poet said:

He attained the caliphate, or it was for him a decree, as Musa came to his Lord according to a measure.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I chose you for Myself﴾ [20:41]. Ibn Abbas said: i.e., I chose you for My revelation and My message. It is said: "istana'tuka" means "khalaqtuka" (I created you), derived from sun'ah (craft). It is also said: I strengthened you and taught you so that you might convey My command and My prohibition to My servants.

(Go, you and your brother, with My signs) [20:42]. Ibn Abbas said: he means the nine signs that were sent down upon him.

(And do not be slack in remembering Me) [20:42]. Ibn Abbas said: do not weaken, i.e., in the matter of the message, and Qatadah said the same. It is also said: do not slacken. The poet said: [it is al-Ajjaj]:

"Muhammad did not weaken since Allah forgave him what had passed and what remained."

Al-wana is weakness and languor, fatigue and exhaustion, and all of this is intended in the verse [from b, j, and y]. Imru' al-Qays said:

As though the great cauldrons before them were domes that they built, never ceasing to boil.

It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: do not delay. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la tahina fi dhikri", and [in it] My praise, My glorification and the conveying of My message.

**First issue:** Concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Go, both of you﴾. In the beginning of the verse He said, "Go, you and your brother, with My signs," and here He said, "Go, both of you." It is said that Allah commanded Musa and Harun in this verse to proceed to call Pharaoh. He first addressed Musa alone, honouring him, and then repeated the command for emphasis. It is also said that this shows that the going of only one of them is not sufficient. And it is said that the first command is to go to all people, and the second is to go to Pharaoh.

**Second issue:** In His saying, Exalted is He: (But speak to him with gentle speech) [20:44], there is evidence for the permissibility of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and that this should be done with gentle speech toward one who has power and is assured of protection. Do you not see that He said: "But speak to him with gentle speech" [20:44], and He said: "Fear not. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see" [20:46]? So how about us, who are more deserving of this? In this way the one who enjoins or forbids attains what is desired and achieves his aim. This is clear.

**Third issue:** People differed regarding the meaning of His saying (gentle). A group, including al-Kalbi and Ikrimah, said: its meaning is that he should be given a kunyah (teknonym). This was also said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. Then it was said: his kunyah was Abu al-Abbas. It was also said: Abu al-Walid. And it was said: Abu Murrah. According to this view, addressing an unbeliever by a kunyah is permissible if he is distinguished and of noble rank and there is hope for his Islam. It may also be permissible even if there is no hope for his Islam, because hope is not a reality that necessitates action. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the noble man of a people comes to you, honour him," and he did not say, "even if you hope for his Islam." Among honouring is calling him by his kunyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Safwan ibn Umayyah: "Descend, Abu Wahb," and he gave him his kunyah. And he said to Sa'd: "Did you not hear what Abu Hubab says?" meaning Abdullah ibn Ubayy. It is narrated in the Israiliyyat (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources) that Musa, peace be upon him, stood at the gate of Pharaoh for a year, not finding a messenger to convey his words, until he went out. What he encountered is what Allah has related to us of that. This was a consolation for those believers who came after him concerning their conduct with the wrongdoers, "and your Lord knows best who are guided." It was also said that Musa said to him: "Believe in what I have brought, and worship the Lord of the worlds, and you will have a youth that does not age until death, and a kingdom that will not be taken from you until death, and your term will be extended four hundred years, and when you die you will enter Paradise." This is the gentle speech. Ibn Mas'ud said: the gentle speech is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then say, "Would you like to purify yourself, and I will guide you to your Lord so you would fear Him?"﴾ [79:18-19]. It has also been said that the gentle speech is Musa's saying: "O Pharaoh, indeed we are two messengers of your Lord, the Lord of the worlds." He named it thus because it was more beloved to him than anything else said to him, as we call a king and similar titles.

I say: gentle speech is speech in which there is no harshness. It is said: "the thing became soft (laana yalinu linan)," and "a thing is layyin (soft), and layn is its lightened form, and the plural is alyina'." If Musa was commanded to say to Pharaoh a gentle speech, then whoever is below him is more worthy of following that in his address and in enjoining good in his speech. Allah, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾ [2:83], as has been explained previously in al-Baqarah, and all praise is due to Allah.

**Fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [20:44]. Its meaning is: in your hope and your expectation. The expectation in it refers only to the side of the humans. This was stated by the great grammarians, including Sibawayh and others. This has been discussed previously at the beginning of al-Baqarah [1/227]. Al-Zajjaj said: "la'alla" (perhaps) is a word of expectation and hope, so He addressed them in terms they understand. It has been said that "la'alla" here has the meaning of a question, and the meaning is: "look and see whether he remembers." It has also been said that it means "kay" (so that). It was also said: it is a report from Allah, Exalted is He, of Harun's statement to Musa: "perhaps he will remember or fear," as al-Hasan said. And it has been said: "la'alla" and "'asa" throughout the Qur'an refer to what has already occurred. Pharaoh did remember when drowning overtook him and he feared, and he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [10:90] [see vol. 8, p. 377 ff.]. But that did not benefit him, as said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq and others. Yahya ibn Mu'adh said concerning this verse: "This is your gentleness toward one who says 'I am the god'; so how would your gentleness be toward one who says 'you are the god'?!" It was also said that Pharaoh inclined to the word of Musa when he called him, and he consulted his wife, and she believed and advised him to believe. Then he consulted Haman, who said: "Do not do it; after you were a possessor you will become a possessed, and after you were a lord you will become one who is lorded over." And he said to him: "I will return you young," so he dyed his beard black, and he was the first to dye.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ [20:45]

Al-Dahhak said: "yafruta" (يَفْرُطَ) means "yu'jila," (he hastens). He said: "yatgha" (يَطْغَى) means "ya'tadi" (he oversteps).

Al-Nahhas said: The implied meaning is "nakhafu an yafruta 'alayna minhu amr" (we fear that some matter will come upon us from him). Al-Farra' said: "faraṭa minhu amr," meaning "badara" (it escaped from him, i.e., it happened hastily). He said: "wa-afrata" means "asraf" (he exceeded). He said: "wa-farraṭa" means "taraka" (he neglected).

The reading of the majority is "yafruṭa" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra', and its meaning is "ya'jalu wa-yubadiru bi-'uqubatina" (he hastens and rushes to punish us). It is said: "faraṭa minni amr," meaning "badara" (a matter escaped from me). From this comes "al-farit" in reference to water, the one who goes ahead of the people to the water; that is, "yu'adhdhibuna 'adhab al-farit fi al-dhanb," (he punishes us with the punishment of one who goes ahead in sin), and this is the one who precedes in it, as stated by al-Mubarrad.

A group of reciters, among them Ibn Muhaysin, read "yafraṭa" with a fatha on the ya' and the ra'. Al-Mahdawi said: "Perhaps it is a dialect." And from him also, with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ra', meaning that a driver of haste carries him toward us.

A group read "yufriṭa" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', and with it Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Muhaysin also read. Its meaning is "yushtiṭu fi adhiyyatina" (he exceeds the bounds in harming us). The rajaz poet said:

*Qad afrata al-'ilju 'alayna wa-'ajal*
(The barbarian has exceeded against us and hastened.)

There are two issues here. The first: when the believers experienced the fear that human beings feel for their own lives, God, glory be to Him, informed them that Pharaoh and his people could not reach them. This verse refutes those who say that a prophet does not feel fear. Fear of enemies is God's way with His prophets and friends, even though they know Him and trust in Him. Al-Basri (may God have mercy on him) spoke well when he said to the one reporting about Amir ibn Abd Allah, who had stopped with his companions by a water source on the road to Syria when a lion came between them and the water. Amir went to the water and took what he needed. He was told, "You have risked your life." He said: "For the spearheads to break apart in my belly is dearer to me than for God to know that I fear anything other than Him." Someone better than Amir feared as well: Musa (peace be upon him), when he was told: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave; indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers.﴾ So he left from there, fearful and watchful. He said: ﴿My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people.﴾ [al-Qasas: 20–21] [See vol. 13, p. 264 onward.] And He said: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful and watchful.﴾ [al-Qasas: 18] [See vol. 13, p. 259.] He also said when the magicians threw down their ropes and staffs: ﴿So Musa sensed fear within himself. We said: Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 67–68]

I say: Among this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) digging of the trench around Madinah to protect the Muslims and their wealth. Although this was an expression of reliance and trust in his Lord, it reached a station that no one else had reached. Then there was what his companions did, which everyone knows: they moved from their homes, at one time to Abyssinia and at another time to Madinah, out of fear for themselves from the polytheists of Makkah, and to flee with their religion so that these polytheists would not turn them away from it through torture. Asma bint Umays said to Umar when he said, "We preceded you in the hijrah (migration), so we have more right to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) than you do": "You are lying, O Umar! No, by God, you were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who fed your hungry and taught your ignorant. We were in the house, or the land, of the distant (al-Bu'ada') and the hateful (al-Bughda') in Abyssinia, all for the sake of God and His Messenger. By God, I will not eat any food or drink any drink until I mention what you said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). We were harmed and we were afraid." The full hadith was narrated by Muslim.

[Note: al-Bu'ada' means distant in lineage; al-Bughda' means hated in religion. Asma's words "kadhabti ya Umar" mean "you erred," since the Arabs used kadhaba in the sense of "erred."]

The scholars said: Whoever reports about himself something contrary to what God has instilled in the souls of the children of Adam [is a liar] [[The addition is required by the context.]]. God has instilled in them the instinct to flee from what harms them, pains them, or destroys them. They said: No harm is greater than a hostile predator in a wilderness to someone who has no weapon with which to defend himself, such as a sword, spear, arrow, bow, or the like.

The second issue: God's statement ﴿Indeed, I am with you both﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46] means with help, support, and power over Pharaoh. This is like saying, "The commander is with so-and-so," when you mean that he protects him. His statement ﴿I hear and I see﴾ is an expression of perception by which nothing is hidden. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 47–50:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So go to him and say, "Indeed, we are the messengers of your Lord."﴾ [20:47] There is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: "So they went to him and said that to him."

(Send with us the Children of Israel.) [20:47] That is, release them.

(And do not torment them.) [20:47] That is, with forced labour and toil in work. The Children of Israel were under Pharaoh in severe torment: he slaughtered their sons, spared (istahya, read as yastahyi in one variant, meaning "kept alive") their women, and burdened them with work in clay and brick and the building of cities beyond what they could bear.

(We have come to you with a sign from your Lord.) [20:47] Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the staff and the hand. It is also said that Pharaoh asked him, "And what is it?" So he put his hand into the opening of his garment and then drew it out white, with a radiance like the radiance of the sun, its light overpowering the light of the sun, and Pharaoh was amazed by it. He did not show him the staff except on the Day of the Festival.

(And peace be upon whoever follows guidance.) [20:47] Al-Zajjaj said: that is, whoever follows guidance is safe from the wrath of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and from His punishment. He said: and it is not a greeting. The evidence for this is that it is not the opening of a meeting or an address.

Al-Farra' said: "Peace upon whoever follows guidance" and "for whoever follows guidance" are the same.

(Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment) meaning destruction and ruin in this world, and abiding in Hell in the Hereafter, (is upon whoever denies) the prophets of Allah (and turns away) from faith. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is the most hopeful verse for the monotheists, because they did not deny and did not turn away.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "Who then is the Lord of you both, O Musa?"﴾ [20:49] Pharaoh mentioned Musa and not Harun because of the ends of verses (ru'us al-ay, the rhyme endings of the verses). It is also said that he singled him out for mention because he was the bearer of the message, the speech and the sign. It is also said that both of them conveyed the message, even though one of them was silent, because at the time of speech only one speaks; when he stops, the other supports and strengthens him. Thus we have here a benefit of knowledge in this construction: when two people are entrusted with a matter, one of them carries it out while the other is present there, existing and not needed at a particular time rather than another, both of them have discharged the matter they were entrusted with and have earned the reward. This is because Allah the Exalted said: "Go, both of you, to Pharaoh" [20:43], and said: "Go, you and your brother" [20:42], and said: "Speak to him" [20:44]. So He commanded both of them to go and to speak. Then He informed us at the time of address, by His saying: "Who then is the Lord of you both" [20:49], that he was present with Musa.

(Musa) said: (Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation) [20:50]. That is, He is known by His attributes, and He has no proper name so that it could be said, "So-and-so." Rather, He is the Creator of the world, the One who endowed every created thing with its form and shape. Had the address been to both of them, they would have said: "Our Lord, we say." "Khalqahu" is the first of the two objects of "a'ta" (gave), meaning He gave His creatures everything they need and by which they are benefited; or the second, meaning He gave everything its form and shape that corresponds to the benefit attached to it, according to the view of al-Dahhak, as will come.

(Then guided) Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sudi said: He gave everything its mate of its own kind, then guided it to its mating, its food, its drink and its dwelling. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: then He guided it to companionship, gathering and marriage. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: He gave everything its well-being and guided it to what makes it well. Mujahid said: He gave everything its form; He did not make the creation of man like the creation of animals, nor the creation of animals like the creation of man, but He created everything and determined it with a measure. A poet said:

*For everything He has a form,*
*And thus Allah does whatever He wills.*

By "creation" (khilqah) he means the form, and this is the view of 'Ata' and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: He gave everything its creation of the benefit attached to it, corresponding to it, meaning the hand for seizing, the foot for walking, the tongue for speech, the eye for seeing, and the ear for hearing. It is also said: He gave everything what He inspired it with of knowledge or craft. Al-Farra' said: He created the man for the woman, and for every male what suits him of females, then He guided the male to the female. The estimate according to this is: He gave everything the like of its creation. I say: this is the meaning of the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The verse, by its generality, encompasses all these sayings.

Za'idah reported from al-A'mash that he recited "alladhi a'ta kulla shay'in khalqahu" with a fatha on the lam, and this is the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq. Nusayr reported it from al-Kisa'i and others, meaning: He gave the children of Adam everything He created for them of what they need. Thus the two readings agree in meaning.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 51–52:**

There are four issues concerning this passage.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿Said he, "Then what is the state of the former generations?"﴾ (20:51). *Al-bal* means *al-hal* (the state, condition), that is, "What is their state and what is their affair?" Moses was informed that knowledge of them is with God, meaning that this is from the knowledge of the unseen about which you have asked, and it is among the things God has reserved for Himself, and none knows it but Him. "I am only a servant like you, and I know of it only what the Knower of the unseen has told me." The knowledge of the circumstances of past generations is recorded with God in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*).

It has also been said that the meaning is: "What is the case with the earlier generations, that they did not acknowledge this?" That is, what happened to them that they perished while they worshipped other than your Lord?

It has also been said: he asked about the deeds of the earlier generations, and he was informed that they are counted with God and preserved with Him "in a Book," that is, they are written down, and He will reward them for them tomorrow. By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet. It has also been said that it is a book held by some of the angels.

**The second issue:** This verse and similar verses, both those already mentioned and those that will come, indicate the recording of knowledge and writing it down, lest it be forgotten, for memory is subject to afflictions such as error and forgetfulness. A person may not retain what he hears, so he records it so that it will not slip away from him.

We have related with a connected chain of transmission from Qatadah that it was said to him: "Shall we write down what we hear from you?" He said: "What prevents you from writing, when the All-Subtle, the All-Aware has informed you that He writes?" Then he recited: ﴿"Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets"﴾ (20:52).

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had finished creating the creation, He wrote in a Book, which is with Him, concerning Himself: 'My mercy prevails over My wrath.'"

Al-Khatib Abu Bakr narrated with a chain of transmission from Abu Hurairah, who said: A man from the Ansar used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ), listening to the hadith and being pleased with it, but he did not retain it. He complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I hear from you hadith that please me, but I do not retain them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Seek help from your right hand," and he gestured toward writing. This is an explicit text.

Most of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*) hold that writing down and recording knowledge is permissible. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that the sermon he delivered during the Hajj be written down for Abu Shah, a man from Yemen, when he asked for it. This is related by Muslim. It is also related that 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb reported from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Bind knowledge by writing it down." Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah said: "Whoever does not write down knowledge, his knowledge does not count as knowledge."

Some people held the prohibition of writing. Abu Nadrah [[So in the manuscripts B, T and Y, and this is correct. Abu Nadrah is al-Mundhir ibn Malik ibn Qut'ah.]] reported: It was said to Abu Sa'id: "Shall we write down this hadith of yours?" He said: "Why do you make it into Qur'an? Rather, memorize as we memorized."

Among those who did not write were al-Sha'bi, Yunus ibn 'Ubayd, Khalid al-Hadhdha' (who said: "I never wrote anything except one hadith, and when I had memorized it, I erased it"), Ibn 'Awn, and al-Zuhri. Some of them did write and then erased what they had memorized, among them Muhammad ibn Sirin and 'Asim ibn Damrah. Hisham ibn Hassan said: "I never wrote down a hadith except the hadith of al-A'maq [[al-A'maq: a place on the outskirts of Madinah; Dabiq: the name of a place, a market in it. The doubt is from the narrator.]], and when I had memorized it, I erased it." I say: We have already mentioned something similar from Khalid al-Hadhdha'. The hadith of al-A'maq is related by Muslim at the end of the book: "The Hour will not come until the Romans land at al-A'maq or at Dabiq." The hadith is mentioned in the Book of Tribulations.

Some of them would memorize and then write down what they had memorized, among them al-A'mash, 'Abd Allah ibn Idris, Hushaym, and others. This is a precaution for memorization. Writing is preferable in general, and the verses and hadiths have come in this form. This is also the view of al-Zajjaj, and that the meaning of "neither errs" (*la yadillu*) is "neither perishes," from the verse: ﴿"Shall we, when we have strayed in the earth..."﴾ (32:10). "Nor forgets" means He is exalted above perishing and forgetting anything.

The second opinion: "neither errs" (*la yadillu*) means "does not make a mistake." This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, meaning He makes no error in His management. Whoever He gives respite, He gives respite for a wisdom, and whoever He hastens, He hastens for a wisdom.

The third opinion: "neither errs" means "does not go absent." Ibn al-A'rabi said: The root of *dalal* is absence. It is said: "The forgetful person went astray (*dalla al-nasi*)" when the memory of a thing was absent from him. He said: the meaning of ﴿"My Lord neither errs nor forgets"﴾ is that nothing is absent from Him and He is not absent from anything.

The fourth opinion, also said by al-Zajjaj, and al-Nahhas said it is the most similar to the meaning: God the Mighty and Majestic informed that He does not need a book, and the meaning is that no knowledge of any thing escapes Him, nor its recognition, and He does not forget what He has known of them. I say: This opinion goes back to the meaning of Ibn al-A'rabi's statement.

The Arabs say: "The thing has lost me (*dallani*) when I did not find it, and I have lost it (*adlaltuhu*) when I left it in a place and you did not find it there."

It is said: "He went astray from the road (*dalla 'an al-tariq*)," and "he caused the thing to go astray (*adalla al-shay'*)" when he lost it. Moses was informed that knowledge of them is with God, meaning that this is from the knowledge of the unseen about which you have asked, and it is among the things God has reserved for Himself, and none knows it but Him. "I am only a servant like you, and I know of it only what the Knower of the unseen has told me." The knowledge of the circumstances of past generations is recorded with God in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*).

It has also been said that the meaning is: "What is the case with the earlier generations, that they did not acknowledge this?" That is, what happened to them that they perished while they worshipped other than your Lord?

It has also been said: he asked about the deeds of the earlier generations, and he was informed that they are counted with God and preserved with Him "in a Book," that is, they are written down, and He will reward them for them tomorrow. By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet. It has also been said that it is a book held by some of the angels.

A person may not retain what he hears, so he records it so that it will not slip away from him.

We have related with a connected chain of transmission from Qatadah that it was said to him: "Shall we write down what we hear from you?" He said: "What prevents you from writing, when the All-Subtle, the All-Aware has informed you that He writes?" The Almighty's saying: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾ [[(Mahdan) in the plural: the recitation of Nafi', and the original reading.]] "Alladhi" (who) is in the nominative case [[According to manuscripts B, J, Z, Y, K and Y.]] as a qualifier (na't) of "Rabbi" (my Lord), meaning: "My Lord does not go astray, He who made..." It may also be the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "He is the One who..." It may also be in the accusative case, with an implied verb "I mean" (a'ni).

The Kufans recited "mahdan" here and in "al-Zukhruf" with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha. The rest recited "mihadan," and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because they agree on the recitation of ﴿Did We not make the earth a cradle?﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 169 and following.]] [al-Naba': 6]. Al-Nahhas said: The plural is preferable, because "mahdan" is a verbal noun (masdar), and this is not a position for a verbal noun except with an ellipsis, meaning "possessor of a cradle." Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever recites "mahdan" may take it as a verbal noun, like "al-farsh" (spreading), meaning "He spread the earth for you as a spreading," and it may also be read with the omission of a modified noun, meaning "possessor of a cradle." Whoever recites "mihadan" may take it as a singular, like "al-firash" (bedding). It may also be the plural of "mahd," used as a noun and then broken into a plural. The meaning of "mihadan" is: a bed and a resting place on which you settle.

﴿And threaded for you therein roads﴾ [20: 53], that is, paths. Its parallel is ﴿And Allah made the earth a spread-out carpet for you, that you may traverse therein broad roads﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 306.]] [Nuh: 19–20]. This is the last of Musa's speech. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We brought forth thereby﴾. It is also said that all of it is from the speech of Musa. The meaning of ﴿thereby﴾ is: by means of tilling and cultivation, because the water sent down is the cause of the growth of plants. The meaning of ﴿pairs﴾ is: kinds and similitudes, that is, varieties of plants of different pairs and colours. Al-Akhfash said: The implied meaning is "diverse pairs of plants." He said: Plants may also be diverse, so "shatta" (diverse) may be an adjective of "pairs" and may also be an adjective of "plants." "Shatta" is derived from "shatta al-shay'," meaning it became scattered. It is said: "amr shatt," meaning a scattered matter. "Shatta al-amr shatan wa shatatan" means it scattered, and "ishtatta" is similar to it, and so is "tashattut." "Shattatahu tashtiyan" means he scattered it. "Ashatta bi qawmi" means my people scattered my affair. "Al-shatit" means the scattered one. Ru'bah said, describing camels:

They came together and bunched up scattered... and they stirred up the rising dust.
[[Al-sakhtit: fine dust, that is, the very high-rising dust. It is also narrated as "al-shakhtit" with a shin.]]

"Thaghr shatit" means a parted (widely spaced) mouth. "Qawm shatta" and "ashya' shatta" (diverse people, diverse things). It is said: "They came ashtatan," meaning scattered, whose singular is "shatt." This was said by al-Jawhari.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Eat, and pasture your cattle﴾ [20: 54] is a command of permission. "Wa-r'aw" (and pasture) comes from "ra'at al-mashiyah al-kala'" (the livestock grazed the pasture), and "ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan," meaning its owner pastured it, that is, let it loose and drove it out. It is intransitive and transitive.

﴿Surely in that are signs for people of intellect﴾ [[Ulu al-nuha]], that is, those of reason. The singular is "nuhyah." He said this to them because they are the ones to whose opinion one resorts. It is also said: because they restrain the self from vile deeds. All of this is from Musa, as an argument against Pharaoh for establishing the Creator, in answer to his saying: ﴿Who then is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ [20: 49]. He made clear that the Creator is only inferred today through His acts.

It is also said: every drop of semen is created from dust, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates this. Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no child born except that some of the dust of its grave has been scattered upon it." We did not write it except from the narration of Abu 'Asim al-Nabil, who is one of the reliable, distinguished people of Basra." This meaning has already been explained in detail in Surat al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 387 and following.]] from Ibn Mas'ud. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth once again﴾ [20: 55].

They say, 'So-and-so son of so-and-so,' using the best of the names by which they used to call him in the world. They ask for it to be opened, and it is opened. Those nearest to God from every heaven escort it to the heaven next to it, until it reaches the seventh heaven. "Shatta" is derived from "shatta al-shay'," meaning it became scattered. It is said: "amr shatt," meaning a scattered matter. "Shatta al-amr shatan wa shatatan" means it scattered, and "ishtatta" is similar to it, and so is "tashattut." "Shattatahu tashtiyan" means he scattered it. "Ashatta bi qawmi" means my people scattered my affair. "Al-shatit" means the scattered one. Ru'bah said, describing camels:

They came together and bunched up scattered... and they stirred up the rising dust.
[[Al-sakhtit: fine dust, that is, the very high-rising dust. It is also narrated as "al-shakhtit" with a shin.]]

"Thaghr shatit" means a parted (widely spaced) mouth. "Qawm shatta" and "ashya' shatta" (diverse people, diverse things). It is said: "They came ashtatan," meaning scattered, whose singular is "shatt." This was said by al-Jawhari.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Eat, and pasture your cattle﴾ [20: 54] is a command of permission. "Wa-r'aw" (and pasture) comes from "ra'at al-mashiyah al-kala'" (the livestock grazed the pasture), and "ra'aha sahibuha ri'ayatan," meaning its owner pastured it, that is, let it loose and drove it out. It is intransitive and transitive.

﴿Surely in that are signs for people of intellect﴾ [[Ulu al-nuha]], that is, those of reason. The singular is "nuhyah." He said this to them because they are the ones to whose opinion one resorts. It is also said: because they restrain the self from vile deeds. All of this is from Musa, as an argument against Pharaoh for establishing the Creator, in answer to his saying: ﴿Who then is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ [20: 49]. He made clear that the Creator is only inferred today through His acts.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿From it We created you﴾ [20: 55] means Adam, peace be upon him, because he was created from the earth. This was said by Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj and others. It is also said: every drop of semen is created from dust, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates this. Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no child born except that some of the dust of its grave has been scattered upon it." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz recorded it in the chapter on Ibn Sirin and said: "This is a strange (gharib) hadith from the narration of 'Awn. We did not write it except from the narration of Abu 'Asim al-Nabil, who is one of the reliable, distinguished people of Basra." This meaning has already been explained in detail in Surat al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 387 and following.]] from Ibn Mas'ud. Ata al-Khurasani said: When the drop enters the womb, the angel appointed over the womb goes and takes some dust from the place where the person will be buried, and scatters it upon the drop, and Allah creates the soul (nasamah) from the drop and from the dust. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth once again﴾ [20: 55].

In the hadith of al-Bara' from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the soul of the believing servant departs, the angels ascend with it, and they do not pass with it by any company of angels without them saying, 'What is this good soul?' They say, 'So-and-so son of so-and-so,' using the best of the names by which they used to call him in the world. They ask for it to be opened, and it is opened. Those nearest to God from every heaven escort it to the heaven next to it, until it reaches the seventh heaven. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, 'Write a book for My servant in 'Illiyyin, and return him to the earth, for I created them from it, and into it I shall return them, and from it I shall bring them forth once again.' Then his soul is returned into his body." He mentioned the hadith. I have mentioned it in full in the book "al-Tadhkirah." It has also been narrated from the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

The meaning of ﴿And into it We shall return you﴾ [20: 55] is: after death. ﴿And from it We shall bring you forth﴾ [20: 55] is: for resurrection and reckoning.

﴿Once again﴾ (taratan ukhra) refers back to His saying ﴿From it We created you﴾ [20: 55], not to "We shall return you." It is like your saying: "I bought a she-camel and a house and another she-camel." The meaning is: We brought you out from the earth, and We shall bring you out from the earth after death once again.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾ [[(Mahdan) in the plural: the recitation of Nafi', and the original reading.]] "Alladhi" (who) is in the nominative case [[According to manuscripts B, J, Z, Y, K and Y.]] as a qualifier (na't) of "Rabbi" (my Lord), meaning: "My Lord does not go astray, He who made..." It may also be the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "He is the One who..." It may also be in the accusative case, with an implied verb "I mean" (a'ni).

The Kufans recited "mahdan" here and in "al-Zukhruf" with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha. The rest recited "mihadan," and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because they agree on the recitation of ﴿Did We not make the earth a cradle?﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 169 and following.]] [al-Naba': 6]. Al-Nahhas said: The plural is preferable, because "mahdan" is a verbal noun (masdar), and this is not a position for a verbal noun except with an ellipsis, meaning "possessor of a cradle." Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever recites "mahdan" may take it as a verbal noun, like "al-farsh" (spreading), meaning "He spread the earth for you as a spreading," and it may also be read with the omission of a modified noun, meaning "possessor of a cradle." Whoever recites "mihadan" may take it as a singular, like "al-firash" (bedding). It may also be the plural of "mahd," used as a noun and then broken into a plural. The meaning of "mihadan" is: a bed and a resting place on which you settle.

﴿And threaded for you therein roads﴾ [20: 53], that is, paths. Its parallel is ﴿And Allah made the earth a spread-out carpet for you, that you may traverse therein broad roads﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 306.]] [Nuh: 19–20]. The Almighty also said: ﴿Who made for you the earth a cradle, and threaded for you therein roads, that you may be guided﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 64.]] [al-Zukhruf: 10]. ﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾ has already been explained. This is the last of Musa's speech. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We brought forth thereby﴾. It is also said that all of it is from the speech of Musa.
