Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 56–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs﴾ [20:56], meaning the miracles indicating the prophethood of Musa. It is also said: the proofs of God indicating His oneness.

(But he denied and refused) [20:56], meaning he did not believe. This indicates that he disbelieved out of obstinacy, because he saw the signs directly, not merely by report. A parallel to it is: "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance" [see vol. 13, p. 163].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Musa?"﴾ [20:57]. When he saw the signs that Musa brought him, he said: they are magic. The meaning is: you have come to make the people imagine that you have brought a sign that obliges them to follow you and to believe in you, so that you may prevail over our land and over us.

(So we will surely bring you magic like it) [20:58], meaning: we will confront you with the like of what you have brought, so that it becomes clear to the people that what you have brought is not from God.

(So make between us and you an appointment) [20:58]. It is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning a promise. It is also said: al-maw'id is a noun for the place of the promise, as the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 43] [see vol. 10, p. 29 onward], so al-maw'id here is a place. It is also said: al-maw'id is a noun for the time of the promise, as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ [Hud: 81] [see vol. 9, p. 81]. The meaning is: set for us a known day, or a known place. Al-Qushayri said: the more apparent view is that it is a masdar, and for this reason He said: (which we will not break) [20:58], meaning we will not break that promise. Breaking a promise (ikhlaf) is to promise something and not fulfil it. Al-Jawhari said: al-mi'ad and al-mawid mean the act of promising, the time, and the place alike.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shayba and al-A'raj read "la nukhlifhu" (we will not break it) with a jazm (sukun), as an answer to His saying "ij'al" (make). Whoever reads it with raf' (damma) treats it as an adjective of "maw'id," and the implied sense is: a promise not to be broken.

(a place, equitable) [20:58]. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read "suwan" with a damma on the sin. The rest read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like 'udan and 'idan, and tuwan and tuwan. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the kasra on the sin, because it is the high, eloquent dialect. Al-Nahhas said: the kasra is more well-known and more common. All of them pronounced the waw with tanwin, though it was narrated from al-Hasan that the sin was read with a damma without tanwin. Its meaning has been disputed. It is said: "suwa" of this place, as al-Kalbi said. It is said: a level place where the matter made clear to the people what we have explained in it, as Ibn Zayd said. Ibn 'Abbas said: half-way. Mujahid said: fair. It is also reported from him, and from Qatada: just between us and you. Al-Nahhas said: the people of tafsir agree that the meaning of "suwan" is fair and just, and this is a good view. Sibawayh said: it is said "suwan" and "siwan," meaning just, that is, a just place in between the two places, in which there is fairness. Its origin is from your saying: he sat in the middle (sawa') of the house with the long vowel, meaning in its midst, and the middle of everything is its most just part. In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and "Thus We made you a midmost community" [al-Baqarah: 143] means just. Zuhayr said:

"Show us a plot in which there is no injustice,
in which equality (al-sawa') makes us equal."

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutabi said: midmost between the two parties. Abu 'Ubayda recited for Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

"Indeed our father had settled in a land
equal (suwan) between Qays of 'Aylan and al-Fizr."

Al-Fizr is Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim. Al-Akhfash said: "suwan" when it means "other than" or "just" has three dialects: if you put a damma or a kasra on the sin, you shorten in both cases; if you put a fatha, you lengthen. You say: makan suwan, siwan, and sawa', meaning just and midmost between the two parties. Musa ibn Jabir said: "We found our father had settled in a land," and so on. It is also said: (a place, suwan) [20:58] means a chosen place. The proponent of this view recited:

"Were my beloved to wish, she would not turn me away,
and were I to wish, I would not pass by her."

You say: I passed by a man other than you (siwak, suwak, and sawa'ik), meaning other than you. They are equal (sawa') in this matter, and if you wish, "sawa'an." They are equal for all, and they are "aswa'," and they are "sawasiyah," like "thamaniyah," contrary to analogy. "Makanan" is in the accusative as the second object of "ja'ala" (made). Its being in the accusative governed by "al-maw'id" is not sound, whether as an object or as an adverb of it, because the verbal noun has been described, and nouns that work like verbs, when described or diminutive, should not govern, since they have left the resemblance to the verb. Nor is it sound to take it as an adverb standing in the position of the second object, because when an adverb follows the verbal noun the Arabs do not treat it like masdars with adverbs, but they allow latitude in it, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾ [Hud: 81], and "Your appointment is the day of adornment" [20:59].

The day of adornment has been disputed. It is said it was a festival day they had, when they adorned themselves and gathered, as said by Qatada, al-Suddi and others. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was the day of 'Ashura'. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: a market day in which they adorned themselves, and Qatada also said this. al-Dahhak said: Saturday. It is said: the day of Nawruz, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. It is said: a day on which the canal is opened, because they used to go out on it to stroll and enjoy themselves, and at that time the Egyptian lands were safe from the Nile. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, al-Sulami and Hubayra from Hafs read "yawmu al-zinah" with a fatha. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr, meaning: on the day of adornment, the fulfilment of our promise. The rest read it with a raf', as the predicate of the subject.

(and that the people be gathered in the forenoon) [20:59], meaning: and that the people be assembled. "An" is in the position of a raf' according to the reading of whoever reads "yawmu" with raf'. The coordination of "wa an yuhsharu" [20:59] strengthens the reading with raf', because "an" cannot be an adverb, although the explicit masdar can be an adverb, like "maqdima al-hajj" (the arrival of the pilgrims), since whoever says "I will come to you at the arrival of the pilgrims" does not say "I will come to you that the pilgrims arrive." Al-Nahhas said: more preferable than this is that it be in the position of the genitive, coordinated with "al-zinah." "Al-duha" is feminine; the Arabs diminutive it without a ha' lest its diminutive resemble "duhwah." Al-Nahhas said this. Al-Jawhari said: duhwat al-nahar is after the rising of the sun, then after it "al-duha," which is when the sun shines, a maqsur word that is feminine and masculine. Whoever makes it feminine takes it to be the plural of duhwah; whoever makes it masculine takes it to be a noun on the pattern fi'l, like "surad" and "nughar." It is an adverb that does not take full declension, like "sahar." You say: I met him "duha" and "duha" when you mean the duha of your day, and you do not give it tanwin. After it is "al-duha'," a masdud masculine word, which is at the height of the day. "Al-duha" is singled out because it is the beginning of the day, so if the matter was extended between them there would be room within the day.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Jahdari and others: "wa an yuhsharu al-nasu duhan" (and that the people be gathered in the forenoon), with the meaning "and that God gather the people," and the like. From some readers: "wa an tahsura al-nas" (and that you, O Fir'awn, gather the people), and from al-Jahdari also: "wa an nahsura" with the nun.

He promised them that day so that the exaltation of God's word, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the unbeliever, and the vanishing of falsehood might occur before the eyes of witnesses, and so that the desire of the one who desires the truth might be strengthened, the edge of the falsifiers and their partisans might be blunted, and the one who narrates this matter might spread knowledge in every desert and town, and it might spread among the gatherings of the people of the tent and the city.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Fir'awn withdrew and gathered his scheme﴾ [20:60], meaning his tricks and his magic, and what is meant is the gathering of the magicians. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were seventy-two magicians, each with ropes and staves. It is also said: they were four hundred. It is also said: they were twelve thousand. It is also said: fourteen thousand. Ibn al-Munkadir said: they were eighty thousand. It is also said: they gathered under a leader called Shim'un. It is also said: his name was Yuhanna, with twelve chiefs, each chief with twenty overseers, each overseer with a thousand magicians. It is also said they were three hundred thousand magicians from al-Fayyum, three hundred thousand magicians from al-Sa'id, and three hundred thousand magicians from the countryside, so they became nine hundred thousand, and their leader was blind.

(Then he came) [20:60], meaning the appointment came.

(Musa said to them) [20:61], meaning he said to Fir'awn and the magicians: (Woe to you) [20:61], an invocation of woe upon them. It is a verbal noun. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative in the sense of "God imposed woe upon them." He said: it may also be a vocative, like His saying: ﴿O woe to us, who raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52] [see vol. 15, p. 39 onward]. (Do not invent against God a lie) [20:61], meaning do not fabricate lies against Him, do not associate partners with Him, and do not say to the miracles that they are magic.

(lest He destroy you with a punishment) [20:61], meaning from Him, that is, He will root you out with destruction.

It is said of it: "sahata" and "as-hata," with the same meaning, and its origin is from the thorough shaving of hair. The Kufans read "fayusihtakum" from "as-hata," and the rest read "fayasahtakum" from "sahata." This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, while the first is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. It is in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition. Al-Farazdaq said:

"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left
of the wealth nothing but a stripped remnant [musahtan],
or a worn-out one [mujallaf]."

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a line whose syntactic parsing the caravans never cease to dispute.

(And he has indeed failed who invented) [20:61], meaning he lost and perished, and whoever claims against God what He has not permitted has failed of mercy and reward.

(And they secretly conferred) Qatadah said: "They said: If what he has brought is magic, we will overcome him; and if it is from Allah, then there will be a matter for him. This is what they kept secret." It was also said that what they kept secret was their saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾ [20:63], "the verses," said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. It was also said that what they kept secret was their saying: "If we are overcome, we will follow him," related by al-Kalbi; the evidence for this is what became apparent of the outcome of their affair. It was also said: Their secret was that when Musa said to them, ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ [20:61], they said: "This is not the word of a magician." And "al-najwa" (secret counsel) may be a noun or a verbal noun (masdar), and its explanation has already been given in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 382 onward].

His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾) [20:63]. Abu 'Amr recited "Inna hadhayni la-sahiran" (إِنَّ هَذَيْنَ لَسَاحِرَانِ). This reading is transmitted from Uthman, Aisha, and others among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and likewise al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others among the Successors (tabi'un). Among the readers, Isa ibn Umar and Asim al-Jahdari are mentioned, according to what al-Nahhas reported. This reading agrees with grammatical rules (i'rab) but differs from the codex (mushaf). Al-Zuhri, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, al-Mufaddal, Aban, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Asim in the transmission of Hafs from him recited ﴿inna hadhan﴾ [20:63] with the particle "inna" lightened (تخفيف إنْ) followed by "la-sahiran," and Ibn Kathir shaddads the nun of "hadhan." This reading is free from contradicting the codex and from faulty grammar, and its meaning would be: "These are only two magicians." Al-Kisa'i said, regarding the reading of Abdullah: "Inna hadhani sahiran," without the lam. Al-Farra' said regarding the variant of Ubayy: "Inna dhani illa sahiran." These are three other readings which are to be understood as tafsir, not as permissible recitations, because they contradict the codex.

I say: For the scholars regarding the reading of the people of Madinah and Kufah there are six opinions, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari at the end of his book al-Radd, and by al-Nahhas in his I'rab, and by al-Mahdawi in his tafsir, and others mixed some of their statements together. Some people declared it erroneous, to the extent that Abu 'Amr said: "Indeed I am ashamed before Allah [exalted is He] to recite ﴿Inna hadhan﴾ [20:63]." Urwah reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿But those firm in knowledge﴾ [4:162], then he said: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [4:162], and in al-Ma'idah ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians﴾ [5:69], and ﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾ [20:63], and she said: "O nephew! This is an error by the scribe." Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There is a lahn (grammatical error) in the mushaf, and the Arabs will set it straight with their tongues." Aban ibn Uthman said: I recited this verse in the presence of Abu Uthman ibn Affan, and he said: "It is a lahn and an error." Someone said to him: "Shall we not change it?" He said: "Leave it, for it does not make the lawful unlawful nor the unlawful lawful."

The first of the six opinions: It is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Zubayd, Khath'am, and Kinanah ibn Zayd, who make the dual's nominative, accusative and genitive with the alif: they say "jaa'a al-Zaydani," "ra'aytu al-Zaydani," and "marartu bi'l-Zaydani." From this is His saying: ﴿nor would have informed you of it﴾ [10:16], according to what has preceded [see vol. 8, p. 320 onward]. Al-Farra' recited for a man from Banu Asad [it is al-Mutalammis, as in al-Lisan]—he said: "I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him":

*So he lowered his head like the bitter one, and if he saw / a way to bite him, the bitter one would have bitten firmly.* [Ṣammama al-shuja' fī 'ḍatihi: i.e., he bit and clenched, and did not release what he bit.]

And they say: "kasarat yadahu" and "rakibtu 'alahu," meaning "yadayhi" and "'alayhi." Their poet said: [it is Hawbar al-Harithi. Al-Hābī is dust that is raised and fine.]

*He took from us, between his two ears, a blow / that called him to the dust of the hābī, barren.*

And another said: [It is said: it belongs to some people of Yemen, and before it:

*O she-camel of a rider you see / they flew above her, and the mount flew over her.
Bind with the two haunches her waist / swift, and swift is her father.*
The haqw is the flank. The nājiyah is the swift one.]

*They flew above them, so the mount flew above her,*

meaning "'alayhinna" and "'alayha." And another said: [He attributed it to al-Jawhari to Abu al-Najm, and before it:

*Woe to Salma, then woe, woe! / She is my desire, if only we had attained her...*
*Would that her eyes were ours and her mouth / for a price we would accept, her father accepts...* etc. Some attributed it to Ru'bah. It was said: it belongs to some people of Yemen, and before it:

*O she-camel of a rider you see...* etc.]

*Indeed her father and her father's father / have reached the furthest point in glory,*

meaning: "inna abaha wa-abā abāha" and "ghayatāha." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: This opinion is among the best ways the verse has been interpreted, since this dialect is well known, and it has been related by one whose knowledge and trustworthiness are accepted, among them Abu Zayd al-Ansari, who used to say: "When Sibawayh says 'I was told by one I trust,' he means me." And Abu al-Khattab al-Akhfash, who is a leader among the leaders of the language, and al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', all of them said this is according to the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b. Abu 'Ubaydah related from Abu al-Khattab that this is the dialect of the Banu Kinanah. Al-Mahdawi said: Others related that it is a dialect of Khath'am. Al-Nahhas said: Among the clearest evidence for this is Sibawayh's saying: "Know that when you make the singular dual, you add to it two additional letters, the first of which is a letter of extension and softness, and it is the letter of i'rab." Abu Ja'far said: Sibawayh's saying "and it is the letter of i'rab" requires that the original should not change, so "inna hadhan" comes according to its original form, so that this be known. Allah exalted has said: ﴿The Shaytan has overcome them﴾ [58:19], and did not say "istaḥāza," so this comes to indicate the original form; likewise "inna hadhan." And one should not give thought to the denial of whoever denied this dialect, since the Imams had transmitted it.

The second opinion: that "inna" is in the sense of "na'am" (yes), as al-Kisa'i related from Asim, who said: "The Arabs use 'inna' in the sense of 'na'am'." Sibawayh related that "inna" comes in the sense of "ajal" (indeed). To this opinion Muhammad ibn Yazid and Isma'il ibn Ishaq al-Qadi inclined. Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj and Ali ibn Sulayman inclining to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: Abu Ishaq was impressed by it. Al-Nahhas said: Ali ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Salam al-Naysaburi related to us; then I met Abdullah ibn Ahmad [this addition is from al-Nahhas's I'rab] and he related to me, saying: Umayr ibn al-Mutawakkil related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Nawfali, from the descendants of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, related to us, saying: Umar ibn Jami' al-Kufi related to us from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali—that is Ibn al-Husayn—from his father, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all, who said: "I cannot count how many times I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say from his pulpit: 'Inna al-hamda lillah, nahmaduhu wa-nasta'inuhu'," then he would say: "I am the most eloquent of Quraysh, and the most eloquent of them after me is Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As." This is because the orators of the Jahiliyyah used to open their speeches with "na'am." And a poet said in the sense of "na'am":

*They said: You betrayed, so I said: "Inna," and perhaps / the betrayer attains high station and cools the burning thirst.*

And Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*The blamers rose early in youth, / blaming me, and I blame them.
And they say: "White hair has overtaken you, / and you have grown old," so I said: "Inna-hu."*

Accordingly, it is permissible that the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "Inna hadhani la-sahiran" be in the sense of "na'am," and it is not put in the accusative. Al-Nahhas said: Dawud ibn al-Haytham recited to me, saying: Tha'lab recited to me:

*Would that I knew whether the lover has a cure / from the anguish of love for them, indeed the meeting.*

Al-Nahhas said: This is a good opinion, except that there is something in it, because one only says "na'am Zayd kharij" (yes, Zayd is going out), and the lam hardly occurs here. Although the grammarians have spoken on this, saying that the lam is intended to be placed before, as he said:

*My maternal uncle, you are indeed, and whoever Jarir is his maternal uncle, / he attains glory and honours the maternal uncles.*

Another:

*Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, shahraba, / she is content from the sheep with a bone of the neck.*

Meaning: "la-khali" and "la-Umm al-Hulays." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning in the verse is "Inna hadhani la-humā sāhirāni," then the subject was deleted. Al-Mahdawi said: Abu Ali and Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni denied it. Abu al-Fath said: The deleted "humā" was not deleted except after it became known, and when it is known, one is sufficed by its knowledge from emphasizing it with the lam, and it is unseemly to delete the emphasized element and leave the emphasizer.

The third opinion: also said by al-Farra' [said by min b, j, t, k]: I found the alif to be a support that is not a root letter of the verb, so I added a nun to it and did not change it, as I said: "alladhi," then I added to it a nun and said: "jā'anī alladhīna 'indaka," "ra'aytu alladhīna 'indaka," and "marartu bi'lladhīna 'indaka."

The fourth opinion: said by some of the Kufans. He said: The alif in "hadhan" is likened to the alif in "yaf'alan," so it was not changed.

The fifth opinion: Abu Ishaq said: The early grammarians say that the hā' here is implied, and the meaning is "innahu hadhani la-sahiran." Ibn al-Anbari said: The hā' which is the object of "inna" was implied, and "hadhani" is the predicate of "inna," and "sahiran" is raised by "humā" the implied [and the estimate is: innahu hadhani lahumā sāhirāni]. The more likely view among the adherents of this answer is that the hā' is the subject of "inna," and "hadhani" is raised by the beginning (mubtada'), and what follows it is the predicate of the beginning.

The sixth opinion: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I asked Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan about this verse, and he said: "If you wish, I will answer you with the answer of the grammarians, and if you wish, I will answer you with my own view." I said: "With your view." He said: Isma'il ibn Ishaq asked me about it, and I said: "The view I hold is that since 'hadha' is said in the position of the nominative, accusative and genitive in one form, and the dual ought not to change for it, the dual is treated like the singular." He said: "How excellent this is; if only someone had preceded you in saying it, so that one might be comforted by it." Ibn Kaysan said: I said to him: "Then the judge says it, so that one may be comforted by it," and he smiled.

This is the exegesis of Qur'an 20:63–64 by al-Qurtubi, read in the context of Pharaoh and the sorcerers.

Allah's words: ﴿They both wish to drive you out of your land by their sorcery and to do away with your exemplary way of life (al-muthla)﴾ [20:63]. This is the speech of Pharaoh to the sorcerers. That is, their aim is to corrupt the religion you hold, just as Pharaoh said: "Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land" [40:26] (see vol. 15, p. 304 onward) [Ghafir: 26]. It is said, "So-and-so is of good tariqa (ṭarīqa)," meaning of good madhhab (school of thought). It was also said: the tariqa of the people is the best of their speech, and this is the path they should follow and take as a model. So the meaning is: "and they will take away your leaders and chiefs," seeking to win them over. Or: "they will take away the Children of Israel," who are the best among them, even though they are your servants, because of their connection to the prophets. Or: "they will take away the people of your tariqa," with the noun omitted. The word al-muthlā (﴿al-muthlā﴾ [20:63]) is the feminine of al-amthal, just as one says al-afḍal and al-fuḍlā. The word ṭarīqa was made feminine according to its form, even though men are meant by it. It is also permissible that the feminine form refers to the group. Al-Kisa'i said: "bi-ṭarīqatikum" [20:63] means "by your sunna (established custom) and your bearing (samt)." And al-muthlā [20:63] is an adjective, like your saying imra'a kubrā (an elder woman). The Arabs say: "So-and-so is on the best path (al-ṭarīqa al-muthlā)," meaning on the upright guidance.

Allah's words: ﴿So muster your scheme﴾ [20:64]. Al-ijmā' means firm resolve and determination upon a matter. One says: "ajma'tu al-khurūj" and "ʿalā al-khurūj," meaning "I resolved." The reading of all the metropolitan reciters is "fa-ajmi'ū," except Abu ʿAmr, who read "fa-ajma'ū" with a connected hamza and a fatha on the mim. He cited Allah's words: ﴿then he gathered his scheme, then came﴾ [20:60]. Al-Nahhas said: It has been related to me from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: Abu ʿAmr must read contrary to this reading, which is the reading most people follow. He said: because he argued from "jama'a" (gathered), and Allah's words, "fa-jama'a kaydahu" [20:60], are established; it is unlikely that the phrase "fa-ajmi'ū" comes after it, whereas it is likely that "fa-ajmi'ū" means "resolve and strive," and since that came earlier, this must have a different meaning. One says: "amrun mujma'un" and "mujma'un ʿalayhi" (a settled matter). Al-Nahhas said: The reading of Abu ʿAmr, "fa-ajma'ū," is sound, meaning "gather every scheme you have and every stratagem, and combine them with your brother." Abu Ishaq also said this. Al-Tha'labi said: The reading with a cut alif and a kasra on the mim has two meanings. The first: in the sense of gathering. You say "ajma'tu al-shay'" and "jama'tuhu" with one meaning. In al-Sihah: "wa-ajma'tu al-shay'a" means "I made it all together." Abu Dhu'ayb said, describing wild asses:
Like them by the cliff between Nubayiʿ [a place or mountain or valley in the land of Hudhayl] ... and the mounts of Dhū al-ʿArjāʾ, a plundered gathering (mujmaʿ).
That is, a gathered thing. The second: it means resolve and firmness, as the poet said:
Would that I knew, though wishes do not profit, whether I shall go out one day while my affair is firmly resolved (mujma').
That is, settled.

Allah's words: ﴿Then come in a row﴾ [20:64]. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "all together." It was also said: "in rows," so that it would be more awe-inspiring for you. It is in the accusative because the verb falls upon it, according to the view of Abu ʿUbayda. He said: One says "ataytu al-ṣaff," meaning the place of prayer. So the meaning, in his view, is: come to the place where you gather on the day of the festival. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I was not able to come to the ṣaff," meaning the place of prayer. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is "then come while the people are lined up," so in this case it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and for this reason it is not pluralized. It was also read "thumma ʾituw" with a kasra on the mim and a ya'. Whoever drops the hamza replaces the hamza with an alif.

Allah's words: ﴿And he has indeed prospered today who prevails﴾ [20:64]. That is, whoever has overcome. All of this is the speech of the sorcerers to one another. It was also said: it is the speech of Pharaoh to them.

*My maternal uncle, you are indeed, and whoever Jarir is his maternal uncle, / he attains glory and honours the maternal uncles.*

Another:

*Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, shahraba, / she is content from the sheep with a bone of the neck.*

Meaning: "la-khali" and "la-Umm al-Hulays." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning in the verse is "Inna hadhani la-humā sāhirāni," then the subject was deleted. Al-Mahdawi said: Abu Ali and Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni denied it. Abu al-Fath said: The deleted "humā" was not deleted except after it became known, and when it is known, one is sufficed by its knowledge from emphasizing it with the lam, and it is unseemly to delete the emphasized element and leave the emphasizer.

The third opinion: also said by al-Farra' [said by min b, j, t, k]: I found the alif to be a support that is not a root letter of the verb, so I added a nun to it and did not change it, as I said: "alladhi," then I added to it a nun and said: "jā'anī alladhīna 'indaka," "ra'aytu alladhīna 'indaka," and "marartu bi'lladhīna 'indaka."

The fourth opinion: said by some of the Kufans. He said: The alif in "hadhan" is likened to the alif in "yaf'alan," so it was not changed.

The fifth opinion: Abu Ishaq said: The early grammarians say that the hā' here is implied, and the meaning is "innahu hadhani la-sahiran." Ibn al-Anbari said: The hā' which is the object of "inna" was implied, and "hadhani" is the predicate of "inna," and "sahiran" is raised by "humā" the implied [and the estimate is: innahu hadhani lahumā sāhirāni]. The more likely view among the adherents of this answer is that the hā' is the subject of "inna," and "hadhani" is raised by the beginning (mubtada'), and what follows it is the predicate of the beginning.

The sixth opinion: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I asked Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan about this verse, and he said: "If you wish, I will answer you with the answer of the grammarians, and if you wish, I will answer you with my own view." I said: "With your view." He said: Isma'il ibn Ishaq asked me about it, and I said: "The view I hold is that since 'hadha' is said in the position of the nominative, accusative and genitive in one form, and the dual ought not to change for it, the dual is treated like the singular." He said: "How excellent this is; if only someone had preceded you in saying it, so that one might be comforted by it." Ibn Kaysan said: I said to him: "Then the judge says it, so that one may be comforted by it," and he smiled.

This is the exegesis of Qur'an 20:63–64 by al-Qurtubi, read in the context of Pharaoh and the sorcerers.

Allah's words: ﴿They both wish to drive you out of your land by their sorcery and to do away with your exemplary way of life (al-muthla)﴾ [20:63]. This is the speech of Pharaoh to the sorcerers. That is, their aim is to corrupt the religion you hold, just as Pharaoh said: "Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land" [40:26] (see vol. 15, p. 304 onward) [Ghafir: 26]. It is said, "So-and-so is of good tariqa (ṭarīqa)," meaning of good madhhab (school of thought). It was also said: the tariqa of the people is the best of their speech, and this is the path they should follow and take as a model. So the meaning is: "and they will take away your leaders and chiefs," seeking to win them over. Or: "they will take away the Children of Israel," who are the best among them, even though they are your servants, because of their connection to the prophets. Or: "they will take away the people of your tariqa," with the noun omitted. The word al-muthlā (﴿al-muthlā﴾ [20:63]) is the feminine of al-amthal, just as one says al-afḍal and al-fuḍlā. The word ṭarīqa was made feminine according to its form, even though men are meant by it. It is also permissible that the feminine form refers to the group. Al-Kisa'i said: "bi-ṭarīqatikum" [20:63] means "by your sunna (established custom) and your bearing (samt)." And al-muthlā [20:63] is an adjective, like your saying imra'a kubrā (an elder woman). The Arabs say: "So-and-so is on the best path (al-ṭarīqa al-muthlā)," meaning on the upright guidance.

Allah's words: ﴿So muster your scheme﴾ [20:64]. Al-ijmā' means firm resolve and determination upon a matter. One says: "ajma'tu al-khurūj" and "ʿalā al-khurūj," meaning "I resolved." The reading of all the metropolitan reciters is "fa-ajmi'ū," except Abu ʿAmr, who read "fa-ajma'ū" with a connected hamza and a fatha on the mim. He cited Allah's words: ﴿then he gathered his scheme, then came﴾ [20:60]. Al-Nahhas said: It has been related to me from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he said: Abu ʿAmr must read contrary to this reading, which is the reading most people follow. He said: because he argued from "jama'a" (gathered), and Allah's words, "fa-jama'a kaydahu" [20:60], are established; it is unlikely that the phrase "fa-ajmi'ū" comes after it, whereas it is likely that "fa-ajmi'ū" means "resolve and strive," and since that came earlier, this must have a different meaning. One says: "amrun mujma'un" and "mujma'un ʿalayhi" (a settled matter). Al-Nahhas said: The reading of Abu ʿAmr, "fa-ajma'ū," is sound, meaning "gather every scheme you have and every stratagem, and combine them with your brother." Abu Ishaq also said this. Al-Tha'labi said: The reading with a cut alif and a kasra on the mim has two meanings. The first: in the sense of gathering. You say "ajma'tu al-shay'" and "jama'tuhu" with one meaning. In al-Sihah: "wa-ajma'tu al-shay'a" means "I made it all together." Abu Dhu'ayb said, describing wild asses:
Like them by the cliff between Nubayiʿ [a place or mountain or valley in the land of Hudhayl] ... and the mounts of Dhū al-ʿArjāʾ, a plundered gathering (mujmaʿ).
That is, a gathered thing. The second: it means resolve and firmness, as the poet said:
Would that I knew, though wishes do not profit, whether I shall go out one day while my affair is firmly resolved (mujma').
That is, settled.

Allah's words: ﴿Then come in a row﴾ [20:64]. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "all together." It was also said: "in rows," so that it would be more awe-inspiring for you. It is in the accusative because the verb falls upon it, according to the view of Abu ʿUbayda. He said: One says "ataytu al-ṣaff," meaning the place of prayer. So the meaning, in his view, is: come to the place where you gather on the day of the festival. It is related from some eloquent Arabs: "I was not able to come to the ṣaff," meaning the place of prayer. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is "then come while the people are lined up," so in this case it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and for this reason it is not pluralized. It was also read "thumma ʾituw" with a kasra on the mim and a ya'. Whoever drops the hamza replaces the hamza with an alif.

Allah's words: ﴿And he has indeed prospered today who prevails﴾ [20:64]. That is, whoever has overcome. All of this is the speech of the sorcerers to one another. It was also said: it is the speech of Pharaoh to them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 62–64 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves﴾ [20:62], meaning they consulted one another, referring to the magicians.

(And they secretly conferred) Qatadah said: "They said: If what he has brought is magic, we will overcome him; and if it is from Allah, then there will be a matter for him. This is what they kept secret." It was also said that what they kept secret was their saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾ [20:63], "the verses," said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. It was also said that what they kept secret was their saying: "If we are overcome, we will follow him," related by al-Kalbi; the evidence for this is what became apparent of the outcome of their affair. It was also said: Their secret was that when Musa said to them, ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ [20:61], they said: "This is not the word of a magician." And "al-najwa" (secret counsel) may be a noun or a verbal noun (masdar), and its explanation has already been given in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 382 onward].

His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾) [20:63]. Abu 'Amr recited "Inna hadhayni la-sahiran" (إِنَّ هَذَيْنَ لَسَاحِرَانِ). This reading is transmitted from Uthman, Aisha, and others among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and likewise al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others among the Successors (tabi'un). Among the readers, Isa ibn Umar and Asim al-Jahdari are mentioned, according to what al-Nahhas reported. This reading agrees with grammatical rules (i'rab) but differs from the codex (mushaf). Al-Zuhri, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, al-Mufaddal, Aban, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and Asim in the transmission of Hafs from him recited ﴿inna hadhan﴾ [20:63] with the particle "inna" lightened (تخفيف إنْ) followed by "la-sahiran," and Ibn Kathir shaddads the nun of "hadhan." This reading is free from contradicting the codex and from faulty grammar, and its meaning would be: "These are only two magicians." The people of Madinah and Kufah recited "Inna hadhani" with "inna" shaddad (تشديد إنَّ) followed by "la-sahiran," so they agreed with the codex but contradicted grammatical rules. Al-Nahhas said: These are three readings which the community has transmitted from the Imams. It is also reported from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Inna hadhani illa sahiran." Al-Kisa'i said, regarding the reading of Abdullah: "Inna hadhani sahiran," without the lam. Al-Farra' said regarding the variant of Ubayy: "Inna dhani illa sahiran." These are three other readings which are to be understood as tafsir, not as permissible recitations, because they contradict the codex.

I say: For the scholars regarding the reading of the people of Madinah and Kufah there are six opinions, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari at the end of his book al-Radd, and by al-Nahhas in his I'rab, and by al-Mahdawi in his tafsir, and others mixed some of their statements together. Some people declared it erroneous, to the extent that Abu 'Amr said: "Indeed I am ashamed before Allah [exalted is He] to recite ﴿Inna hadhan﴾ [20:63]." Urwah reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿But those firm in knowledge﴾ [4:162], then he said: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ [4:162], and in al-Ma'idah ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians﴾ [5:69], and ﴿Indeed, these two are but magicians﴾ [20:63], and she said: "O nephew! This is an error by the scribe." Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There is a lahn (grammatical error) in the mushaf, and the Arabs will set it straight with their tongues." Aban ibn Uthman said: I recited this verse in the presence of Abu Uthman ibn Affan, and he said: "It is a lahn and an error." Someone said to him: "Shall we not change it?" He said: "Leave it, for it does not make the lawful unlawful nor the unlawful lawful."

The first of the six opinions: It is the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Zubayd, Khath'am, and Kinanah ibn Zayd, who make the dual's nominative, accusative and genitive with the alif: they say "jaa'a al-Zaydani," "ra'aytu al-Zaydani," and "marartu bi'l-Zaydani." From this is His saying: ﴿nor would have informed you of it﴾ [10:16], according to what has preceded [see vol. 8, p. 320 onward]. Al-Farra' recited for a man from Banu Asad [it is al-Mutalammis, as in al-Lisan]—he said: "I have never seen anyone more eloquent than him":

*So he lowered his head like the bitter one, and if he saw / a way to bite him, the bitter one would have bitten firmly.* [Ṣammama al-shuja' fī 'ḍatihi: i.e., he bit and clenched, and did not release what he bit.]

And they say: "kasarat yadahu" and "rakibtu 'alahu," meaning "yadayhi" and "'alayhi." Their poet said: [it is Hawbar al-Harithi. Al-Hābī is dust that is raised and fine.]

*He took from us, between his two ears, a blow / that called him to the dust of the hābī, barren.*

And another said: [It is said: it belongs to some people of Yemen, and before it:

*O she-camel of a rider you see / they flew above her, and the mount flew over her.
Bind with the two haunches her waist / swift, and swift is her father.*
The haqw is the flank. The nājiyah is the swift one.]

*They flew above them, so the mount flew above her,*

meaning "'alayhinna" and "'alayha." And another said: [He attributed it to al-Jawhari to Abu al-Najm, and before it:

*Woe to Salma, then woe, woe! / She is my desire, if only we had attained her...*
*Would that her eyes were ours and her mouth / for a price we would accept, her father accepts...* etc. Some attributed it to Ru'bah. It was said: it belongs to some people of Yemen, and before it:

*O she-camel of a rider you see...* etc.]

*Indeed her father and her father's father / have reached the furthest point in glory,*

meaning: "inna abaha wa-abā abāha" and "ghayatāha." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: This opinion is among the best ways the verse has been interpreted, since this dialect is well known, and it has been related by one whose knowledge and trustworthiness are accepted, among them Abu Zayd al-Ansari, who used to say: "When Sibawayh says 'I was told by one I trust,' he means me." And Abu al-Khattab al-Akhfash, who is a leader among the leaders of the language, and al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', all of them said this is according to the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b. Abu 'Ubaydah related from Abu al-Khattab that this is the dialect of the Banu Kinanah. Al-Mahdawi said: Others related that it is a dialect of Khath'am. Al-Nahhas said: Among the clearest evidence for this is Sibawayh's saying: "Know that when you make the singular dual, you add to it two additional letters, the first of which is a letter of extension and softness, and it is the letter of i'rab." Abu Ja'far said: Sibawayh's saying "and it is the letter of i'rab" requires that the original should not change, so "inna hadhan" comes according to its original form, so that this be known. Allah exalted has said: ﴿The Shaytan has overcome them﴾ [58:19], and did not say "istaḥāza," so this comes to indicate the original form; likewise "inna hadhan." And one should not give thought to the denial of whoever denied this dialect, since the Imams had transmitted it.

The second opinion: that "inna" is in the sense of "na'am" (yes), as al-Kisa'i related from Asim, who said: "The Arabs use 'inna' in the sense of 'na'am'." Sibawayh related that "inna" comes in the sense of "ajal" (indeed). To this opinion Muhammad ibn Yazid and Isma'il ibn Ishaq al-Qadi inclined. Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj and Ali ibn Sulayman inclining to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: Abu Ishaq was impressed by it. Al-Nahhas said: Ali ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Salam al-Naysaburi related to us; then I met Abdullah ibn Ahmad [this addition is from al-Nahhas's I'rab] and he related to me, saying: Umayr ibn al-Mutawakkil related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Nawfali, from the descendants of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, related to us, saying: Umar ibn Jami' al-Kufi related to us from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali—that is Ibn al-Husayn—from his father, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all, who said: "I cannot count how many times I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say from his pulpit: 'Inna al-hamda lillah, nahmaduhu wa-nasta'inuhu'," then he would say: "I am the most eloquent of Quraysh, and the most eloquent of them after me is Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As." Abu Muhammad al-Khaffaf said: Umayr said: Its i'rab according to the people of Arabic and grammar is "inna al-hamda lillah" with the accusative, except that the Arabs make "inna" in the sense of "na'am," as if he, ﷺ, meant: "Yes, the praise is for Allah." This is because the orators of the Jahiliyyah used to open their speeches with "na'am." And a poet said in the sense of "na'am":

*They said: You betrayed, so I said: "Inna," and perhaps / the betrayer attains high station and cools the burning thirst.*

And Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*The blamers rose early in youth, / blaming me, and I blame them.
And they say: "White hair has overtaken you, / and you have grown old," so I said: "Inna-hu."*

Accordingly, it is permissible that the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "Inna hadhani la-sahiran" be in the sense of "na'am," and it is not put in the accusative. Al-Nahhas said: Dawud ibn al-Haytham recited to me, saying: Tha'lab recited to me:

*Would that I knew whether the lover has a cure / from the anguish of love for them, indeed the meeting.*

Al-Nahhas said: This is a good opinion, except that there is something in it, because one only says "na'am Zayd kharij" (yes, Zayd is going out), and the lam hardly occurs here. Although the grammarians have spoken on this, saying that the lam is intended to be placed before, as he said:

*My maternal uncle, you are indeed, and whoever Jarir is his maternal uncle, / he attains glory and honours the maternal uncles.*

Another:

*Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, shahraba, / she is content from the sheep with a bone of the neck.*

Meaning: "la-khali" and "la-Umm al-Hulays." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning in the verse is "Inna hadhani la-humā sāhirāni," then the subject was deleted. Al-Mahdawi said: Abu Ali and Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni denied it. Abu al-Fath said: The deleted "humā" was not deleted except after it became known, and when it is known, one is sufficed by its knowledge from emphasizing it with the lam, and it is unseemly to delete the emphasized element and leave the emphasizer.

The third opinion: also said by al-Farra' [said by min b, j, t, k]: I found the alif to be a support that is not a root letter of the verb, so I added a nun to it and did not change it, as I said: "alladhi," then I added to it a nun and said: "jā'anī alladhīna 'indaka," "ra'aytu alladhīna 'indaka," and "marartu bi'lladhīna 'indaka."

The fourth opinion: said by some of the Kufans. He said: The alif in "hadhan" is likened to the alif in "yaf'alan," so it was not changed.

The fifth opinion: Abu Ishaq said: The early grammarians say that the hā' here is implied, and the meaning is "innahu hadhani la-sahiran." Ibn al-Anbari said: The hā' which is the object of "inna" was implied, and "hadhani" is the predicate of "inna," and "sahiran" is raised by "humā" the implied [and the estimate is: innahu hadhani lahumā sāhirāni]. The more likely view among the adherents of this answer is that the hā' is the subject of "inna," and "hadhani" is raised by the beginning (mubtada'), and what follows it is the predicate of the beginning.

The sixth opinion: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I asked Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan about this verse, and he said: "If you wish, I will answer you with the answer of the grammarians, and if you wish, I will answer you with my own view." I said: "With your view." He said: Isma'il ibn Ishaq asked me about it, and I said: "The view I hold is that since 'hadha' is said in the position of the nominative, accusative and genitive in one form, and the dual ought not to change for it, the dual is treated like the singular." He said: "How excellent this is; if only someone had preceded you in saying it, so that one might be comforted by it." Ibn Kaysan said: I said to him: "Then the judge says it, so that one may be comforted by it," and he smiled.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 65–71:

Allah's words: ﴿They said, "O Musa..."﴾ He means the magicians.

("Either you throw") your staff from your hand ("or we will be the first to throw"). They showed courtesy toward Musa, and that was the cause of their faith.

("He said, 'Rather, you throw.' Then their ropes...") 20:66. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning "so they threw," which the meaning indicates. Al-Hasan recited "wa-'usiyyahum" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn ("wa-ʿuṣīyuhum"). Harun al-Qari said: this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, "wa-ʿuṣīyuhum," and al-Hasan takes it that way. The rest recite with a kasrah, following the kasrah of the ṣād. Similar forms are dulī and dilī, qusī and qisī.

("It is imagined to him, because of their magic, that they were running") 20:66. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Haywah, Ibn Dhakwan, and Rawh from Yaʿqub recited "tukhayyalu" with a tāʾ, referring it to the staffs and ropes, since they are feminine. That is because they had smeared the staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun reached them, they quivered and moved. so Shaybān never sneezed except with a cut-off nose.

They cut and crucified until they died, may Allah have mercy on them. Ibn Muhaysin recited here and in al-A'raf "fa-la-uqatti'anna" [20:71] and "wa-la-usalliban-nakum" with a fatḥah on the alif and the lightened form, from qaṭaʿa and ṣalaba.

﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾ [20:71] Meaning: me or the Lord of Musa.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 65–71:

Allah's words: ﴿They said, "O Musa..."﴾ He means the magicians.

("Either you throw") your staff from your hand ("or we will be the first to throw"). They showed courtesy toward Musa, and that was the cause of their faith.

("He said, 'Rather, you throw.' Then their ropes...") 20:66. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning "so they threw," which the meaning indicates. Al-Hasan recited "wa-'usiyyahum" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn ("wa-ʿuṣīyuhum"). Harun al-Qari said: this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, "wa-ʿuṣīyuhum," and al-Hasan takes it that way. The rest recite with a kasrah, following the kasrah of the ṣād. Similar forms are dulī and dilī, qusī and qisī.

("It is imagined to him, because of their magic, that they were running") 20:66. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Haywah, Ibn Dhakwan, and Rawh from Yaʿqub recited "tukhayyalu" with a tāʾ, referring it to the staffs and ropes, since they are feminine. That is because they had smeared the staffs with mercury, and when the heat of the sun reached them, they quivered and moved. Al-Kalbi said: It was imagined to Musa that the earth was full of snakes, and that they were crawling on their bellies. It was also recited "takhayyalu," meaning "tatakhayyalu," whose pattern is that of "tukhayyalu." Whoever recites "yukhayyilu" with a yāʾ refers it to the plotting. It was also recited "nukhayyilu" with a nūn, on the basis that Allah is the One who makes it appear for the trial and testing. It is also said that the subject is "annahā tasʿā" (that it was running). "Anna" is in the position of a nominative, meaning "its running was imagined to him," as al-Zajjaj said. Al-Farra' claimed that its position is accusative, meaning "bi-annahā," and then the bāʾ was deleted. The meaning in the first view is: their magic and plotting made the staffs appear to him until he thought they were running. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever recites with a tāʾ makes "anna" in the accusative position, meaning "it was imagined to him as something having running." He said: it is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position as a substitute for the pronoun in "tukhayyalu," which refers to the ropes and staffs, and the substitution there is a substitution of inclusion. "Tasʿā" means "walks."

Allah's words: ﴿So Musa sensed within himself a fear﴾ That is, he concealed it. It is also said: he found it. It is also said: he perceived it, that is, from the snakes, and that was according to what arises in human nature, as mentioned before. It is also said: he feared that the people would be tempted before he threw his staff. It is also said: he feared, when the revelation was delayed about throwing the staff, that the people would disperse before that and be tempted. Some people of realities said: if the cause was that when Musa, peace be upon him, met the magicians and said to them, "Woe to you! Do not invent a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment" (20:61), he turned and saw Jibril on his right, and he said to him, "O Musa, be gentle with the friends of Allah." Musa said, "O Jibril, these are magicians who have come with great magic to nullify the miracle, to support the religion of Pharaoh, and to reject the religion of Allah, and you say: be gentle with the friends of Allah!" Jibril said: "They will be with you from now until the afternoon prayer, and after the afternoon prayer they will be in Paradise." When he said that to him, fear arose in the soul of Musa, and it occurred to him: what tells me what Allah's knowledge concerning me is? Perhaps I am now in a state while Allah's knowledge concerning me is contrary to it, as it was with those. When Allah knew what was in his heart, Allah revealed to him: ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior﴾ [20:68], that is, the victor over them in this world, and in the high ranks of Paradise, by the prophethood and election that Allah has given you. The original form of "khīfatan" was "khawfatan," and the wāw became a yāʾ because of the kasrah of the khāʾ.

Allah's words: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made﴾ [20:69] [Talaqqafa with a shaddah is the recitation of Nafi'.] He did not say "throw your staff." It is permissible that this is a diminutive of it, meaning: do not be concerned with the multitude of their ropes and staffs, and throw the small single stick, small in body, that is in your right hand, for by the power of Allah it will swallow them, despite its singleness and their multitude, its smallness and their greatness. It is also permissible that this is an exaltation of it, meaning: do not be impressed by these many large bodies, for in your right hand there is something greater than all of them, and these, despite their multitude, are the least and most insignificant thing before it. So throw it, and it will swallow them by Allah's permission and annihilate them. "Talqaf" with a jazm is the answer to the command, as if he said: if you throw it, it will swallow, that is, take and devour. Al-Sulami and Hafs recited "talqafu," with the lām silent, from laqifa yalqafu laqfan. Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Haywah al-Shami, and Yahya ibn al-Harith recited "talqafu" with the tāʾ deleted and the fāʾ raised, meaning "fa-innahā tatalaqqafu" (for it will swallow). The address is to Musa. It is also said: it is to the staff. Al-Laqf is taking quickly; it is said: laqiftu al-shay' (with kasrah) alqafuhu laqfan, and talaqqaftu it too, meaning I took it quickly. From Yaʿqub: it is said a man is laqif thaqif, meaning light and skillful. Al-Laqaf (with a fatḥah on the qāf) is the collapse of a wall. And the pool laqifa laqfan, meaning it collapsed from its bottom and widened. Talaqqafa, talaqqama, and talahama have the same meaning. This was already mentioned in (al-A'raf) [see vol. 7, p. 257 onward]. Laqimtu al-luqmah (with kasrah) laqman, and talaqqamtuha when I swallowed it slowly. Likewise lahimahu (with kasrah) when he swallowed it. ﴿What they have made﴾ means what they made. Similarly ﴿What they have made is only a plot of a sorcerer﴾ — "kaydu" with a ḍammah and "siḥrin" with a kasrah on the sīn and sukūn on the ḥāʾ, which is the recitation of the Kufans except ʿAsim. In it there are two views: first, that "kayd" is an annex to "siḥr" following it without any deletion; second, that there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning "kaydu dhī siḥrin" (the plot of one possessing magic). The rest recited "kayda" with a fatḥah, the object of the making, and "mā" is a restrictive particle, and the hā' of "sāḥir" is not elided in the annex. In reality, according to this recitation, the plot is annexed to the sorcerer, not to the magic. And it is permissible to open "anna" with a fatḥah, meaning "because what they made is the plot of a sorcerer."

﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed wherever he comes﴾ [20:69] That is, he does not win or escape wherever he comes from the earth. It is also said: wherever he schemes. The ruling on the sorcerer and the meaning of magic have already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [see vol. 2, p. 43 onward], so consider it there.

Allah's words: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ [20:70] Because of what they saw of the great matter and the breaking of custom with the staff, for it swallowed all that they had contrived of ropes and staffs, which were a load of three hundred camels, and then it returned to being a staff, and no one knows where the ropes and staffs went except Allah the Exalted. This meaning has already been discussed in (al-A'raf) [vol. 7, p. 259], and the matter of the staff is complete there.

﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa." He said, "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission?"﴾ [20:70–71] That is, in Him. It is said: "amana lahu" and "amana bihi" (both mean believed in him). From this: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26]. In al-A'raf he said: "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?" [see vol. 13, p. 339]. It is a denunciation from him against them, meaning: you have transgressed and done what I did not command you to do.

﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ That is, your head in teaching, and he overcame you only because he is more skilled in it than you. Pharaoh only said this to confuse the people, so that they would not follow them and believe as they believed. Otherwise Pharaoh knew that they had not learned from Musa; rather, they knew magic before Musa's arrival and birth.

﴿I will surely cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [20:71] That is, upon the trunks of palm trees. Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

They crucified al-ʿAbdi upon a palm trunk,
so Shaybān never sneezed except with a cut-off nose.

They cut and crucified until they died, may Allah have mercy on them. Ibn Muhaysin recited here and in al-A'raf "fa-la-uqatti'anna" [20:71] and "wa-la-usalliban-nakum" with a fatḥah on the alif and the lightened form, from qaṭaʿa and ṣalaba.

﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾ [20:71] Meaning: me or the Lord of Musa.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 72–76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said﴾ meaning the magicians, ﴿"We will not prefer you﴾ [20:72], i.e., we will not choose you, ﴿over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾ [20:72]. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means from certainty and knowledge. 'Ikrimah and others said: when they prostrated, God showed them their places in Paradise in their prostration, and therefore they said: "We will not prefer you" [20:72]. The wife of Pharaoh (Asiya) used to ask who had prevailed, and it was said to her: Musa and Harun have prevailed. She said: "I believe in the Lord of Musa and Harun." Pharaoh sent for her and said: Look at the greatest rock; if she persists in her saying, then throw it upon her. When they came to her, she raised her gaze to the sky and saw her place in Paradise, so she persisted in her saying, and her soul was taken, and the rock was thrown upon her body, and there was no soul in her body. It is also said: the chief of the magicians said to one whom he trusted, when he saw what he saw of Musa's staff: Look at this serpent, has it become frightened (takhawwafat)? So it is a jinn, or has it not become frightened? Then it is from the craft of the Maker to whom no made thing is hidden. He said: It has not become frightened. He said: "I believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa."

﴿And the One who originated us﴾ [20:72]: it has been said that it is coordinated with "what has come to us of the clear proofs" [20:72], i.e., we will not prefer you over what has come to us of the clear proofs, nor over the One who originated us, i.e., created us. It has also been said that it is an oath, i.e., by God, we will not prefer you.

﴿So decree what you will decree﴾ [20:72]. The estimated meaning: what you are one who decrees. The "mā" here is not the one that occurs with a verb in the sense of a verbal noun, because that one is joined to verbs, whereas this one is a relative joined to a subject and predicate.

Ibn 'Abbas said: do what you are going to do. It has also been said: judge what you are judging, i.e., of cutting off and crucifixion. The yā' is dropped from qādin in pausal connection because of its quiescence and the quiescence of the tanwin. Sibawayh preferred to retain it in pause, because the reason for the meeting of two quiescent letters has ceased.

﴿You only decree this worldly life﴾ [20:72], i.e., your command only takes effect in it. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the meaning: you only decree within the enjoyment of this worldly life, or during this worldly life, so the object is understood as elided. It may also be that the estimate is: you only decree the affairs of this worldly life, so it is in the accusative as an object, and "mā" is a particle preventing the operation of inna. Al-Farra' permitted the nominative, by making "mā" mean "alladhi" and dropping the hā' from taqdi, and "this worldly life" is nominative.

﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord﴾ [20:73], i.e., we have affirmed God alone, having no partner, and what Musa brought to us.

﴿That He may forgive us our sins﴾ [20:73], meaning the polytheism they had been upon.

﴿And the magic you compelled us to﴾ [20:73]. "Mā" is in the accusative position, coordinated with "al-khaṭāyā" (the sins). It has also been said: it has no position, and it is a negation, i.e., that He may forgive us our sins of magic, and what you compelled us to. Al-Nahhas said: the first is better. Al-Mahdawi said: there is remoteness in it, because of their saying: "Indeed for us there will surely be a reward if we are the victors" [7:113, see vol. 7 p. 258], and this is not the speech of those compelled; and because compulsion is not a sin, although it is possible that they were compelled to learn it as children. Al-Hasan said: they were taught magic as children, then they practised it afterward by choice. It is also possible that "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, with the predicate omitted, and the estimate: "and what you compelled us to of magic is removed from us." And "of magic" on this view and the first view is connected to "you compelled us" [20:73]; and on the view that "mā" is a negation it is connected to "our sins" [20:73].

﴿And God is better and more enduring﴾ [20:73], i.e., His reward is better and more enduring, so the noun was elided; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It has also been said: God is better for us than you, and more enduring in punishment for us than your punishment for us, and this is the answer to his saying: "And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring" [20:71]. It has also been said: God is better for us if we obey Him, and more enduring in punishment than you if we disobey Him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ [20:74]. It has been said: this is from the speech of the magicians when they believed. It has also been said: it is the beginning of speech from God, may He be exalted and majestic. The pronoun in "innahu" returns to the matter and affair. It is also permissible to read "inna man ya'ti", and from it is the poet's saying:

Indeed whoever enters the church one day... will meet in it gazelles and antelopes.

[The line is by al-Akhtal, who was Christian.]

He meant "innahu man yadkhul," i.e., the matter is this: that the criminal enters the Fire, and the believer enters Paradise. The criminal is the disbeliever. It has also been said: the one who commits sins and acquires them. The first is more fitting, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live﴾ [20:74], and this is the description of the disbelieving, denying, obstinate one, as previously explained in Surat al-Nisa' [see vol. 5 p. 253] and elsewhere; so he gains no benefit from his life and finds no rest in his death. The poet said:

Oh, for a soul that does not die so that its wretchedness ends, nor lives a life that has any sweetness.

It has also been said: the soul of the disbeliever is suspended in his throat; God informed about him that he does not die by its departure, nor live by its settling. And the meaning of:

﴿Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ [20:74]: whoever comes to the appointed time of his Lord. And the meaning of ﴿and whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾ [20:75]: i.e., he dies upon it and meets Him affirming Him.

﴿Who has done good deeds﴾ [20:75]: i.e., and has done the "ṣāliḥāt," meaning the acts of obedience and what he was commanded and forbidden.

﴿Those will have the high ranks﴾ [20:75]: i.e., the lofty ones, which descriptions fall short of. His saying: ﴿and whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾ [20:75] indicates that the criminal here means the polytheist.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [20:76] is an explanation of "the ranks" and a substitute for them; and "'adn" means residence. Its explanation has already been given [see vol. 10 p. 396].

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾ [20:76], i.e., beneath their chambers and couches, ﴿rivers﴾ of wine, honey, milk and water. This has already been mentioned.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ [20:76], i.e., remaining, eternal.

﴿That is the recompense of one who purifies himself﴾ [20:76], i.e., who purifies himself from disbelief and sins. Whoever says this is from the speech of the magicians said: perhaps the magicians heard it from Musa or from the Children of Israel, since there were groups of them in Egypt, and there was also among them the believer from the family of Pharaoh. I say: it is possible that this was an inspiration from God to them, which made them speak thus when they believed, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 77–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to Musa, "Travel with My servants by night"﴾ [20:77]. The discussion of this has already been given in full.

(So strike for them a dry path through the sea) [20:77], meaning dry, with no mud or water in it. The striking of the sea by Musa and his kunya for it (Abu Musa? no) — hold on; the text reads: the striking of the sea by Musa, and his drowning of Fir'awn, have already been mentioned in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 389 onward.]], so there is no point in repeating them.

(Do not fear being overtaken) [20:77], meaning being caught up with by Fir'awn and his soldiers. "Nor fear" — Ibn Jurayj said: the companions of Musa said to him, "This is Fir'awn, who has overtaken us, and this is the sea, which has surrounded us." So Allah, exalted is He, sent down: ﴿Do not fear being overtaken, nor be afraid﴾ [20:77], meaning: do not fear being overtaken by Fir'awn, nor fear drowning in the sea, that it might seize you if it engulfs you.

Hamzah recited "lā takhaf" (do not fear), taking it as a response to the imperative. The sense is: if you strike for them a path in the sea, do not fear. "Wa lā takhshā" [20:77] is then a new sentence, as if to say: "nor are you afraid." Or it may be jussive, with the alif being the lengthened form of a fatha, as in His saying: ﴿fa-aḍallūnā al-sabīlā﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67] (see vol. 14, p. 249). Or it may be in the manner of the poet's saying: [[This is ʿAbd Yaghuth ibn Waqqas, one of the poets of the Jahiliyyah. The verse begins: "wa-taḍḥaku minnī shaykhatun ʿabshiyyatun" (And an old woman of ʿAbs laughs at me).]]

"As if you had not seen before me a Yemeni captive,"

with the vowel dropped on the assumption that it is elided as a sound letter's vowel would be. This is the view of al-Farra'. Another poet said:

You satirized Zabban, then came back apologizing for the satire, but you did not satirize Zabban and you did not leave it.

Another poet said [[The verse is from lines of Qays ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhaymah ibn Rawahah al-ʿAbsi, who had a quarrel with al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad over a coat of mail; he drove off al-Rabi''s camels and sold them in Makkah to ʿAbd Allah ibn Jadʿan al-Qurashi.]]:

"Has it not reached you, though news spreads, of what the she-camels of Banu Ziyad encountered?"

Al-Nahhas said: It is among the most grievous errors to interpret the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, by the anomalies of poetry. Moreover, what the poets bring does not resemble the verse in any respect, because the yā' and wāw differ from the alif: they take vowels, whereas the alif does not. A poet, when compelled, may treat them as vocalized and then drop the vowel for the jazm, but this is impossible with the alif. The first reading is clearer, because what follows it, "wa lā takhshā" [20:77], is agreed upon without jazm.

There are three interpretations of it. The first: "lā takhāf" [20:77] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the addressee, meaning: strike for them a dry path in the sea, neither fearing nor dreading. The second: it is in the position of a qualifier (naʿt) of the path, since it is conjoined to "yabasan" (dry), which is a qualifier; the meaning would be: you do not fear in it, the returning pronoun having been omitted from the qualifier. The third: it is a separate predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, the meaning being: and you do not fear.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Fir'awn pursued them with his soldiers﴾ [20:78], meaning he followed them with his soldiers. It is also read "fa-ittabaʿahum" with the shaddah, in which case the bāʾ in "bi-junūdihi" makes the verb reach its second object, because ittabaʿa is transitive to one object. The sense is: he followed them so as to overtake them, with his soldiers, just as one says: "the commander rode with his sword," meaning with his sword. As for the reading without the shaddah, "fa-atbaʿa," it is transitive to two objects; the bāʾ may be extra, or the verb may be confined to one object. It is said: tabiʿahu, atbaʿahu, and laḥiqahu, alḥaqahu have the same meaning. His saying "bi-junūdihi" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: he followed them, driving his soldiers.

(Then there covered them from the sea that which covered them) [20:78], meaning there befell them from the sea what drowned them. It is repeated to express magnitude and to affirm the certainty of the matter.

(And Fir'awn led his people astray and did not guide them) [20:79], meaning he led them away from right guidance and did not guide them to any good or to any deliverance, because he had assumed that Musa, peace be upon him, and those with him could not escape him, since the sea lay before them. When Musa struck the sea with his staff, it split into twelve paths, and between the paths the water stood up like mountains. In Surah al-Shu'ara': ﴿each part was like a great mountain﴾ (see vol. 13, p. 100 onward), meaning a great mountain. So each tribe took a path. Allah revealed to the masses of water: "Interlace," and they became interwoven so that some of them could see one another and hear one another's speech. This was among the greatest miracles and the mightiest signs. When Fir'awn approached and saw the paths in the sea and the water standing, he imagined that the sea had done this out of awe of him, so he and his companions entered, and the sea closed over them.

It is said that His saying, "and did not guide them" [20:79], is an emphasis on his leading them astray. It is also said that it answers Fir'awn's statement: ﴿I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾ [Ghafir: 29] (see vol. 15, p. 305 onward), so Allah, exalted is He, refuted him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "and did not guide them" means he did not guide himself; rather he destroyed himself and his people.

"As if you had not seen before me a Yemeni captive,"

with the vowel dropped on the assumption that it is elided as a sound letter's vowel would be. This is the view of al-Farra'. Another poet said:

You satirized Zabban, then came back apologizing for the satire, but you did not satirize Zabban and you did not leave it.

Another poet said [[The verse is from lines of Qays ibn Zuhayr ibn Judhaymah ibn Rawahah al-ʿAbsi, who had a quarrel with al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad over a coat of mail; he drove off al-Rabi''s camels and sold them in Makkah to ʿAbd Allah ibn Jadʿan al-Qurashi.]]:

"Has it not reached you, though news spreads, of what the she-camels of Banu Ziyad encountered?"

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 80–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, We have delivered you from your enemy﴾ [20:80]. When He delivered them from Pharaoh, He said this to them so that they would be thankful to Him.

(And We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount) [20:80]. "Janib" (side) is in the accusative as the second object (al-maf'ul al-thani) of "wa'adna" (We made an appointment). It is not good for it to be in the accusative as a adverb of place (zarf), because it is a purely definite place-noun (zarf makan mahd ghayr mubham). Verbs and verbal nouns pass to adverbs of place without a preposition only when those adverbs are indefinite (mubhama). Makki said: This is a principle on which there is no disagreement, and the sense of the verse is: "And We made an appointment with you for the coming to the side of the Mount," then the modified noun was deleted. al-Nahhas said: That is, We commanded Musa to command you to go out with him so that He might speak to him in your presence and you would hear the speech. It was also said: After the drowning of Pharaoh, Musa promised to come to the right side of the Mount, where He would give him the Torah. So the promise was made to Musa, but they were addressed with it because the promise was for their sake. Abu 'Amr read "wa-wa'adnakum" without an alif, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, because the promise (al-wa'd) comes only from God, Exalted, to Musa specifically, whereas mutual promising (al-muwa'adah) can only be between two parties. This meaning has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [see vol. 1 pp. 394 and 406]. "Al-Ayman" (the right) is in the accusative because it is an adjective (na't) of "janib." The Mount has no right or left, so when one says, "Take from the right side of the Mount," the meaning is: "Take on your right from the Mount." The Mount was on Musa's right when He came to him.

(And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail) [20:80]. That is, in the wilderness (al-tih). This has already been discussed [from manuscripts b, ṭ, and y].

(Eat of the good things with which We have provided you) — that is, of the delicious provision. It was also said: of its lawful portion, since no human labor is involved in it, so no doubt (shubhah) enters into it.

(And do not transgress) — that is, do not let abundance and well-being lead you to disobey, because transgression (al-tughyan) is going beyond what is not permitted. It was also said: The meaning is: do not disbelieve the blessing, and do not forget the thanks due to the Benefactor for it upon you. It was also said: That is, do not exchange it for something else, as He said: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:61]. It was also said: Do not store any of it for more than a day and a night. Ibn 'Abbas said: then it would spoil on them what they had stored, and had it not been for that, food would never have spoiled.

(Lest My anger should descend upon you) [20:81]. That is, it is obligatory and descends. It is in the subjunctive (mansub) after the fa' (fa') as the answer to the prohibition in His saying: "and do not transgress."

(Then My anger descends upon you, and whoever has My anger descend upon him has indeed fallen) [20:81]. al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read "fa-yahilla" [20:81] with a ḍammah on the ḥa', and "wa-man yahlil" [20:81] with a ḍammah on the first lam. The rest read with a kasrah, and both are dialectal variants. Abu 'Ubaydah and others related that it is said: ḥalla yaḥillu when it is obligatory (wajaba), and ḥalla yaḥullu when it descends (nazala). Likewise al-Farra' said: the ḍammah is from al-ḥulūl in the sense of falling/alighting, and the kasrah is from obligation (al-wujub). The two meanings are close, except that the kasrah is preferable, because they have agreed on His saying: ﴿And upon him a lasting punishment descends﴾ [Hud 11:39]. The anger of God is His retribution, His vengeance, and His punishment.

"Then he has indeed fallen" [20:81]. al-Zajjaj said: then he has perished, that is, he has gone to the abyss (al-hawiyah), which is the bottom of the Fire, from hawa yahwi hawiyyan, meaning he fell from a height to a lower place; and hawa fulan means he died. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash informed us, saying: Tha'labah ibn Muslim narrated to us from Ayyub ibn Bashir, from Shufayy al-Asbahi [diminutive; Ibn Mati' with a Tā' with two dots above, al-Asbahi], who said: Indeed in Hell there is a mountain called Sa'ud, upon which the disbeliever climbs for forty autumns before he reaches its top. God, Exalted, said: ﴿I will drive him to a steep ascent (sa'ud)﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:17]. And indeed in Hell there is a palace called Hawa, from which the disbeliever is thrown from its top, and he falls for forty autumns before he reaches its base [in k: its bottom]. God, Exalted, said: "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has indeed fallen" [20:81]. He mentioned the hadith, and we have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed I am Oft-Forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [20:82]. That is, from polytheism.

(And believes and does righteous deeds, then remains guided) [20:82]. That is, he remains upon his faith until he dies upon it. This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri, Qatadah and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, his faith is not doubted. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari and Ibn 'Abbas also said: he remained upon the Sunnah and the Community (al-jama'ah). This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Anas said: he adhered to the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Mawardi related it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. A fifth opinion: he hit upon the right action (asaba al-'amal). This was said by Ibn Zayd, and from him also: he sought knowledge so that he would be guided as to how to act. al-Mahdawi mentioned the first, and al-Tha'labi the second. al-Sha'bi, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: he knew that there is a reward for that and a punishment for neglecting it; this was also said by al-Farra'. An eighth opinion: "then remains guided" [20:82] concerning the guardianship (wilayah) of the People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ); this was said by Thabit al-Bunani. The first opinion is the best of these opinions, God willing, and all the others return to it. Waki' related from Sufyan: We used to hear in His saying, mighty and majestic: "And indeed I am Oft-Forgiving to whoever repents" [20:82], meaning from polytheism; "and believes" [20:82], meaning after polytheism; "and does righteous deeds" [20:82], meaning he prayed and fasted; "then remains guided" [20:82], meaning he died upon that.
