(Eat of the good things with which We have provided you) — that is, of the delicious provision. It was also said: of its lawful portion, since no human labor is involved in it, so no doubt (shubhah) enters into it.

(And do not transgress) — that is, do not let abundance and well-being lead you to disobey, because transgression (al-tughyan) is going beyond what is not permitted. It was also said: The meaning is: do not disbelieve the blessing, and do not forget the thanks due to the Benefactor for it upon you. It was also said: That is, do not exchange it for something else, as He said: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:61]. It was also said: Do not store any of it for more than a day and a night. Ibn 'Abbas said: then it would spoil on them what they had stored, and had it not been for that, food would never have spoiled.

(Lest My anger should descend upon you) [20:81]. That is, it is obligatory and descends. It is in the subjunctive (mansub) after the fa' (fa') as the answer to the prohibition in His saying: "and do not transgress."

(Then My anger descends upon you, and whoever has My anger descend upon him has indeed fallen) [20:81]. al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read "fa-yahilla" [20:81] with a ḍammah on the ḥa', and "wa-man yahlil" [20:81] with a ḍammah on the first lam. The rest read with a kasrah, and both are dialectal variants. Abu 'Ubaydah and others related that it is said: ḥalla yaḥillu when it is obligatory (wajaba), and ḥalla yaḥullu when it descends (nazala). Likewise al-Farra' said: the ḍammah is from al-ḥulūl in the sense of falling/alighting, and the kasrah is from obligation (al-wujub). The two meanings are close, except that the kasrah is preferable, because they have agreed on His saying: ﴿And upon him a lasting punishment descends﴾ [Hud 11:39]. The anger of God is His retribution, His vengeance, and His punishment.

"Then he has indeed fallen" [20:81]. al-Zajjaj said: then he has perished, that is, he has gone to the abyss (al-hawiyah), which is the bottom of the Fire, from hawa yahwi hawiyyan, meaning he fell from a height to a lower place; and hawa fulan means he died. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash informed us, saying: Tha'labah ibn Muslim narrated to us from Ayyub ibn Bashir, from Shufayy al-Asbahi [diminutive; Ibn Mati' with a Tā' with two dots above, al-Asbahi], who said: Indeed in Hell there is a mountain called Sa'ud, upon which the disbeliever climbs for forty autumns before he reaches its top. God, Exalted, said: ﴿I will drive him to a steep ascent (sa'ud)﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:17]. And indeed in Hell there is a palace called Hawa, from which the disbeliever is thrown from its top, and he falls for forty autumns before he reaches its base [in k: its bottom]. God, Exalted, said: "And whoever has My anger descend upon him has indeed fallen" [20:81]. He mentioned the hadith, and we have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed I am Oft-Forgiving to whoever repents﴾ [20:82]. That is, from polytheism.

(And believes and does righteous deeds, then remains guided) [20:82]. That is, he remains upon his faith until he dies upon it. This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri, Qatadah and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, his faith is not doubted. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari and Ibn 'Abbas also said: he remained upon the Sunnah and the Community (al-jama'ah). This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Anas said: he adhered to the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi, and al-Mawardi related it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. A fifth opinion: he hit upon the right action (asaba al-'amal). This was said by Ibn Zayd, and from him also: he sought knowledge so that he would be guided as to how to act. al-Mahdawi mentioned the first, and al-Tha'labi the second. al-Sha'bi, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: he knew that there is a reward for that and a punishment for neglecting it; this was also said by al-Farra'. An eighth opinion: "then remains guided" [20:82] concerning the guardianship (wilayah) of the People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ); this was said by Thabit al-Bunani. The first opinion is the best of these opinions, God willing, and all the others return to it. Waki' related from Sufyan: We used to hear in His saying, mighty and majestic: "And indeed I am Oft-Forgiving to whoever repents" [20:82], meaning from polytheism; "and believes" [20:82], meaning after polytheism; "and does righteous deeds" [20:82], meaning he prayed and fasted; "then remains guided" [20:82], meaning he died upon that.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi on Surah 20, verses 83–89:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ [20:83], meaning: what drove you to get ahead of them? It is said that by "the people" He meant all of the Children of Israel. On this view, it is said that Harun (Aaron) was appointed as successor over the Children of Israel, and Musa went out with seventy men for the appointed time (al-miqat). So His words: ﴿They are right behind me﴾ [20:84] do not mean that they were walking behind him in his direction. Rather, he meant that they were close to me, waiting for my return to them. It is also said: No, rather Harun had been ordered to follow the Children of Israel, keeping to his trail, and they would join him. Some said: By "the people" He meant the seventy whom he had chosen, and when Musa drew near to the Tur (the mountain), he went ahead of them out of longing to hear the speech of Allah, [Mighty and Majestic]. [Manuscript variant: "Exalted" in one copy.] It is also said: When he set out for Tur Sina (Mount Sinai) by the appointment, he longed for his Lord, and the distance became long for him because of the intensity of his longing for Allah the Exalted. The matter became so burdensome for him that he tore his garment. Then he could not bear it, so he left them behind and went on alone. When he stood in his place, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ [20:83]. So (ﷺ) remained perplexed about how to answer this question, because of the sincerity of longing that overcame him, so he turned away from answering it. He alluded to it with his words: ﴿They are right behind me﴾ [20:84]. He had been asked about the cause that hastened him, using the word "mā" (what), so he informed of their coming by the trail. Then he said: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [20:84]. Thus he alluded to mention of longing and its sincerity, turning it toward seeking Allah's good pleasure. [Manuscript variant: "and its redirection" in some copies.] ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Maʿmar, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [20:84], that he said: "Out of longing." ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, used to say, when she went to her bed: "Bring me al-Majid," and the Mushaf would be brought to her, and she would take it to her chest and sleep with it, consoling herself with that. This was narrated by Sufyan from Maʿsar, from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to, when the sky rained, take off his clothes and expose himself until the rain reached him, and he would say: "Indeed it is newly come from my Lord." So this came from the Messenger (ﷺ) and from those after him, as a form of longing. For this reason Allah, Blessed is His name, said, as is narrated from Him: "The longing of the righteous for My meeting has become long, and I am more longing for their meeting." Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah knew, but He said: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people﴾ [20:83] out of mercy toward Musa, and as an honor to him by this speech, and to calm his heart, and in tenderness (riqqah) toward him. [Riqqah here means compassion.] So he answered his Lord: ﴿They are right behind me﴾ [20:84]. Abu Hatim said, Isa said: The Banu Tamim say "hum ula'" with the word shortened and without the extending mad, while the people of the Hijaz say "ula'" with the mad extended. Al-Farra' related ﴿hum ula'i ʿala athari﴾ [20:84], and Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj claimed that this has no sound basis. Al-Nahhas said: He is as he said, because this is not something that is put in an idafah construction, to be like "hudaya" (my guidance). It cannot be free of one of two aspects: either it is an ambiguous noun, so its idafah is impossible, or it has the meaning of "alladhina" (those who), so it is not put in idafah either, because what follows it completes it, and it is definite. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr and Ruways, from Yaʿqub, read ﴿ʿala ithri﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah and a sukun on the thaʾ, and it has the meaning of athar (trace); both are dialects. ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [20:84] means: I hastened to the place where You commanded me to go, that You may be pleased with me. It is said: a man is ʿajil, ʿujul, ʿajul, and ʿajlan, clearly characterized by haste, and haste is the opposite of slowness.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed We have tested your people after you﴾ [20:85], meaning: We tested them and examined them by having them seek evidence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And al-Samiri misled them﴾ [20:85], meaning: he called them to error, or he was its cause. It is said: "We tested them" means "We cast them into trial," that is: We made the worship of the calf appear attractive to them. For this reason Musa said: ﴿It is only Your trial﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:155]. [See vol. 7, p. 294 onward.] Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: al-Samiri was from a people who worshipped cows, [meaning, from the people of India, as in some reports], and he arrived in the land of Egypt and entered the religion of the Children of Israel outwardly, while in his heart was what he had of the worship of cows. It is said he was a man from the Copts, and he was a neighbor of Musa, who believed in him and went out with him. It is also said: He was a great man among the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe known as al-Samirah, who are well known in al-Sham (Greater Syria). Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He was from the people of Kerman.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ [20:86]. This is a circumstantial clause (hal), and its explanation has already been given in full in (al-Aʿraf) [see vol. 7, p. 286 onward].

﴿He said: "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"﴾ [20:86]. He, Mighty and Majestic, promised them Paradise if they remained upon His obedience, and promised them that He would make them hear His speech in the Torah through the tongue of Musa, so that they would act by what is in it and deserve the reward of their deeds. It is also said: He promised them victory and triumph. It is also said: His promise was His words: ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to whoever repents and believes﴾ [20:82], and so on.

﴿Has the time been long for you?﴾ [20:86], meaning: Have you forgotten, as has been said? A thing may be forgotten because the period has been long.

﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ [20:86]. "Yahilla" means: be due and descend. "Ghadab" means punishment and retribution. The meaning is: Did you wish to do an act that would be the cause of Allah's wrath descending upon you? Because no one seeks Allah's wrath, but a person may commit what becomes a cause of anger. [Manuscript variant: "wrath of the Lord" in some copies.]

﴿So you broke your appointment with me﴾ [20:86], because they had promised him that they would remain upon the obedience of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from the Tur. It is also said: He had promised them, as he went, to wait for the appointed time, but they hesitated.

﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power"﴾ [20:87]. It is read with a fathah on the mim, and this is the reading of Nafiʿ, ʿAsim and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: Its meaning is "by our capacity." Ibn Zayd said: We did not possess ourselves, meaning we were compelled. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read "bi-malkina" with a kasrah on the mim. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because it is the higher dialect. It is a verbal noun from "malaktu al-shayʾa amlikuhu milkan" (I possessed the thing). The verbal noun is in the idafah form with the agent, and the object is omitted, as if he said: "By our possession of the right course, but we erred," so it is an acknowledgment from them of error. Hamzah and al-Kisai read "bi-mulkina" with a dammah on the mim, and the meaning is "by our authority," that is, we had no power, so we broke your appointment. Then it is said: His words "They said" are general, meaning the specific: those who remained steadfast in the obedience of Allah until he returned to them from the Tur said: ﴿We did not break our appointment with you by our own power﴾ [20:87]. They were twelve thousand, while all of the Children of Israel were six hundred thousand.

﴿But we were burdened﴾ [20:87] with a dammah on the ha' and a shaddah on the mim with a kasrah. It is read this way by Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Hafs and Ruways. The rest read both letters with a fathah, lightly. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because they carried the ornaments of the people with them, and what they carried was against their will.

﴿Burdens﴾ [20:87], that is, loads, ﴿of the ornaments of the people﴾ [20:87], that is, of their jewelry. They had borrowed it when they wished to go out with Musa, peace be upon him, and gave them the impression that they would gather for a festival of theirs or a wedding feast. It is also said: It was what they had taken from the household of Pharaoh when the sea cast them onto the shore. They were called "burdens" because they were sins, meaning it was not lawful for them to take them, and spoils of war were not lawful for them. Also, "awzar" in the language means loads.

﴿So we threw it﴾ [20:87], that is, the burden of the jewelry that was with us became heavy on us, so we cast it into the fire to melt, meaning we threw it in. It is also said: We threw it to al-Samiri, so that he would come back and see his opinion in it. Qatadah said: When the people were slow to hear back from Musa, al-Samiri said to them: "He has only been delayed on your account, because of the jewelry you have." So they gathered it and handed it over to al-Samiri, and he threw it into the fire and fashioned a calf from it for them. Then he cast upon it a handful of the trace of the horse of the Messenger, who was Jibril, peace be upon him. Maʿmar said: The horse on which Jibril rode was alive, and when he cast the handful upon it, it became a calf with a body that made a lowing sound. "Khuwar" is the sound of cattle. Ibn ʿAbbas said: When the jewelry poured out into the fire, al-Samiri came and said to Harun: "O Prophet of Allah, shall I cast what is in my hand?" He thought it was like some of the other jewelry that had come with others. Then he threw dust into it and said: "Be a calf with a body that has a lowing sound." It became as he said, as a trial and temptation, and it lowed one single lowing, and did not follow it with another like it. It is also said: Its lowing and its voice were by the wind, because he had made holes in it, and when the wind entered its belly, it lowed, and there was no life in it. This is the view of Mujahid. According to the first view, it was a calf of flesh and blood, and this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Hammad narrated from Simak, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Harun passed by al-Samiri while he was making the calf, and said: "What is this?" He said: "It benefits and does not harm." Harun said: "O Allah, give him what he asks of You according to what is in his heart." Then al-Samiri said: "O Allah, I ask You that it may low." And whenever it lowed, they prostrated, and the lowing came about because of Harun's supplication. Ibn ʿAbbas said: It lowed the way a living calf lows. It is also narrated that Musa said: "O my Lord, this al-Samiri has brought forth for them a calf with a body and a lowing sound from their jewelry. Who made the body and the lowing?" Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: "I did." Musa, peace be upon him, said: "By Your might and Your majesty, Your exaltedness, Your loftiness and Your sovereignty, none has misled them but You." He said: "You have spoken truly, O Wisest of the wise." All of this has already been mentioned in full in Surah al-Aʿraf [see vol. 7, p. 284 onward].

﴿So they said: "This is your god and the god of Musa"﴾ [20:88], meaning: al-Samiri said it, and whoever followed him, and they were inclined toward anthropomorphism, when they said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:138]. ﴿But he forgot﴾ [20:88], meaning Musa left his god behind and went off seeking him, so he did not know where he was and went astray on the way to his Lord. It is also said: The meaning is that Musa left his god here and went out seeking him, meaning Musa left his god here. Israʾil narrated from Simak, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: That is, Musa forgot to tell you that He is his god. It is also said: The address is a report about al-Samiri, meaning al-Samiri abandoned what Musa had commanded him regarding faith, and so he went astray. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said this.

Then Allah the Exalted, arguing against them, said: ﴿Do they not see﴾ [20:89], meaning: do they not reflect and consider? [In (anna), a manuscript variant.] ﴿That it does not return to them a word﴾ [20:89], meaning it does not speak to them. It is also said: It does not return to the lowing and the sound.

﴿And it does not possess for them any harm or benefit﴾ [20:89]. How then could it be a god? The One whom Musa, peace be upon him, worships harms and benefits, rewards and gives, and withholds. The phrase ﴿that it does not return﴾ [20:89], its estimated form is "that it does not return," and so the verb is in the nominative, and "anna" was lightened and the pronoun was omitted. This is the preferred usage with verbs of seeing, knowing and thinking. The poet said:

"Among youths of Indian swords, who have known
That everyone who goes barefoot or wears sandals is doomed."

It may also be omitted with the shaddah, as the poet said:

"If you were a Dabbi, you would have known my kinship,
But I am a Zanji with enormous lips."

That is, "but you are."

﴿Or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ [20:86]. "Yahilla" means: be due and descend. "Ghadab" means punishment and retribution. The meaning is: Did you wish to do an act that would be the cause of Allah's wrath descending upon you? Because no one seeks Allah's wrath, but a person may commit what becomes a cause of anger. [Manuscript variant: "wrath of the Lord" in some copies.]

﴿So you broke your appointment with me﴾ [20:86], because they had promised him that they would remain upon the obedience of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, until he returned to them from the Tur. It is also said: He had promised them, as he went, to wait for the appointed time, but they hesitated.

﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power"﴾ [20:87]. It is read with a fathah on the mim, and this is the reading of Nafiʿ, ʿAsim and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar. The rest read both letters with a fathah, lightly. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because they carried the ornaments of the people with them, and what they carried was against their will.

It is also said: It was what they had taken from the household of Pharaoh when the sea cast them onto the shore. Maʿmar said: The horse on which Jibril rode was alive, and when he cast the handful upon it, it became a calf with a body that made a lowing sound. "Khuwar" is the sound of cattle. It is also said: The meaning is that Musa left his god here and went out seeking him, meaning Musa left his god here. Israʾil narrated from Simak, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: That is, Musa forgot to tell you that He is his god. It is also said: The address is a report about al-Samiri, meaning al-Samiri abandoned what Musa had commanded him regarding faith, and so he went astray. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said this.

[In (anna), a manuscript variant.] ﴿That it does not return to them a word﴾ [20:89], meaning it does not speak to them. It is also said: It does not return to the lowing and the sound.

That is, "but you are."

So His words: ﴿They are right behind me﴾ [20:84] do not mean that they were walking behind him in his direction. Rather, he meant that they were close to me, waiting for my return to them. The matter became so burdensome for him that he tore his garment. Then he could not bear it, so he left them behind and went on alone. When he stood in his place, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ [20:83]. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 90–93:

Allah's words: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before [Musa returned]﴾ [20:90], meaning before Musa came and returned to them. ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it﴾ [20:90], meaning you are being tried and led astray by it, that is, by the calf.

﴿And your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ [20:90], not the calf.

﴿So follow me﴾ in worshipping Him.

﴿And obey my command﴾ [20:90], not the command of the Samiri. Or: follow me on my way to Musa and leave the calf. But they disobeyed him and ﴿said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us"﴾ [20:91], meaning we will not cease to remain upon the worship of the calf. ﴿Until Musa returns to us﴾ [20:91], so that he may see whether he worships it as we have worshipped it. They imagined that Musa worshipped the calf. So Harun withdrew from them with twelve thousand men who had not worshipped the calf. When Musa returned and heard the shouting and tumult, for they were dancing around the calf, he said to the seventy men with him, "This is the sound of trial." When Harun saw this, he seized his head by its hair with his right hand and his beard with his left, in anger, and ﴿Musa said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray﴾ [20:92], meaning they had erred from the path and disbelieved.

﴿That you did not follow me﴾ [20:93]. The "lā" [in alla tattabi'an] is superfluous, meaning "that you did not follow my command and my instruction." It has also been said: what prevented you from following me in denouncing them? It has also been said: the meaning is, why did you not fight them, since you knew that if I had been among them I would have fought them over their disbelief? It has also been said: what prevented you from joining me when they were tried?

﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ [20:93]. He means that your remaining among them while they worshipped other than Allah, the Exalted, is disobedience on your part toward me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: the meaning is, why did you not part from them? Your parting from them would have been a rebuke and a deterrent to them. As for the meaning of "Did you then disobey my command?" it has been said: his command is what Allah, the Exalted, relates of him: ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 142]. When he remained with them and did not strive to prevent them or to denounce them, he attributed to him disobedience and opposition to his command.

Issue: All of this is a basis for enjoining good and forbidding evil, for changing wrongdoing, and for separating from its people. Whoever remains among them, especially when he is content with their ruling, is like them. This matter has already been discussed in Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf and al-Anfal.

The Imam Abu Bakr al-Tartushi, may God have mercy on him, was asked: "What does our master the jurist say about the doctrine of the Sufis? Let him be informed, may God preserve his lifespan, that a group of men gather and frequently mention God, the Exalted, and mention Muhammad (ﷺ). Then they strike a stick upon a piece of leather, and some of them stand up, dancing and entering ecstasy until one of them falls unconscious. They bring something for them to eat. Is attending with them permissible or not? Give us a fatwa, and may you be rewarded, [may God have mercy on you]." And this saying they recite:

"O shaykh, refrain from sins ...
before separation and slipping.

Act righteously for yourself
while righteous deeds still benefit you.

As for youth, it has passed,
and the whiteness of your head has come down."

Regarding this and similar matters, the answer, may God have mercy on you: the doctrine of the Sufis is idleness, ignorance and misguidance. Islam is nothing but the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger. As for dancing and ecstatic swaying, the first to introduce it were the companions of the Samiri, when he made for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound. They stood dancing around it and swaying in ecstasy. So it is the religion of the disbelievers and the worshippers of the calf. As for the stick, the first to adopt it were the heretics (zanadiqa), so that they might occupy the Muslims away from the Book of God, the Exalted. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sit with his companions as though birds were upon their heads from gravity. Therefore the ruler and his deputies should prevent them from attending the mosques and other places. It is not lawful for anyone who believes in God and the Last Day to attend with them or to help them in their falsehood. This is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others among the imams of the Muslims. And success is from God.

When Harun saw this, he seized his head by its hair with his right hand and his beard with his left, in anger, and ﴿Musa said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray﴾ [20:92], meaning they had erred from the path and disbelieved.

﴿That you did not follow me﴾ [20:93]. The "lā" [in alla tattabi'an] is superfluous, meaning "that you did not follow my command and my instruction." It has also been said: what prevented you from following me in denouncing them? It has also been said: the meaning is, why did you not fight them, since you knew that if I had been among them I would have fought them over their disbelief? It has also been said: what prevented you from joining me when they were tried?

﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ [20:93]. He means that your remaining among them while they worshipped other than Allah, the Exalted, is disobedience on your part toward me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: the meaning is, why did you not part from them? Your parting from them would have been a rebuke and a deterrent to them. As for the meaning of "Did you then disobey my command?" it has been said: his command is what Allah, the Exalted, relates of him: ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 142]. When he remained with them and did not strive to prevent them or to denounce them, he attributed to him disobedience and opposition to his command.

Issue: All of this is a basis for enjoining good and forbidding evil, for changing wrongdoing, and for separating from its people. Whoever remains among them, especially when he is content with their ruling, is like them. This matter has already been discussed in Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf and al-Anfal.

The Imam Abu Bakr al-Tartushi, may God have mercy on him, was asked: "What does our master the jurist say about the doctrine of the Sufis? Let him be informed, may God preserve his lifespan, that a group of men gather and frequently mention God, the Exalted, and mention Muhammad (ﷺ). Then they strike a stick upon a piece of leather, and some of them stand up, dancing and entering ecstasy until one of them falls unconscious. They bring something for them to eat. Is attending with them permissible or not? Give us a fatwa, and may you be rewarded, [may God have mercy on you]." And this saying they recite:

"O shaykh, refrain from sins ...
before separation and slipping.

Act righteously for yourself
while righteous deeds still benefit you.

As for youth, it has passed,
and the whiteness of your head has come down."

Regarding this and similar matters, the answer, may God have mercy on you: the doctrine of the Sufis is idleness, ignorance and misguidance. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*) on Surah 20, verses 94–98 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head!﴾ Ibn Abbas said: He took his hair with his right hand and his beard with his left, because zeal for God had overcome him, meaning: do not do this, lest they suppose that it is from you contempt or punishment. It has also been said that Musa (peace be upon him) only did this without contempt or punishment, as a man takes hold of his own beard. This has been treated in full in (Surat) al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, pp. 289 ff., and pp. 286 and 253.]]. God, Mighty and Majestic, knows best what His Prophet (peace be upon him) intended.

﴿I feared that you would say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel"﴾ [20:94]. That is: I feared that I would leave them and go out, while you had commanded me to go out with them. If I had gone out, some people would have followed me and others would have stayed behind with the calf, and perhaps the matter would have led to the shedding of blood. And I feared that if I restrained them, fighting would break out and you would blame me for that. This was Harun's answer to Musa, regarding his words: ﴿Did you disobey my command?﴾ [20:93]. In al-A'raf it is said: ﴿The people overpowered me and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾ [7:150], because you had commanded me to be with them. This has already been mentioned.

﴿And you did not observe my word﴾ [20:94]: you did not act on my instruction to protect them, because you had commanded me to be with them. This was said by Muqatil. Abu Ubayda said: you did not wait for my covenant and my return.

Musa then left him and turned to al-Samiri, and said: ﴿What is your affair, O Samiri?﴾ [20:95]. That is: what is your matter and your situation, and what drove you to what you have done? Qatadah said: al-Samiri was a notable among the Children of Israel, from a tribe called Samirah, but the enemy of God became a hypocrite after he had crossed the sea with Musa. When the Children of Israel passed by the Amalekites, who were devoted to their idols, they said: ﴿O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [7:138]. Al-Samiri seized this opportunity, knowing that they inclined toward worshipping the calf, so he made a calf.

He answered Musa, saying: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ [20:96]. That is: I saw what they did not see. I saw Jibril (peace be upon him) on the steed of life, and it was placed in my soul that I should take a handful from his footprint. Whatever I threw onto anything became living, with flesh and blood. So when they asked you to make a god for them, my soul made that appealing to me.

Ali (may God be pleased with him) said: When Jibril descended to ascend with Musa (peace be upon him) to the heaven, al-Samiri saw him among the people and took a handful from the hoofprint of the horse. It was also said that al-Samiri said: I saw Jibril on the horse, and it was throwing its step as far as the eye could see, so it was placed in my soul to take a handful from its trace, and whatever I threw onto anything became alive with spirit and blood. It was also said: he saw Jibril on the day he descended upon a mare in heat (*ramakah wadiq*). [[Al-ramakah: a mare, and the female horse kept for breeding; it is an arabicized word. Here it means the mare. Al-wadiq: the one in heat, desiring the stallion.]] The horses of Pharaoh went ahead into the sea's waters. It is also said that the mother of al-Samiri, when she gave birth to him, put him in a cave for fear that Pharaoh would kill him, and Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and placed the hand of al-Samiri in the mouth of al-Samiri, so he sucked honey and milk, and [Jibril] kept coming to him, and from then on he recognized him. This meaning has already been mentioned in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 274.]].

It is also said that al-Samiri heard the speech of Musa (peace be upon him) when he made two images of wax, one a bull and the other a horse, and he threw them into the Nile seeking the grave of Yusuf (peace be upon him), which was in a stone coffin in the Nile. The bull brought it to him on its horn. Then al-Samiri spoke with that speech which he had heard from Musa, and threw the handful into the belly of the calf, and it lowed.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Khalaf read ﴿what you did not perceive﴾ with a *ta'* (second person, addressing). The rest read it with a *ya'* (third person, narrative). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿so I took a handful﴾ (*faqabasttu qabsatan*) with an unpointed *sad* (ص). It is also reported from al-Hasan that he vowelled the *qaf* of *qabdatan* with a *damma* while the *sad* is unpointed. The rest read *qabadtu qabdatan* with the pointed *dad* (ض). The difference between them is that *al-qabd* is with the whole palm, and *al-qabs* is with the tips of the fingers; similar are *al-khadm* and *al-qadm*. *Al-qubdah* with a *damma* on the *qaf* is the amount grasped, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Al-Jawhari did not mention *qubsah* with a *damma* on the *qaf* and an unpointed *sad*; he mentioned only *al-qubdah* with a *damma* on the *qaf* and a pointed *dad*, which is what one grasps of something. It is said: he gave him a *qubdah* of sawiq or dates, meaning a handful of it; it may also come with a *fatha*. He said: *al-qabd*, with a *kasra* on the *qaf* and an unpointed *sad*, is a large number of people. Al-Kumayt said:

For you are the two mosques of God, the visited ones, and the pebbles;
for you is a *qibs* from between the wealthy and the poor.
[[That is, between the rich and the poor.]]

﴿So I threw it﴾ [20:96]: that is, I cast it into the calf.

﴿And thus my soul made it appealing to me﴾ [20:96]: that is, it adorned it for me. This was said by al-Akhfash. Ibn Zayd said: my soul spoke to me. The meanings are close.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "Go!"﴾ [20:97]: that is, Musa said to him: Go, away from us. ﴿For in life it is yours to say, "No contact"﴾ [20:97]: that is, "Do not touch me, and I will not touch anyone, all my life." So Musa banished him from his people and commanded the Children of Israel not to mix with him, nor approach him, nor speak to him, as a punishment for him. [And God knows best [[From K.]]]. The poet said:

The Tamim are like the family of al-Samiri, and his saying,
"No, no contact," for al-Samiri does not desire contact.

Al-Hasan said: God made the punishment of al-Samiri that no one should touch him or be touched by him, as a punishment for him and for those who were of his kind until the Day of Resurrection. It is as if God, Mighty and Majestic, intensified the trial upon him by making him unable to touch anyone, and unable to be touched by anyone, and made that a punishment for him in this world. It is said: he was afflicted with *waswasah* (whisperings), and the origin of *waswasah* dates from that time. Qatadah said: their remnants to this day say it, "No contact," and if anyone from outside touches one of them, both of them become feverish at once. It is also said that Musa intended to kill al-Samiri, and God, Exalted, said to him: Do not kill him, for he is generous. It is also said that when Musa said to him, "Go, for in life it is yours to say, 'No contact,'" he feared and fled, and began to wander in the wilderness with beasts of prey and wild animals, finding no one who would touch him, until he became like one who says, "No contact," because he was far from people and people were far from him. As the poet said:

Bearer of banners with them spears [...],
until the Azd say, "No, no contact."
[[Thus in the sources, and we have not located it.]]

Issue: This verse is a basis for the banishment of the people of innovation and sin, their abandonment, and not mixing with them. The Prophet (peace be upon him) did this to Ka'b ibn Malik and the three who stayed behind [[In K: "and his two companions."]]. Regarding one who seeks refuge in the Sacred Precinct while owing a killing, some jurists hold that he is not to be killed there, but he is not to be dealt with, sold to, or bought from, and he is pressured to leave. Of this kind is banishment as a *hadd* (prescribed punishment) for fornication. All of this has been fully discussed in its proper place, so there is no point in repeating it. All praise is due to God alone.

Harun al-Qari said: In the language of the Arabs, *la misas* is with a *kasra* on the *sin* and a *fatha* on the *mim*. The grammarians have discussed it. Sibawayh said: it is built on the *kasra*, as one says *idrib al-rajul* ("strike the man"). Abu Ishaq said: *la misas* is a negation, and the *sin* was given a *kasra* because the *kasra* is a sign of the feminine; you say *fa'alti ya imra'ah* ("you did, O woman"). [[Thus in al-Nahhas. What is in the originals reads: *fa'alat al-mar'ah*.]] Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: when a word is defective in three respects, it must be built (indeclinable); when it is defective in two respects, it must be non-declinable, because after non-declension only building remains. So *misas* and *dirak* are defective in three respects: it is *ma'dul* (altered from its original form), it is feminine, and it is definite. When building became necessary for it, and the *alif* before the *sin* was quiescent, the *sin* was given a *kasra* due to the meeting of two quiescent letters, as you say *idrib al-rajul*. I saw Abu Ishaq holding that this statement is wrong, and he argued against Abu al-Abbas that if one named a woman *Fir'awn*, he would have to build it, and no one says this. Al-Jawhari said in *al-Sihah*: As for the Arabs' saying *la misas*, in the pattern of *qatam*, it is built on the *kasra* because it is altered from the verbal noun, which is *al-mass* (touching). Abu Haywah read *la misas*.

﴿And indeed you have a appointment you will not fail to keep﴾ [20:97]: meaning the Day of Resurrection. *Al-mawid* is a verbal noun, that is, you have a promise of your punishment. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read *tukhlifahu* with a *kasra* on the *lam*, which has two meanings. One: you will come to it, and you will not find it failed, as you say *ahmadtuhu*, meaning I found him praiseworthy. The second, as a threat: you must inevitably arrive at it. The rest read it with a *fatha* on the *lam*, meaning: God will not fail you in it.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And look at your god to which you remained devoted﴾ [20:97]: that is, you continued and persisted in it. ﴿Devoted﴾ [20:97]: that is, staying constantly, and its origin is *zalalta*. The poet said:

Except that the noble camels among the mounts
feel it, and toward it they are *shus* [wide-eyed, sidelong].
[[Abu Zubayd. *Al-shus* (with vowel marking) — Ibn Sida said: that one looks with one eye and tilts his face toward the side of the eye he looks with; this is natural, or it results from pride, arrogance or anger.]]

That is, *ahassna* (they feel it). Likewise al-A'mash read it with two *lams* according to the original form. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *zilta* with a *kasra* on the *za'*. It is said: *zallaltu af'alu kadha* when you do it during the day, and *zaltu* and *zilt*. Whoever says *zalt* drops the first *lam* for lightness, and whoever says *zilt* transfers the vowel of the *lam* onto the *za'*.

﴿We will surely burn it﴾ [20:97]: the common reading is with a *damma* on the *nun* and a shadda on the *ra'*, from *harraqa yuharriqu*. Al-Hasan and others read with a *damma* on the *nun*, a sukun on the *ha'*, and a light *ra'*, from *ahraqahu yuhriquhu*. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin and Ashhab al-Uqayli read *lanahrquannahu* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, lightly, from *harqtu al-shay'a ahruquhu harqan*, meaning: I filed it and rubbed some of it against another. From this comes their saying *harqa nabahu yuhriquhu* and *yahrquhu*, meaning he ground it until a grinding sound was heard. So the meaning of this reading is: *lanabriданnahu bi-al-mabarid*, "we will file it with files." The file is called *al-mihraq*. The first two readings mean burning with fire, and it is possible to combine these meanings in it. Al-Suddi said: he slaughtered the calf and blood flowed from it as blood flows from a calf when slaughtered, then he filed its bones with a file and burned it. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "we will slaughter it, then we will surely burn it." When flesh and blood are burned they become ash, so it can be scattered into the sea. As for gold, it does not become ash. It was also said: Musa knew what would turn the gold into ash, and that was one of his signs.

*Lananfa'annahu* [20:97] means "we will scatter it." Abu Raja read *lananfusannahu* with a *damma* on the *sin*; both are dialects. *Al-nasf* is shaking a thing so that the wind carries it away, which is winnowing. *Al-minsaf* is what grain is winnowed with, and it is an object whose front is inclined with its top raised. *Al-nusafah* is what falls from it. It is said: "Separate the *nusafah* and collect the pure." It is also said: "So-and-so came to us as if his beard were a *minsaf*," related by Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim. *Al-minsafah* is a tool with which a building is pulled down. *Nasafa al-bina' nasfan* means he tore down the building. *Nasafa al-ba'ir al-kala'* means the camel uprooted the pasture with its roots when it pulled it out completely. *Intasaftu al-shay'* means I uprooted the thing. This is from Abu Zayd.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi on Surah 20, verses 94–98 (Part 2 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no god. He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ [20:98]. Not the calf. That is, His knowledge encompasses everything. He does an act out of knowledge. The word *ʿilman* is in the accusative as a *tafsir* (specification, the grammatical term for a clarifying accusative).

Mujahid and Qatadah read it as *wasiʿa kulla shayʾin ʿilman* [20:98], with a verb in the past tense.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*) on Surah 20, verses 94–98 (part 1 of 2):

[[Abu Zubayd. *Al-shus* (with vowel marking) — Ibn Sida said: that one looks with one eye and tilts his face toward the side of the eye he looks with; this is natural, or it results from pride, arrogance or anger.]]

That is, *ahassna* (they feel it). Likewise al-A'mash read it with two *lams* according to the original form. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *zilta* with a *kasra* on the *za'*. It is said: *zallaltu af'alu kadha* when you do it during the day, and *zaltu* and *zilt*. Whoever says *zalt* drops the first *lam* for lightness, and whoever says *zilt* transfers the vowel of the *lam* onto the *za'*.

﴿We will surely burn it﴾ [20:97]: the common reading is with a *damma* on the *nun* and a shadda on the *ra'*, from *harraqa yuharriqu*. Al-Hasan and others read with a *damma* on the *nun*, a sukun on the *ha'*, and a light *ra'*, from *ahraqahu yuhriquhu*. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin and Ashhab al-Uqayli read *lanahrquannahu* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, lightly, from *harqtu al-shay'a ahruquhu harqan*, meaning: I filed it and rubbed some of it against another. From this comes their saying *harqa nabahu yuhriquhu* and *yahrquhu*, meaning he ground it until a grinding sound was heard. So the meaning of this reading is: *lanabriданnahu bi-al-mabarid*, "we will file it with files." The file is called *al-mihraq*. The first two readings mean burning with fire, and it is possible to combine these meanings in it. Al-Suddi said: he slaughtered the calf and blood flowed from it as blood flows from a calf when slaughtered, then he filed its bones with a file and burned it. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "we will slaughter it, then we will surely burn it." When flesh and blood are burned they become ash, so it can be scattered into the sea. As for gold, it does not become ash. It was also said: Musa knew what would turn the gold into ash, and that was one of his signs.

*Lananfa'annahu* [20:97] means "we will scatter it." Abu Raja read *lananfusannahu* with a *damma* on the *sin*; both are dialects. *Al-nasf* is shaking a thing so that the wind carries it away, which is winnowing. *Al-minsaf* is what grain is winnowed with, and it is an object whose front is inclined with its top raised. *Al-nusafah* is what falls from it. It is said: "Separate the *nusafah* and collect the pure." It is also said: "So-and-so came to us as if his beard were a *minsaf*," related by Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim. *Al-minsafah* is a tool with which a building is pulled down. *Nasafa al-bina' nasfan* means he tore down the building. *Nasafa al-ba'ir al-kala'* means the camel uprooted the pasture with its roots when it pulled it out completely. *Intasaftu al-shay'* means I uprooted the thing. This is from Abu Zayd.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi on Surah 20, verses 94–98 (Part 2 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no god. He encompasses all things in knowledge﴾ [20:98]. Not the calf. That is, His knowledge encompasses everything. He does an act out of knowledge. The word *ʿilman* is in the accusative as a *tafsir* (specification, the grammatical term for a clarifying accusative).

Mujahid and Qatadah read it as *wasiʿa kulla shayʾin ʿilman* [20:98], with a verb in the past tense.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 99–104:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾ The kaf is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: as We have related to you the account of Musa, thus We relate to you, a relating like this, of reports of what has already passed, so that it may be a consolation for you and to show the truth of your prophethood.

﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ [20:99] means the Qur'an. The Qur'an was called a reminder (dhikr) because of the remembrance (dhikr) contained in it, just as the Messenger was called a reminder, because the reminder (dhikr) used to descend upon him. It has also been said that ﴿a reminder from Us﴾ [20:99] means honour (sharaf), as Exalted is He said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you﴾ [43:44], that is, an honour and a elevation of your name.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾ [20:100], that is, from the Qur'an, so that he does not believe in it and does not act upon what is in it. ﴿Indeed, he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ [20:100], that is, a great sin and a heavy load.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ [20:101] means remaining in it, that is, in its recompense, and its recompense is Hell.

﴿And evil will it be for them as a load on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [20:101] means: how evil is the load that they carry on the Day of Resurrection. Dawud ibn Rufay' read: "fa-innahu yuhammalu" (it will be made to carry).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Day the Horn is blown﴾ The reading of the majority is "yunfakhu" with a damma on the yaa, as a passive verb. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a nun, as an active verb (the nun of the first person). Abu 'Amr supported this by the saying of Exalted is He: "wa-nahshuru" with a nun. From Ibn Hurmuz: "yanfukhu" with a fatha on the yaa, meaning Israfil blows. Abu 'Iyad read "fi al-sur". The rest read "fi al-sur". This has been discussed in full earlier in (al-An'am) [see vol. 7, p. 20 onward] and in the book (al-Tadhkirah). Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wa-yuhsharu" with a damma on the yaa, "al-mujrimun" in the nominative, contrary to the Mushaf. The rest read: ﴿And We will gather the criminals﴾ [20:102], that is, the polytheists.

(Zurqan) [20:102] is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "al-mujrimin". Al-zaraq is the opposite of kohl (collyrium). The Arabs regard blue eyes as an ill omen and disparage them, meaning their creation is disfigured by the blueness of their eyes and the blackness of their faces. Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: "zurqan" means blind. Al-Azhari said [i.e., ...] they are thirsty, their eyes having turned blue from the intensity of thirst; al-Zajjaj also said this, saying: because the blackness of the eye changes and turns blue from thirst. It has also been said that it is false hope when it is followed by disappointment; it is said: "my eye has turned white from the long wait for such-and-such." A fifth opinion: the meaning of the blueness is the staring of the gaze from intense fear. The poet said:

Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Mu'kabar,
As every Dabbi is blue from baseness.

It is said: a man with blue eyes (azraq al-'ayn), and a woman is zarqa'a, clearly blue-eyed. The noun is zurqa. His eye turned blue (zarigat 'aynuhu) with the kasra, and azraqqat 'aynuhu, izraqaqan, and azra'arrat 'aynuhu, izriqaqan. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about His saying: "And We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed" [20:102], and in another place He said: "And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf" [17:97]. He said: the Day of Resurrection has states; in one state they will be blue-eyed, and in another state blind.

(Yatakhafatuna baynahum) [20:103]. The root of khafat in the language is stillness; then whoever lowers his voice is called khafit. [The meaning is] they whisper to one another, as Mujahid said, that is, some say to others in the place of standing, secretly. (In labithtum) means: how long you remained, that is, in the world; it has also been said: in the graves. (Illa 'ashran) [20:103] means ten nights. It has also been said: he meant the period between the two blasts, which is forty years, during which the punishment is lifted from the disbelievers, according to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, so they consider that period short. Or the period of their stay in the world, because of the intensity of what they see of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. And it appears to the most just of them, that is, the most upright in speech, the most intelligent and the most knowledgeable in his own estimation, that they remained only one day, meaning their stay in the world, according to Qatadah; so the estimate is: "except like a day." It has also been said: because of the intensity of the terror of the arrival, they forgot the delights of the world they had been in, and saw it as a day. It has also been said: by the day of their staying he meant the period between the two blasts, or their stay in the graves, as previously mentioned. "Ashran" and "yawman" are accusative, governed by "labithtum".

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 105–110:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will ask you about the mountains﴾ [20:105], meaning: about the condition of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection.

(So say) [This appears with a fa' (فَـ) in the source: فقد [[من ك.]]] This occurs with a fa', and every question in the Qur'an is introduced by "Say" without a fa' except this one. The reason is that the meaning is: "If they ask you about the mountains, then say," so the sentence contains the sense of a conditional. Allah knew that they would ask him about them, so He answered them before the question was asked. Those are questions that had already occurred, which they asked of the Prophet ﷺ, and the answer came immediately after the question; therefore it was without a fa'. This is a question they had not yet asked him, so understand it.

(He will scatter them) [20:105] means: He will make them fly. Ibn al-A'rabi and others said: He will uproot them from their roots, then make them into sand that flows like a stream, then make them like carded wool that the winds scatter this way and that. He said: "Ihn" (wool) is only the dyed kind. Then they become like scattered dust.

(And leave it) [20:106] means: He will leave their places (as) a level plain, bare and smooth [20:106]. Al-qa' is level ground without plants or buildings, as Ibn al-A'rabi said. Al-Jawhari said: al-qa' is the level part of the earth, and its plural is aqw', aqwa' and qi'an. The waw became a ya' because the letter before it is kasra. Al-Farra' said: al-qa' is a pool of standing water, and al-safsaf is the bare, barren land. Al-Kalbi said: it is the place where there is no vegetation. It was also said: it is the level part of the earth, as if it were in one row in its evenness; this was said by Mujahid. The meaning of al-qa' and al-safsaf is one and the same: al-qa' is an uncovered place, and al-safsaf is a level, smooth place. Sibawayh recited (the verse is by al-A'sha, who described the distance between himself and the patron he was heading to, in order to deserve his reward. Al-dakdak is level sand. Al-a'qad is the plural of 'uqdah, which is sand that is packed and piled up):

"How many a safsaf lies between you and your house,
and dakdak of sand and its 'aqad."

Qa'an [20:106] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and al-safsaf (is in apposition to it).

(You will not see) [20:107] is in the place of a descriptive clause.

(Any crookedness in it) [20:107]. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-'iwaj is irregularity in the paths. Al-amt is the nabak. Abu Amr said: al-amt is al-nibak, which are small hills, whose singular is nabak; that is, it is a level land with no depression and no elevation. You say: "It became full, and there was no amt in it," and "I filled the waterskin fully, with no amt in it," meaning no slackness in it. In the language, al-amt is an elevated place. Ibn Abbas said: "'iwajan" means a slope. He said: al-amt is a trace, like the thong of a sandal. He also said, regarding "'iwajan": a valley; and "wa la amtan": a hillock. He also said: al-'awaj is depression, and al-amt is elevation. Qatadah said: "'iwajan" means a fissure.

(Nor any elevation) [20:107], that is, a mound. Yaman said: al-amt is the cracks in the earth. It was also said: al-amt is when a place is thick in the open plain or in the mountain and thin in another place; this was related by al-Suli.

I say: This verse falls under the category of incantations (ruqa), by which warts are treated. These are what we call "al-baraziq," whose singular is "buruqah." They appear on the body, especially on the hand. You take three stalks of barley straw, with a knot at the end of each stalk. You pass each knot over the warts while reciting the verse once, then you bury the stalks in a damp place, and they rot and the warts rot, so no trace of them remains. I tested this on myself and on others, and I found it beneficial, God willing, (in the source: "beneficial, by God, and praise be to God." In another manuscript: "beneficial, by God's permission, and praise be to God.").

The words of the Exalted: ﴿On that day they will follow the summoner﴾ [20:108], meaning Israfil, peace be upon him, when he blows into the Trumpet. (There is no crookedness in it) [20:108], meaning: they have no deviation from it. That is, from his summons they do not turn aside or veer off, but rush toward it and do not swerve from it. Most scholars hold this view. It was also said: "There is no crookedness in it" means: for his summons. It was also said: they follow the summoner with a following that has no crookedness; so the verbal noun is implied, and the meaning is: they follow the voice of the summoner to the gathering. Its parallel is the verse: ﴿And listen on the day the caller calls from a nearby place﴾ [50:41], and so on. This will come later. (see vol. 17, p. 26).

(And the voices will be hushed) [20:108], meaning they will be humbled and silent. From Ibn Abbas, who said: When the news of al-Zubayr came, the villages of Medina and the mountains humbled themselves, so every tongue there was silent out of awe.

(Before the Most Merciful) means: because of Him.

(You will hear nothing but a whisper) [20:108]. Al-hams is a hidden sound, said Mujahid. From Ibn Abbas: a hidden sensation. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: it is the sound of footsteps, some upon others, going to the gathering. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"And they walk with us, whispering."

He means the sound of camels' hooves in their march. The lion is called al-hamus, because it whispers in the darkness, i.e., it treads with a hidden step. Ru'bah, describing himself as strong, said:

"A lion who crushes the lion that whispers, and the two dark ones [he called the elephant and the buffalo two dark ones because of their color, which is dun],
the elephant and the buffalo."

Hamasa al-ta'am means he chewed food with his mouth closed. The rajaz poet said:

"I have seen something strange since yesterday,
old women like the ghouls, five of them,
eating what I make, whispering, whispering."

It was also said: al-hams is the moving of the lips and tongue. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "So they will not speak except in a whisper." The meanings are close: that is, no speech, no words and no sound of footsteps are heard from them. The root h-m-s is basically concealment in whatever form it takes, and from it come the whispered letters (al-huruf al-mahmusah), which are ten, gathered by your saying: "Hathhahu shakhsun fasakata" (someone urged him, and he fell silent). A letter is called mahmus only because the pressure from its point of articulation weakens so that breath flows with it.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿On that day intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [20:109]. "Man" (whom) is in the accusative position as an exceptive clause excluded from the first, meaning: intercession will benefit no one except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted.

(And whose word He approves) [20:109], meaning: He approves his word in intercession. It was also said: the meaning is that intercession benefits only the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who had a word that is approved. Ibn Abbas said: it is the word "There is no god but Allah."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾, meaning the matters of the Hour.

(And what is behind them) means the matters of this world; this was said by Qatadah. It was also said: He knows what they will come to of reward or punishment. "And what is behind them" means what they left behind them in the world. Then it was said: the verse is general, covering all creation. It was also said: the intended ones are those who follow the summoner. And praise be to God.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they will not encompass Him with knowledge﴾ [20:110]. The pronoun in "bihi" (by Him) refers to God Exalted; no one encompasses Him in knowledge, since encompassing implies limitation, and God is exalted above being limited. It was also said: it refers to knowledge, meaning no one encompasses by knowledge what God knows. Al-Tabari said: the pronoun in "aydihim" (before them), "khalfahum" (behind them) and "yuhitun" (encompass) refers to the angels; God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them or behind them.

(And the voices will be hushed) [20:108], meaning they will be humbled and silent. From Ibn Abbas, who said: When the news of al-Zubayr came, the villages of Medina and the mountains humbled themselves, so every tongue there was silent out of awe.

(Before the Most Merciful) means: because of Him.

(You will hear nothing but a whisper) [20:108]. Al-hams is a hidden sound, said Mujahid. From Ibn Abbas: a hidden sensation. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: it is the sound of footsteps, some upon others, going to the gathering. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"And they walk with us, whispering."

He means the sound of camels' hooves in their march. The lion is called al-hamus, because it whispers in the darkness, i.e., it treads with a hidden step. Ru'bah, describing himself as strong, said:

"A lion who crushes the lion that whispers, and the two dark ones [he called the elephant and the buffalo two dark ones because of their color, which is dun],
the elephant and the buffalo."

Hamasa al-ta'am means he chewed food with his mouth closed. The rajaz poet said:

"I have seen something strange since yesterday,
old women like the ghouls, five of them,
eating what I make, whispering, whispering."

It was also said: al-hams is the moving of the lips and tongue. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "So they will not speak except in a whisper." The meanings are close: that is, no speech, no words and no sound of footsteps are heard from them. The root h-m-s is basically concealment in whatever form it takes, and from it come the whispered letters (al-huruf al-mahmusah), which are ten, gathered by your saying: "Hathhahu shakhsun fasakata" (someone urged him, and he fell silent). A letter is called mahmus only because the pressure from its point of articulation weakens so that breath flows with it.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿On that day intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [20:109]. "Man" (whom) is in the accusative position as an exceptive clause excluded from the first, meaning: intercession will benefit no one except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted.

(And whose word He approves) [20:109], meaning: He approves his word in intercession. It was also said: the meaning is that intercession benefits only the one for whom the Most Merciful has permitted intercession, and who had a word that is approved. Ibn Abbas said: it is the word "There is no god but Allah."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾, meaning the matters of the Hour.

(And what is behind them) means the matters of this world; this was said by Qatadah. It was also said: He knows what they will come to of reward or punishment. "And what is behind them" means what they left behind them in the world. Then it was said: the verse is general, covering all creation. It was also said: the intended ones are those who follow the summoner. And praise be to God.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they will not encompass Him with knowledge﴾ [20:110]. The pronoun in "bihi" (by Him) refers to God Exalted; no one encompasses Him in knowledge, since encompassing implies limitation, and God is exalted above being limited. It was also said: it refers to knowledge, meaning no one encompasses by knowledge what God knows. Al-Tabari said: the pronoun in "aydihim" (before them), "khalfahum" (behind them) and "yuhitun" (encompass) refers to the angels; God informed those who worship them that they do not know what is before them or behind them.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 111–112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾ [20:111]. That is, they will be abased and submissive. This is what Ibn al-A'rabi and others said. From this it is said of a captive: ʿanin (a captive). Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"The King over the throne of heaven, the Guardian, / Before His might the faces are abased and prostrate."

And he also said:

"My face and all my creation have humbled themselves / Among those who prostrate to His face, thanked."

Al-Jawhari said: ʿanā yaʿnū means he submitted and was humbled, and aʿnāhu means someone else made him so. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: "And faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting" [20:111]. It is also said: ʿanā fīhim fulān asīran, meaning so-and-so remained among them as a captive and was detained. ʿannāhu ghayruhu taʿniyatan means he detained him. Al-ʿānī is the captive; qawm ʿunāh and niswa ʿawān (plural forms). ʿanat umūr means matters that have befallen. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "ʿanat" means humbled. Mujahid said: it means humbled in fear (khasha'at). Al-Mawardi: the difference between humiliation (dhull) and humility (khushu') — though their meanings are close — is that dhull is being humbled in oneself, while khushu' (submission) is to be lowered before one who is obeyed. Al-Kalbi said: "ʿanat" means knew. ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi: submitted. Talq ibn Habib said: it is placing the forehead and nose on the ground in prostration. Al-Nahhas: regarding "And faces will be humbled" [20:111], there are two views on its meaning. The first: this refers to the Hereafter. ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "And faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting" [20:111] that he said: it is bowing and prostration. The linguistic meaning of ʿanat is subjugation and overpowering, and from it comes the phrase the lands were opened ʿanwatan, meaning by force. The poet said:

"They did not take them by force out of affection, / But the strike of the Indian sword compelled them."

It is also said that it derives from ʿanā, meaning fatigue, and that the faces are mentioned to signify people, because the signs of humiliation are most evident in the face.

(Before the Living, the Self-Subsisting) [20:111]. Regarding al-Qayyum there are three interpretations. The first: He is the One who sustains the management of creation. The second: He is the One who watches over every soul for what it has earned. The third: He is the Everlasting who does not cease or perish. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah).

(And he has indeed failed who carries injustice) [20:111]. That is, he who carries shirk (polytheism) has lost.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer﴾ [20:112], because deeds are not accepted without faith. The "min" in His saying "min al-salihat" is for partitive (tab'id), meaning some of the righteous deeds. It is also said it is for genus (jins).

(So he will not fear) [20:112]. Ibn Kathir, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read "yakhaf" with jazm (apocopation) as an answer to His saying: "And whoever does [evil]" (20:110). The rest read "yakhafu" with raf' (nominative) as a statement, meaning: so he does not fear, or: indeed he does not fear.

(Injustice) means diminution of the reward of his obedience, and no addition to his sins.

(Nor oppression) [20:112] by reduction of his right. Al-hadm is diminution and breaking; it is said: I took that from my right, meaning I reduced and abandoned it. This (food) digests (yahdimu) the food, meaning reduces its weight. A woman with hadim al-kashh is one with a slender waist and a flat belly. Al-Mawardi: the difference between injustice (zulm) and hadm is that zulm is withholding the whole of a right, while hadm is withholding part of it; hadm is nevertheless a form of injustice, though they differ in one respect. Al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi said:

"Indeed the lowly and the base are a group / whose master is the oppressed, the wronged."

Al-Jawhari said: a man who is hadim and muhtadam means one who is wronged. Tahadamahu means he wronged him, and ihtadamahu, when he wronged him and broke his right.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 113–114:

Allah's words: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, as We have explained to you in this surah of clarification, ﴿We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [20:113], that is, in the language of the Arabs.

﴿And We have diversified therein of the warning﴾ [20:113], that is, We have made clear what it contains of intimidation, threat, reward and punishment.

﴿That perhaps they will fear Allah﴾, that is, that they will fear Allah, so they avoid His disobedience and beware of His punishment.

﴿Or it causes them to remember﴾ [20:113], that is, an admonition. Qatadah said: caution and scrupulousness. It was also said: honour, so "dhikr" here means honour, like His words: "And indeed it is a reminder (dhikr) for you and your people" [43:44] [see vol. 16, p. 93]. It was also said: that is, so that they may remember the punishment with which they were threatened. al-Hasan recited "aw nuhdithu" with a nun, and it is related from him that the thā' is read both with a damma and with a jazm.

Allah's words: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the Sovereign, the Truth﴾ [20:114]. When the servants recognised the magnitude of His blessings, and the sending down of the Qur'an, He declared Himself free of children and rivals, saying: "So exalted is Allah", that is, Allah is majestic, ﴿the Sovereign, the Truth﴾ [20:114], that is, the Possessor of truth.

﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is completed﴾ [20:114]. He taught His Prophet how to receive the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, would hurry ahead of Jibril and recite before Jibril had finished the revelation, out of eagerness to memorise and out of concern for the Qur'an, fearing forgetfulness. So Allah forbade him from that and sent down: "And do not hasten with the Qur'an" [20:114]. This is like His words: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [75:16], as will come. Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid that he said: Do not recite it before you have clarified it. It was also said: "And do not hasten" [20:114] means: do not ask for its descent, ﴿before its revelation to you is completed﴾ [20:114], that is, before its revelation comes to you. It was also said: the meaning is, do not convey it to the people before the explanation of its interpretation comes to you. al-Hasan said: It was revealed concerning a man who slapped his wife's face, and she came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking retaliation (qisas), and the Prophet ﷺ granted her retaliation, and then the verse "Men are in charge of women" [4:34] was revealed. This is why He said: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [20:114], that is, in understanding, because he, peace be upon him, had ruled for retaliation, and Allah rejected that. Ibn Mas'ud and others read "min qabli an naqdiya" with a nun and a kasra on the dad, and "wahyahu" with a fatha.
