Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 115:

Regarding His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot﴾ (20:115). Al-A'mash recited ﴿fa-nasiya﴾ (20:88) with a sukun on the ya', according to a variant transmitted from him. It has two meanings. The first is "left," that is, he abandoned the command and the covenant. This is the view of Mujahid and most of the exegetes, and from it comes the verse ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ (9:67) [See vol. 18, p. 43.]. The second meaning [added by the editor for context] is that Ibn Abbas said: "Nasiya" here is from forgetfulness and oblivion, and man was named "insan" because he was given a covenant and then forgot it. Ibn Zayd said: he forgot what Allah had covenanted with him concerning that matter, and had he had resolve (azm), he would not have obeyed His enemy Iblis. According to this view, it is possible that Adam, peace be upon him, was at that time overtaken by forgetfulness, even though forgetfulness is lifted from us today.

The meaning of "min qabl" (before) is: before he ate from the tree, because he had been forbidden from it. The purpose is to console the Prophet ﷺ: the obedience of the children of Adam to Satan is an ancient matter. That is, if these people break the covenant, Adam too was given a covenant and forgot it. This is related by al-Qushayri, and likewise by al-Tabari, meaning: and if these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers, and obey Iblis, then their father Adam did so long ago.

Ibn Atiyya said: this interpretation is weak, because making Adam an example for the disbelievers who deny Allah is nothing, and Adam only disobeyed through interpretation (ta'wil). In this there is an affront to him ﷺ. Rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is either that it begins a narrative with no connection to what precedes it, or that its connection is this: when He covenanted with Muhammad ﷺ not to hasten with the Qur'an, He gave him the example of a prophet before him who was covenanted and forgot, and was punished, so that the warning would be stronger and the covenant with Muhammad ﷺ more emphatic. The "covenant" here means a charge. "Forgot" means "left," and forgetting in the sense of heedlessness is not possible here, because punishment does not attach to one who forgets.

"Azm" (resolve) is persistence upon a conviction in whatever matter it may be. Adam, peace be upon him, had held the conviction not to eat from the tree, but when Iblis whispered to him, he did not hold firm to his conviction. What was covenanted to Adam was that he should not eat from the tree, and he was also informed that Iblis was his enemy.

Scholars differed on the meaning of His statement: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ (20:115). Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: We found in him no patience against eating from the tree, and no steadfastness in observing the command. Al-Nahhas said: this is also the meaning in the language. It is said: "li-fulan azm," meaning patience and firmness in guarding against sins until he is safe from them. From this comes the verse ﴿So be patient, as the resolute messengers were patient﴾ (46:35) [See vol. 16, p. 220.].

It is also related from Ibn Abbas and Atiyya al-Awfi: vigilance (hifz) over what he was commanded, meaning he did not guard himself from what I had forbidden him, until he forgot and was removed from knowledge of that by abandoning inquiry. This is because Iblis said to him: "If you eat it, you will be immortal in Paradise," meaning this very tree. He did not obey him, so Iblis invited him to a tree like that one, one that fell under the general scope of the prohibition, and he should have inferred the prohibition concerning it but did not. He thought it was not included in the prohibition, so he ate it by interpretation. One who knows that a thing is disobedience is not one who has forgotten it.

Ibn Zayd said: "azman" means guarding the command of Allah. Al-Dahhak said: it means determination in the matter. Ibn Kaysan said: it means persistence, without concealing an intention to return to the sin. Al-Qushayri said: the first view is closer to the sense of the statement. For this reason some said: Adam was not among the Resolute Messengers (ulu al-azm), because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ (20:115). But the majority said: the messengers were the Resolute Messengers. In a report: "There is no prophet who has not erred or intended a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." So if Adam had been removed from the number of the Resolute Messengers because of his sin, all the prophets would be removed except Yahya.

Abu Umamah said: the intellects of the children of Adam, from the time Allah created creation until the Day of Resurrection, were gathered and placed in one pan of a scale, and the forbearance (hilm) of Adam was placed in the other pan, and it would outweigh them. And Allah, blessed and exalted, has said: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ (20:115).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 116–119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused﴾. This has been discussed fully in (Surat al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 291 onward.]].

(Then We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you from the Garden, [for then you would be distressed]" [20:117]). It is a prohibition, and its meaning is: do not accept from him, for that would be a cause of your expulsion "from the Garden," "so that you would be distressed" [20:117]. He says: you and your wife, because the cause of distress is equal for both of them, and He did not say "so that you both would be distressed," because the meaning is well known, and Adam, peace be upon him, is the one addressed and is the intended one. Also, since he was the one who toiled for it and earned it, he was more specifically associated with the distress. It was also said: the expulsion applies to both of them, while the distress is for Adam alone, which is bodily distress. Do you not see that He followed it with His saying: "Indeed, it is yours that you do not hunger therein, nor go naked" [20:118], that is, in the Garden, "and that you do not thirst therein, nor are exposed to the sun" [20:119]. So He informed him that in the Garden he has all of this: clothing, food, drink, and shelter, and that if you neglect the commandment and obey the enemy, I will expel you both from the Garden, and you will be distressed with toil and exhaustion, that is, you will hunger, be naked, thirst, and be struck by the sun, because you will be returned to the earth when you are expelled from the Garden. He specified the distress for him and did not say "so that you both would be distressed" to teach us that the maintenance of the wife is upon the husband. From that day, the provision of women became due from husbands, and since Eve's maintenance was upon Adam in this way, the maintenance of her daughters is upon the sons of Adam by right of marriage. In this verse He also informed us that the maintenance that is owed to a woman by her husband is these four: food, drink, clothing, and shelter. So when he gives her these four, he has fulfilled his obligation toward her; if he gives more beyond that, he is rewarded. But these four are indispensable for her, because by them the life is sustained. Al-Hasan said: what is meant by His saying "so that you would be distressed" [20:117] is the distress of this world; the son of Adam is seen only as one who toils. Al-Farra' said: it is that he eats from the labor of his hands. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: a red bull was sent down to Adam, and he would plow with it, wiping the sweat from his brow; that is his distress which Allah, blessed and exalted, mentioned. It was also said: when he was sent down from the Garden, one of the first of his distresses was that Jibril sent down to him some grains from the Garden and said: "O Adam, sow this." So he plowed and sowed, then reaped, then threshed, then winnowed, then ground, then kneaded, then baked, and then he sat down to eat after the toil, and his loaf rolled from his hand until it reached the foot of the mountain, and Adam ran after it until he was exhausted and his brow was sweating. He said: "O Adam, thus is your sustenance with toil and distress, and the sustenance of your offspring after you, for as long as you are in this world."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is yours that you do not hunger therein, nor go naked. And that you do not thirst therein, nor are exposed to the sun﴾ [20:118–119]. In this there are two issues. The first: His saying ﴿Indeed, it is yours that you do not hunger therein﴾ [20:118], that is, in the Garden, "nor go naked" [20:118]. "And that you do not thirst therein" [20:119], that is, you do not become thirsty. Ẓama' is thirst. "Nor are exposed to the sun" [20:119], that is, you do not come out into the sun and feel its heat, for there is no sun in the Garden; rather there is an extended shade, as between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun. Abu al-'Aliyah said: the daytime of the Garden is like this, and he pointed to the time of the worshippers' dawn prayer. Abu Zayd said: "ḍaḥā al-ṭarīq yaḍḥū ḍuḥūwan" means when the road appears and becomes clear to you. "ḍaḥiytu" (with kasra) "ḍaḥan" means I was sweating. "ḍaḥiytu" also, for the sun, "ḍaḥā'an mamdūdan" means I came out into it; and "ḍaḥaytu" (with fatḥa) is similar, and the future is "aḍḥā" in both dialects. ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

A man saw her when the sun was overhead, so he was exposed to it, and in the evening he was in the shade.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 120–122:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ [20:120]. This was discussed in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 177.]].

(He said), meaning Satan: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [20:120]. This indicates direct speech, and that he entered Paradise inside the serpent, as explained earlier in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 308 onward.]]. The tree was identified there, along with what the scholars said about it, so there is no point in repeating it.

﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden﴾ [20:121]. This was discussed fully in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 180.]]. Al-Farra' said: "Taffaqa" in Arabic means "aqbala" (they began). He said: it was also said that they began to stick leaves of the fig tree onto themselves.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ [20:121]. There are six issues in this.

**The first issue:** Allah's words ﴿disobeyed﴾ [20:121] were discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 305.]] in the discussion on the sins of the prophets. One of our later scholars said: What should be said is that Allah has informed us that some of them committed sins, attributed them to them, rebuked them for them, and they themselves informed of this about their own souls, disowned them, sought forgiveness for them and repented. All of this occurs in many places and, taken as a whole, does not admit of interpretation, even if individual instances may admit of it. None of this diminishes their ranks. Those matters that occurred from them were rare, done in error or forgetfulness, or due to an interpretation that prompted them. Relative to others, they are good deeds, but for them they are sins, relative to their ranks and the loftiness of their standing. A minister may be held accountable for what a governor is rewarded for. Therefore, they feared this on the Day of Resurrection, while knowing their security, safety and well-being. He said: This is the truth. Al-Junayd spoke well when he said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." May the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them. Although the texts have testified that some sins occurred from them, this did not harm their ranks nor diminish their station. Rather, He made amends for them, chose them, guided them, praised them, purified them, selected them and chose them, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

**The second issue:** The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about Adam, except when we mention it within the context of Allah's words about him, or the words of His Prophet. As for initiating this on one's own account, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers, those like us, so how much more regarding our father, the most ancient, greatest, most noble, foremost prophet, whom Allah the Exalted excused, accepted repentance from, and forgave. I say: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, and descent, and others, is even more deserving of prohibition. It is not permissible to begin with any of those, except within the recitation of His Book or the sunnah of His Messenger. For this reason, Imam Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever describes any aspect of the Essence of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained"﴾ [5:64], and gestures with his hand to his neck, his hand should be cut off. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened Allah the Exalted to himself.

**The third issue:** The imams narrated, and the wording is from al-Bukhari [[In the originals: the wording is from al-Bukhari. The correction is from Sahih Muslim.]], from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Adam and Musa debated. Musa said: 'O Adam, you are our father. You disappointed us and expelled us from the Garden.' Adam said to him: 'O Musa, Allah the Mighty and Majestic chose you with His speech and wrote for you with His hand. O Musa, do you blame me for a matter that Allah decreed upon me forty years before He created me?' So Adam overcame Musa in argument three times." [[Thrice: i.e., the Prophet ﷺ said "fa-hajja Adam Musa" (Adam overcame Musa) three times.]] Al-Muhallab said: His words "fa-hajja Adam Musa" mean he overcame him with argument. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: The argument of Adam over Musa, peace be upon them both, in this story was valid only because Allah the Exalted had forgiven Adam his error and accepted his repentance. So it was not permissible for Musa to reproach him for a sin that Allah the Exalted had forgiven him. For this reason, Adam said: "You are Musa, whom Allah gave the Torah, in which is the knowledge of everything. Did you find in it that Allah decreed disobedience upon me and decreed repentance from it for me, and thereby removed blame from me? Do you blame me? By Allah, He does not blame me." In a similar manner, Ibn Umar argued against the one who said to him: "Uthman fled on the day of Uhud." Ibn Umar said: "There is no sin upon Uthman, because Allah the Exalted has pardoned him by His words: ﴿And Allah has certainly pardoned them﴾ [3:155]." [[See vol. 4, p. 243.]]

It has also been said: Adam, peace be upon him, is a father, and reproaching him is not an act of righteousness toward him, even if it were something by which others may be reproached. Allah the Blessed and Exalted says regarding two disbelieving parents: ﴿And accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ [31:15]. [[See vol. 14, p. 63.]] For this reason, when Abraham, peace be upon him, was told by his father, who was a disbeliever: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you. And leave me for a long time.﴾ He said: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [19:46]. [[See p. 111 of this part.]] How much more so regarding a father who is a prophet, whom his Lord chose, accepted the repentance of, and guided.

**The fourth issue:** As for one who commits sins and has not been granted forgiveness, the scholars unanimously agree that it is not permissible for him to argue with an argument like Adam's, saying: "Do you blame me for having killed, or committed adultery, or stolen, when Allah has decreed that upon me?" The community is unanimous on the permissibility of praising the good-doer for his goodness, blaming the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing, and enumerating his sins against him.

**The fifth issue:** Allah's words ﴿so he went astray﴾ [20:121] mean that his life was corrupted. This was related by al-Naqqash and preferred by al-Qushayri. I heard our shaykh, the reciter Abu Ja'far al-Qurtubi, say: ﴿so he went astray﴾ [20:121] means his life was corrupted by his descent to this world. Al-ghayy (going astray) means corruption. This is a good interpretation, and it is better than the interpretation of one who says ﴿so he went astray﴾ [20:121] means he erred, from al-ghayy, which is the opposite of rushd (right guidance). It was also said: it means he was ignorant of the place of his right guidance, that is, he was ignorant that this tree was the one he had been forbidden, and al-ghayy means ignorance. It is also reported from some of them that ﴿so he went astray﴾ [20:121] means he was choked from eating too much. Al-Zamakhshari said: Even if this is valid according to the dialect of those who turn a preceding kasra-ed yā' into an alif, saying "fanā" and "baqā" for "fanīya" and "baqiya," and they are the Banu Tayy, it is a corrupt interpretation.

**The sixth issue:** Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: Some people said: it is said that Adam disobeyed and went astray, but he is not called "ʿāṣin" (a disobedient one) or "ghāwin" (a misguided one), just as one who sews once is called "khāṭ" (a sewer) but is not called "khayyāṭ" (a tailor) unless the sewing is repeated from him. It was also said: a master may use toward his slave, when he disobeys, expressions that it is not permissible for others to use. This is an overreach. Whatever of this is attributed to the prophets, it is either minor sins, the abandonment of what is better, or before prophethood. I say: This is good. Imam Abu Bakr ibn Furak, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said: This occurred from Adam before prophethood. The evidence for this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him﴾ [20:122]. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verses 120–122:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ [20:120]. This was discussed in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 177.]].

(He said), meaning Satan: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [20:120]. This indicates direct speech, and that he entered Paradise inside the serpent, as explained earlier in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 308 onward.]]. The tree was identified there, along with what the scholars said about it, so there is no point in repeating it.

﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden﴾ [20:121]. This was discussed fully in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 180.]]. Al-Farra' said: "Taffaqa" in Arabic means "aqbala" (they began). He said: it was also said that they began to stick leaves of the fig tree onto themselves.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ [20:121]. There are six issues in this.

**The first issue:** Allah's words ﴿disobeyed﴾ [20:121] were discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 305.]] in the discussion on the sins of the prophets. One of our later scholars said: What should be said is that Allah has informed us that some of them committed sins, attributed them to them, rebuked them for them, and they themselves informed of this about their own souls, disowned them, sought forgiveness for them and repented. All of this occurs in many places and, taken as a whole, does not admit of interpretation, even if individual instances may admit of it. None of this diminishes their ranks. Those matters that occurred from them were rare, done in error or forgetfulness, or due to an interpretation that prompted them. Relative to others, they are good deeds, but for them they are sins, relative to their ranks and the loftiness of their standing. A minister may be held accountable for what a governor is rewarded for. Therefore, they feared this on the Day of Resurrection, while knowing their security, safety and well-being. He said: This is the truth. Al-Junayd spoke well when he said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." May the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them. Although the texts have testified that some sins occurred from them, this did not harm their ranks nor diminish their station. Rather, He made amends for them, chose them, guided them, praised them, purified them, selected them and chose them, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

**The second issue:** The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: It is not permissible for any of us today to report this about Adam, except when we mention it within the context of Allah's words about him, or the words of His Prophet. As for initiating this on one's own account, it is not permissible for us regarding our nearer fathers, those like us, so how much more regarding our father, the most ancient, greatest, most noble, foremost prophet, whom Allah the Exalted excused, accepted repentance from, and forgave. I say: If this is impermissible regarding a created being, then reporting the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as the hand, the foot, the finger, the side, and descent, and others, is even more deserving of prohibition. It is not permissible to begin with any of those, except within the recitation of His Book or the sunnah of His Messenger. For this reason, Imam Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever describes any aspect of the Essence of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as His words: ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained"﴾ [5:64], and gestures with his hand to his neck, his hand should be cut off. The same applies to hearing and sight, which should be cut off from him, because he has likened Allah the Exalted to himself.

**The third issue:** The imams narrated, and the wording is from al-Bukhari [[In the originals: the wording is from al-Bukhari. The correction is from Sahih Muslim.]], from Abu Hurairah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Adam and Musa debated. Musa said: 'O Adam, you are our father. You disappointed us and expelled us from the Garden.' Adam said to him: 'O Musa, Allah the Mighty and Majestic chose you with His speech and wrote for you with His hand. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 20, verses 123–127:**

Allah's words: ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you"﴾ [20:123]. This is addressed to Adam and Iblis. "From it" means from the Garden. He had said to Iblis, ﴿Get out of it, disgraced and expelled﴾ [7:18]. So perhaps he was removed from the Garden to a place in the sky, and then sent down to the earth.

﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾. This was discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 319 onward.]]. That is, you (Adam) are an enemy to the serpent and to Iblis, and those two are enemies to you. This shows that His words ﴿Go down﴾ [20:123] are not addressed to Adam and Hawwa' (Eve), because the two of them were not enemies to each other. The descent of Adam includes the descent of Hawwa'.

﴿Whenever there comes to you guidance from Me﴾, that is, right guidance and true speech. This was discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 328 onward.]].

﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾, meaning the Messengers and the Books.

﴿He will neither go astray nor be unhappy﴾ [20:123]. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah guarantees that whoever recites the Qur'an and acts by what is in it will not go astray in this world, nor be unhappy in the Hereafter. Then he recited the verse. And it is also reported from him: Whoever recites the Qur'an and follows what is in it, Allah will guide him out of error and protect him on the Day of Resurrection from the evil of the reckoning. Then he recited the verse.

﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾ [20:124].

That is, from My religion, from reciting My Book, and from acting by what is in it. It is also said: from the proofs I have sent down. It is possible that "remembrance" here refers to the Messenger, since he was the one who brought the remembrance.

﴿Indeed, he will have a constricted life﴾ [20:124]. That is, a narrow life. It is said: "a dank dwelling" and "a dank life" (ḍank), which is used for the singular, dual, masculine, feminine and plural alike. 'Antarah said:

"If they overtake me, I will charge back; if they seek to be gentle, I will press on; and if they find me in a narrow dwelling, I will descend into it."

He also said:

"Were death to take a form, it would take my form, when they descend into a narrow dwelling."

It was also read as "ḍankā" on the pattern of fa'lā. The meaning is that Allah, glorified and exalted, has joined with the religion submission, contentment, and reliance upon Him and upon His allotment. So its follower spends from what Allah has provided him with generosity and ease, and lives a spacious life (rāfigh), as Allah says: ﴿We shall surely give him a good life﴾ [16:97]. As for one who turns away from the religion, greed dominates him, always driving him to seek more of the world, and stinginess is imposed on him, holding back his hand from spending. So his life is constricted and his condition is dark. As one of them said: No one turns away from the remembrance of his Lord without his time becoming dark for him, his provision becoming disordered, and his life becoming constricted.

'Ikrimah said: ﴿constricted﴾ [20:124] means unlawful earnings. Al-Hasan said: it means the food of ḍarī' (a thorny plant) and zaqqūm (the tree of Hell). A fourth view, which is the correct one, is that it is the punishment of the grave. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hurayrah narrated it as marfū' (traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)). We have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah. Abu Hurayrah said: The grave of the disbeliever is constricted until his ribs interlock, and this is the constricted life.

﴿And We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [20:124]. It is said: blind in one state and seeing in another. This was discussed at the end of (Subhan) [[See vol. 10, p. 333.]] [17:1]. It is also said: blind to the proof, as Mujahid said. It is said: blind to the paths of good, unable to be guided to any of them. It is also said: blind to any device for averting punishment from himself, like a blind man who has no way of dealing with what he cannot see.

﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was seeing?"﴾ [20:125]. That is, for what sin did You punish me with blindness?

﴿And I was seeing﴾ [20:125], that is, in the world. It seems he thought he had no sin. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: that is, "Why have You raised me blind" to my proof, "and I was seeing," that is, knowing of my proof. Al-Qushayri said: this is far-fetched, since the disbeliever had no proof in this world.

﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them"﴾ [20:126]. That is, Allah, exalted is He, says to him: ﴿Thus Our signs came to you﴾ [20:126], that is, Our indications of Our oneness and Our power.

﴿But you forgot them﴾ [20:126], that is, you abandoned them, did not reflect on them, and turned away from them.

﴿And thus today you are forgotten﴾ [20:126], that is, you are left in punishment, meaning Hell.

﴿And thus We recompense the one who transgresses﴾ [20:127], that is, just as We recompensed the one who turned away from the Qur'an, and from reflecting on created things and contemplating them, and exceeded the limit in disobedience.

﴿And did not believe in the signs of his Lord﴾ [20:127], that is, did not affirm them.

﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe﴾ [20:127], that is, more terrible than the constricted life and the punishment of the grave.

﴿And more lasting﴾, that is, more enduring and more permanent, because it does not end and does not come to an conclusion.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 128–130:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has it not become clear to them﴾ (20:128). He means the people of Makkah, i.e., has it not become clear to them the news of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, who walk in their dwellings when they travel and go out for trade, seeking livelihood, so they see the lands of the past nations and the bygone generations in ruins? That is, do they not fear that there may befall them the like of what befell the disbelievers before them?

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sulami and others recited "نَهْدِ لَهُمْ" (nahdi lahum) with the nun, and this is clearer. As for "يَهْدِ" (yahdi) with the ya', it is problematic because of the subject (al-fa'il). The Kufans said: the subject is "كَمْ" (kam). Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because "كَمِ" (kami) is an interrogative, so what precedes it does not govern it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Or has the matter not become clear to them by Our destroying those whom We destroyed?" The literal sense of "يَهْدِ" is "to guide," so the subject is "al-huda" (the guidance), its estimate being: "Has not guidance become clear to them?" Al-Zajjaj said: "كَمْ" is in a position of accusative governed by "أَهْلَكْنا" (ahlakna, "We destroyed").

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable﴾ (20:129). In it there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir); that is: "And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord and an appointed term, it would have been inevitable." This was said by Qatadah. "Al-lizam" is constant adherence, i.e., the punishment would have been necessarily attached to them. The noun of "kana" is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: "wa ajalun musamma" (and an appointed term) is conjoined to "kalimah" (word). Qatadah said: the intended meaning is the Resurrection. This was also said by al-Qutabi. It was said: their delay is until the day of Badr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ (20:130). He commanded him, exalted is He, to be patient over their statements: "He is a sorcerer," "He is a soothsayer," "He is a liar," and other such things. The meaning is: do not concern yourself with them, for their punishment has a fixed time that neither advances nor delays. Then it was said: this is abrogated by the verse of fighting (al-qital). It was also said: it is not abrogated, since the disbelievers were not completely uprooted after the verse of fighting, but most of them remained.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun﴾ [20:130]. Most of the commentators said: this refers to the five prayers. "Before the rising of the sun" (qabla tulu' al-shams) [20:130] is the Fajr prayer; "and before its setting" (wa qabla ghurubiha) [20:130] is the 'Asr prayer; "and during the hours of the night" (wa min ana'i al-layl) [20:130] is the 'Isha' (al-'atamah); "and the extremes of the day" (wa atraf al-nahar) [20:130] is the Maghrib and the Zuhr, because Zuhr is at the end of the first extremity of the day and the beginning of the last extremity, so it lies at both ends of it, and the third extremity is the setting of the sun, which is the time of Maghrib. It was also said: the day divides into two parts, separated by the zawal (decline of the sun), and each part has two extremities; at the zawal there are two extremities, the last of the first part and the first of the last part, so he spoke of the two extremities as "atraf" (extremities) in the manner of ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ (al-Tahrim: 4). Ibn Fawrak indicated this line of reasoning in al-Mushkil. It was also said: "al-nahar" (the day) is a generic noun, so each day has an extremity, and the plural form refers to the repetition in every day. "Ana'i al-layl" means its hours; the singular of "al-anaa'" is "inj," "ina," and "ana." A group said: the intended meaning of the verse is the voluntary prayer (salat al-tatawwu'), as said by al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be pleased﴾ [20:130], with a fatha on the ta' (la'allaka tarda), i.e., that you may be rewarded for these deeds with that with which you are pleased. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited "turda" with a damma on the ta' (tur·da), i.e., that you may be given what pleases you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 20, verse 128–130:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has it not become clear to them﴾ (20:128). He means the people of Makkah, i.e., has it not become clear to them the news of those whom We destroyed before them of the generations, who walk in their dwellings when they travel and go out for trade, seeking livelihood, so they see the lands of the past nations and the bygone generations in ruins? That is, do they not fear that there may befall them the like of what befell the disbelievers before them?

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sulami and others recited "نَهْدِ لَهُمْ" (nahdi lahum) with the nun, and this is clearer. As for "يَهْدِ" (yahdi) with the ya', it is problematic because of the subject (al-fa'il). The Kufans said: the subject is "كَمْ" (kam). Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because "كَمِ" (kami) is an interrogative, so what precedes it does not govern it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Or has the matter not become clear to them by Our destroying those whom We destroyed?" The literal sense of "يَهْدِ" is "to guide," so the subject is "al-huda" (the guidance), its estimate being: "Has not guidance become clear to them?" Al-Zajjaj said: "كَمْ" is in a position of accusative governed by "أَهْلَكْنا" (ahlakna, "We destroyed").

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable﴾ (20:129). In it there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir); that is: "And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord and an appointed term, it would have been inevitable." This was said by Qatadah. "Al-lizam" is constant adherence, i.e., the punishment would have been necessarily attached to them. The noun of "kana" is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: "wa ajalun musamma" (and an appointed term) is conjoined to "kalimah" (word). Qatadah said: the intended meaning is the Resurrection. This was also said by al-Qutabi. It was said: their delay is until the day of Badr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ (20:130). He commanded him, exalted is He, to be patient over their statements: "He is a sorcerer," "He is a soothsayer," "He is a liar," and other such things. The meaning is: do not concern yourself with them, for their punishment has a fixed time that neither advances nor delays. Then it was said: this is abrogated by the verse of fighting (al-qital). It was also said: it is not abrogated, since the disbelievers were not completely uprooted after the verse of fighting, but most of them remained.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun﴾ [20:130]. Most of the commentators said: this refers to the five prayers. "Before the rising of the sun" (qabla tulu' al-shams) [20:130] is the Fajr prayer; "and before its setting" (wa qabla ghurubiha) [20:130] is the 'Asr prayer; "and during the hours of the night" (wa min ana'i al-layl) [20:130] is the 'Isha' (al-'atamah); "and the extremes of the day" (wa atraf al-nahar) [20:130] is the Maghrib and the Zuhr, because Zuhr is at the end of the first extremity of the day and the beginning of the last extremity, so it lies at both ends of it, and the third extremity is the setting of the sun, which is the time of Maghrib. It was also said: the day divides into two parts, separated by the zawal (decline of the sun), and each part has two extremities; at the zawal there are two extremities, the last of the first part and the first of the last part, so he spoke of the two extremities as "atraf" (extremities) in the manner of ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ (al-Tahrim: 4). Ibn Fawrak indicated this line of reasoning in al-Mushkil. It was also said: "al-nahar" (the day) is a generic noun, so each day has an extremity, and the plural form refers to the repetition in every day. "Ana'i al-layl" means its hours; the singular of "al-anaa'" is "inj," "ina," and "ana." A group said: the intended meaning of the verse is the voluntary prayer (salat al-tatawwu'), as said by al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be pleased﴾ [20:130], with a fatha on the ta' (la'allaka tarda), i.e., that you may be rewarded for these deeds with that with which you are pleased. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited "turda" with a damma on the ta' (tur·da), i.e., that you may be given what pleases you.

**Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to, as pairs of them, the splendor of the life of this world, that We may test them therein.﴾ (20:131)** The meaning of this has already been discussed in (Surat) al-Hijr [[See vol. 10, p. 56 onward.]]. *Azwājan* (pairs) is the object of *matta'nā* (We have given enjoyment). *Zahrata* (splendor) is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the object). Al-Zajjaj said: *zahrata* is in the accusative by virtue of the meaning of *matta'nā*, because its meaning is "We made the life of this world a splendor for them," or by a hidden verb, which is *ja'alnā* (We made), meaning "We made for them the splendor of the life of this world." This is also from al-Zajjaj. It has also been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the *hā'* in *bihi* (with it), according to the position (*ʿalā al-mawḍiʿ*), as you say: "I passed by him, your brother." Al-Farra' indicated that it is in the accusative as a *ḥāl*, and its governing word is *matta'nā*. He said: as you say, "I passed by him, the poor man." And its implied meaning is: "We have given them enjoyment by it, a splendor in the life of this world and an adornment in it." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun), like *ṣun'a Allāh* (the work of Allah) and *wa'da Allāh* (the promise of Allah), but this is open to question. The better view is that it is in the accusative as a *ḥāl*, and the tanwin is dropped because it is unvoweled, and the lām of *al-ḥayāh* is unvoweled, as is read: ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ (36:40), with *al-nahāra* in the accusative governed by *sābiq*, on the assumption that the tanwin is dropped because of its being unvoweled and the lām being unvoweled. And *al-ḥayāh* is in the genitive as a *badal* of *mā* in His words *ilā mā matta'nā bihi* (to what We have given enjoyment to). The meaning is then: "And do not extend your eyes toward the life of this world in its splendor," that is, in the state of its splendor. It is not good for *zahratun* to be a *badal* of *mā* according to the position in His words *ilā mā matta'nā*, because *li-naftinahum* (that We may test them) is connected to *matta'nā*, and *zahrata al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* means its adornment by vegetation. *Al-zahrah*, with a fatḥah on the *zāy* and the *hā'*, is the blossom of plants. *Al-zuhrah*, with a ḍammah on the *zāy* and a fatḥah on the *hā'*, is the star (Venus). *Banū Zuhrah* is with a sukūn on the *hā'*, as Ibn ʿUzayz said. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read *zahara* with a fatḥah on the *hā'*, like *nahr* and *nahar*. It is said: *sirāj zāhir*, meaning it has a sheen. And *zahr al-ashjār* (the blossoms of trees) is what pleases the eye of their colors. In a hadith: The Prophet (ﷺ) was *azhar al-lawn*, meaning of bright complexion. It is said of everything that shines: *zāhir*, and it is the finest of colors.

**﴿That We may test them therein﴾** means: that We may try them. It has been said: that We may make that a trial and misguidance for them. The meaning of the verse is: O Muhammad, do not give any weight to the splendor of this world, for it has no permanence.

**"Do not extend"** (*wa-lā tamuddanna*) is more emphatic than "do not look" (*lā tanẓuranna*), because one who extends his gaze is driven to that by a persistent greed, whereas one who merely looks may not have that with him.

**Question:** Some people said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is what Abu Rafi', the freedman of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), narrated. He said: A guest came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he (ﷺ) sent me to a Jewish man and said: "Say to him: Muhammad says to you, a guest has come to us and some of what he needs has not been found with us, so sell me such-and-such flour, or lend it to me until the new moon of Rajab." He said: "No, not unless there is a pledge." So I returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "By Allah, I am trustworthy in heaven and trustworthy on earth. Had he lent it to me or sold it to me, I would have paid it back to him. Go with my coat of mail to him." And the verse was revealed as a consolation to him regarding the world.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This cannot be the occasion of revelation, because the surah is Makkan and the story mentioned is Madinan, from the last part of the Prophet's life (ﷺ), since he died while his coat of mail was pledged with a Jew in this very story that was mentioned. Rather, the apparent view is that the verse is coherent with what precedes it. Allah the Exalted rebuked them for not taking heed from the earlier nations, then threatened them with a deferred punishment, then commanded His Prophet to regard their affairs as insignificant, to be patient with their words, to turn away from their wealth and what is in their hands of the world, since that is cut off from them and is heading toward disgrace.

I say: Likewise is what is reported of him (ﷺ), that he passed by the camels of the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, whose urine and dung had dried on their thighs (*ʿabasat fī abwālihā*) [[ʿAbasat fī abwālihā means that their urine and dung dried on their thighs, and that happens only because of fat.]] [and their dung [[The addition is from al-Nihāyah by Ibn al-Athīr.]]] from fatness, so he covered himself with his garment and went on, in accordance with the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to, as pairs of them﴾ (20:131), and the rest of the verse. Then He consoled him, saying: ﴿But the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring﴾ (20:131), meaning: the reward of Allah for patience and for indifference to the world is more excellent, because it endures while the world perishes. It has also been said: by this provision is meant what Allah opens to the believers of lands and spoils of war.

**Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer, and be steadfast in it﴾ (20:132).** He commanded him to command his family to pray, to perform it along with them, to be steadfast upon it and to persevere in it. This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and his entire community is included in its general meaning, while his household is included in particular. After the revelation of this verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to go every morning to the house of Fatimah and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, and say: "The prayer! The prayer!" It is also narrated that ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him), whenever he saw something of the news of rulers and their conditions, would hurry to his home and enter it, reciting: ﴿And do not extend your eyes…﴾ (20:131) up to His words: ﴿…and more enduring﴾ (20:131). Then he would call out to prayer: "Prayer, may Allah have mercy on you!" and he would pray. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) used to wake the people of his house for the night prayer and pray while reciting the verse as an example.

So whenever hardship befell his household, he (ﷺ) would command them to pray. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me. I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed, Allah is the Provider﴾ (51:56–58) [[See vol. 17, p. 55.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verses 133–135:

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?") 20:133. This refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, meaning: "Why does Muhammad not bring us a sign that necessitates necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri)?" Or "a clear sign, like the she-camel and the staff." Or "Why does he not bring us the signs that we propose, just as the prophets before him brought them?"

Allah said: (Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?) 20:133. This refers to the Torah, the Gospel and the earlier books, and this is the greatest sign, since it informs of what is in them. "Al-suhuf" is also read with a single letter (al-suhuf, unstressed). It was also said: "Has there not come to them the sign that indicates his prophethood, through what they found in the earlier books of good tidings?" It was also said: "Has there not come to them Our destruction of the nations who disbelieved and proposed signs? So what assures them that if the signs come to them, their condition will not be the condition of those people?"

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Hafs read: "Awa-lam ta'tihim" with the (feminine) ta', because "al-bayyina" is feminine. The rest read it with the ya', because the verb comes first, and because "al-bayyina" is "al-bayan" and "al-burhan," so they took it according to the meaning. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Al-Kisa'i related "Awa-lam ta'tihim bayyinatu ma fi al-suhuf al-ula" and said: "It is also permissible in this case to read 'bayyinatu ma fi al-suhuf al-ula'." Al-Nahhas said: "If you put tanwin on 'bayyina' and read it in the nominative, you make 'ma' a substitute for it. If you read it in the accusative, it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), and the meaning is: 'Has there not come to them what is in the former scriptures, clarified?'"

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before this) 20:134, that is, before the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the revelation of the Qur'an, (they would have said) that is, on the Day of Resurrection, (Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?) 20:134, that is, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?"

(So we would have followed Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced.) 20:134. It is also read "nadhilla wa nakhza" in the passive voice (the verbs being in the passive form). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the one who dies in the interval (between prophets), the insane and the infant: "The one who dies in the interval will say: 'No book and no messenger came to me.'" Then he recited: "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before this, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?'" (to the end of the verse). "The insane will say: 'My Lord, You did not give me intellect by which I could discern good and evil.' The infant will say: 'My Lord, I did not reach action.' Then a fire will be raised for them, and He will say to them: 'Approach it and enter it.' He said: 'Whoever was among those whom Allah knew to be fortunate, had he reached action, will approach it or enter it, and whoever was among those whom Allah knew to be wretched, had he reached action, will hold back from it.'" [Note: from B, J, Z, T, K, Y.] "Then Allah, blessed and exalted, will say: 'It was I whom you disobeyed, so how would it have been had My messengers come to you?'" It is also related as a statement of Abu Sa'id (mawquf), and there is something to be examined in it, which we have clarified in the book "al-Tadhkira." With this, those who say that children and others will be tested in the Hereafter argued.

"Fa-nattabi'a" (so we would follow) 20:134 is in the subjunctive, after an answer of restriction (jawab al-takhsis). "Ayatika" (Your signs) means what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. "Min qabli an nadhilla" (before we are humiliated) 20:134, that is, "in punishment." "Wa nakhza" (and disgraced) 20:134, that is, "in Hell," as Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said: "Min qabli an nadhilla" (before we are humiliated) 20:134 means "in this world through punishment," and "wa nakhza" (and disgraced) 20:134 means "in the Hereafter through its punishment."

(Say, "Each is waiting.") 20:135, that is, say to them, O Muhammad, "Each is waiting," meaning all the believers and disbelievers are awaiting the turns of time and to whom victory will belong.

(So wait; you will know who are the companions of the even path and who has been guided.) 20:135. This refers to the straight religion and guidance. The meaning is: "You will know by victory who has been guided to the religion of truth." It was also said: "You will know on the Day of Resurrection who has been guided to the path of Paradise." In this there is a kind of warning, intimidation and threat with which the surah is concluded. It is also read "fa-sawfa ta'lamun" (so you will surely know). Abu Rafi' said: "I memorized it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," as al-Zamakhshari mentioned. "Man" (who) is in the nominative position according to al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: "It is permissible for it to be in the accusative position, like: 'And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer'" [see vol. 3, p. 66]. Abu Ishaq said: "This is an error, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it, and 'man' here is an interrogative in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and the meaning is: 'You will know the companions of the even path: are we or are you?'" Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Farra' holds that the meaning of 'man ashab al-sirat al-sawi' (who are the companions of the even path) is 'who has not gone astray,' and that the meaning of 'wa man ihtada' (and who has been guided) is 'who went astray and then was guided.'"

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and 'Asim al-Jahdari read "fa-sa-ya'lamuna min ashab al-sirat al-sawa" with a shadda on the waw, followed by the feminine alif, in the pattern fu'la without a hamza. The feminine gender of "al-sirat" is rare and anomalous. Allah the Exalted said: (Guide us to the straight path) (al-Fatiha 1:6), where it came masculine in this and in other places. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on surah 20, verses 133–135:

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?") 20:133. This refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, meaning: "Why does Muhammad not bring us a sign that necessitates necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri)?" Or "a clear sign, like the she-camel and the staff." Or "Why does he not bring us the signs that we propose, just as the prophets before him brought them?"

Allah said: (Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?) 20:133. This refers to the Torah, the Gospel and the earlier books, and this is the greatest sign, since it informs of what is in them. "Al-suhuf" is also read with a single letter (al-suhuf, unstressed). It was also said: "Has there not come to them the sign that indicates his prophethood, through what they found in the earlier books of good tidings?" It was also said: "Has there not come to them Our destruction of the nations who disbelieved and proposed signs? So what assures them that if the signs come to them, their condition will not be the condition of those people?"

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Hafs read: "Awa-lam ta'tihim" with the (feminine) ta', because "al-bayyina" is feminine. The rest read it with the ya', because the verb comes first, and because "al-bayyina" is "al-bayan" and "al-burhan," so they took it according to the meaning. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Al-Kisa'i related "Awa-lam ta'tihim bayyinatu ma fi al-suhuf al-ula" and said: "It is also permissible in this case to read 'bayyinatu ma fi al-suhuf al-ula'." Al-Nahhas said: "If you put tanwin on 'bayyina' and read it in the nominative, you make 'ma' a substitute for it. If you read it in the accusative, it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), and the meaning is: 'Has there not come to them what is in the former scriptures, clarified?'"

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before this) 20:134, that is, before the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the revelation of the Qur'an, (they would have said) that is, on the Day of Resurrection, (Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?) 20:134, that is, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?"

(So we would have followed Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced.) 20:134. It is also read "nadhilla wa nakhza" in the passive voice (the verbs being in the passive form). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning the one who dies in the interval (between prophets), the insane and the infant: "The one who dies in the interval will say: 'No book and no messenger came to me.'" Then he recited: "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before this, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?'" (to the end of the verse). "The insane will say: 'My Lord, You did not give me intellect by which I could discern good and evil.' The infant will say: 'My Lord, I did not reach action.' Then a fire will be raised for them, and He will say to them: 'Approach it and enter it.' He said: 'Whoever was among those whom Allah knew to be fortunate, had he reached action, will approach it or enter it, and whoever was among those whom Allah knew to be wretched, had he reached action, will hold back from it.'" [Note: from B, J, Z, T, K, Y.] "Then Allah, blessed and exalted, will say: 'It was I whom you disobeyed, so how would it have been had My messengers come to you?'" It is also related as a statement of Abu Sa'id (mawquf), and there is something to be examined in it, which we have clarified in the book "al-Tadhkira." With this, those who say that children and others will be tested in the Hereafter argued.

"Min qabli an nadhilla" (before we are humiliated) 20:134, that is, "in punishment." "Wa nakhza" (and disgraced) 20:134, that is, "in Hell," as Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said: "Min qabli an nadhilla" (before we are humiliated) 20:134 means "in this world through punishment," and "wa nakhza" (and disgraced) 20:134 means "in the Hereafter through its punishment."

(Say, "Each is waiting.") 20:135, that is, say to them, O Muhammad, "Each is waiting," meaning all the believers and disbelievers are awaiting the turns of time and to whom victory will belong.

(So wait; you will know who are the companions of the even path and who has been guided.) 20:135. This refers to the straight religion and guidance. The meaning is: "You will know by victory who has been guided to the religion of truth." It was also said: "You will know on the Day of Resurrection who has been guided to the path of Paradise." In this there is a kind of warning, intimidation and threat with which the surah is concluded. It is also read "fa-sawfa ta'lamun" (so you will surely know). Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Farra' holds that the meaning of 'man ashab al-sirat al-sawi' (who are the companions of the even path) is 'who has not gone astray,' and that the meaning of 'wa man ihtada' (and who has been guided) is 'who went astray and then was guided.'"
